- triangle $OAP$, with base $OA = 1$ and height $\sin t$: area $\tfrac12\sin t$;
- the sector $OAP$ of the unit circle with angle $t$: area $\tfrac12 r^2 t = \tfrac12 t$ (Module 1);
- triangle $OAT$, with legs $1$ and $\tan t$: area $\tfrac12\tan t$.

The triangle $OAP$ lies inside the sector, which lies inside triangle $OAT$, and each region is
strictly bigger than the one before. So $\tfrac12\sin t < \tfrac12 t < \tfrac12\tan t$, and doubling gives the
claim.

```plot
{"x": [-0.2, 1.4], "y": [-0.2, 1.1], "equal": true, "curves": [{"x": "cos(t)", "y": "sin(t)", "t": [0, 1.5708]}], "polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [1, 0], [0.7648, 0.6442]]}, {"points": [[0, 0], [1, 0], [1, 0.8423]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0.7648, 0.6442], "to": [0.7648, 0], "dashed": true}], "points": [[0, 0], {"at": [1, 0], "label": "A"}, [0.7648, 0.6442], {"at": [1, 0.8423], "label": "T"}], "labels": [{"at": [-0.08, 0.07], "text": "O"}, {"at": [0.72, 0.76], "text": "P"}, {"at": [0.64, 0.3], "text": "sin t"}], "caption": "t = 0.7: triangle OAP (area ½ sin t) sits inside the sector OAP (area ½ t), which sits inside triangle OAT (area ½ tan t)"}
```

The same order holds for the lengths themselves: the height $\sin t$ is shorter than the arc $t$ that
reaches the same height, and the arc is shorter than the tangent segment $AT = \tan t$. The area
argument is the one that is easy to make airtight, which is why textbooks use it.

## Squeezing the ratio sin t / t

Divide all three parts of $\sin t < t < \tan t$ by $\sin t$ (positive for $0 < t < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$):
$$1 < \frac{t}{\sin t} < \frac{1}{\cos t}.$$
Taking reciprocals reverses the inequalities:
$$\cos t < \frac{\sin t}{t} < 1.$$

As $t$ shrinks toward 0, the point $(\cos t, \sin t)$ slides toward $(1, 0)$, so $\cos t$ gets as close
to 1 as you like. The ratio $\tfrac{\sin t}{t}$ is trapped between $\cos t$ and 1, so it is forced toward
1 as well. The general principle, that a quantity trapped between two others that approach the same
number must approach that number too, is the **[[squeeze theorem]]**. In calculus notation:
$$\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin t}{t} = 1.$$

| $t$ | $0.5$ | $0.2$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.01$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\cos t$ | $0.8776$ | $0.9801$ | $0.9950$ | $0.9988$ | $0.99995$ |
| $\tfrac{\sin t}{t}$ | $0.9589$ | $0.9933$ | $0.9983$ | $0.9996$ | $0.99998$ |

Negative $t$ give the same values: $\sin t$ and $t$ are both odd, so
$\tfrac{\sin(-t)}{-t} = \tfrac{-\sin t}{-t} = \tfrac{\sin t}{t}$. The ratio is an even function.

**Radians are essential.** The proof used the sector area $\tfrac12 t$, which is true only when $t$ is
in radians. In degrees, $\sin x^\circ = \sin\tfrac{\pi x}{180}$, so $\tfrac{\sin x^\circ}{x}$ approaches
$\tfrac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745$, not 1. On a graph, the fact $\tfrac{\sin t}{t} \to 1$ says that the curve
$y = \sin t$ leaves the origin with slope exactly 1, hugging the line $y = t$. That clean slope is the
main reason calculus measures angles in radians.

```plot
{"x": [-1.5, 1.5], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "equal": true, "functions": [{"f": "sin(x)"}, {"f": "x", "label": "y = t", "dashed": true}, {"f": "tan(x)", "label": "y = tan t", "from": -1.0, "to": 1.0}], "labels": [{"at": [1.15, 0.6], "text": "y = sin t"}], "caption": "Near 0 the graphs of sin t, t and tan t are almost indistinguishable; farther out sin t falls below the line and tan t rises above it"}
```

## Approximations and how good they are

For small $|t|$ (in radians) the inequality and the squeeze give
$$\sin t \approx t, \qquad \tan t \approx t.$$
Replacing a curve near a point by a straight line like this is a **[[linear approximation]]**.
Cosine needs one more term, because $\cos t \approx 1$ throws away all the information. The chord from
$A$ to $P$ gives it: its length squared is $(1 - \cos t)^2 + \sin^2 t = 2 - 2\cos t$, and the chord of
angle $t$ is $2\sin\tfrac{t}{2}$ (the half-chord is a sine). So
$$1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2\tfrac{t}{2} \approx 2\left(\tfrac{t}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{t^2}{2}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad \cos t \approx 1 - \frac{t^2}{2}.$$
Because $\left|\sin\tfrac{t}{2}\right| < \left|\tfrac{t}{2}\right|$ for $t \ne 0$, this estimate is always a little too low: $\cos t > 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$ for $t \ne 0$.

To judge an approximation, use its **[[relative error]]**: the size of the error divided by the size of
the true value, $\dfrac{|\text{approximation} - \text{true value}|}{|\text{true value}|}$, often written as a percent.

| $t$ (radians) | $\sin t$ | error of $\sin t \approx t$ | $\tan t$ | error of $\tan t \approx t$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $0.5$ | $0.4794$ | $4.29\%$ | $0.5463$ | $8.48\%$ |
| $0.2$ | $0.1987$ | $0.67\%$ | $0.2027$ | $1.34\%$ |
| $0.1$ | $0.0998$ | $0.17\%$ | $0.1003$ | $0.33\%$ |
| $0.05$ | $0.04998$ | $0.04\%$ | $0.05004$ | $0.08\%$ |

The errors shrink fast: halving $t$ cuts them to about a quarter. Calculus explains the pattern (and
we state it here without proof): the error of $\sin t \approx t$ is about $\tfrac{t^3}{6}$, of $\tan t \approx t$
about $\tfrac{t^3}{3}$, and of $\cos t \approx 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$ about $\tfrac{t^4}{24}$. Dividing by $t$, the relative
errors are about $\tfrac{t^2}{6}$ and $\tfrac{t^2}{3}$. Solving numerically, $\sin t \approx t$ is within 1% for
$|t| < 0.244$ (about $14^\circ$), and $\tan t \approx t$ for $|t| < 0.173$ (about $9.9^\circ$).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Deciding whether to use a small-angle approximation
  accDescr: Start with an angle. If it is in degrees, first convert it to radians by multiplying by pi over 180. Then ask whether its size is below about 0.17 radians, roughly 10 degrees, for 1 percent accuracy. If yes, use sine of t approximately t, tangent of t approximately t, and cosine of t approximately 1 minus t squared over 2. If no, compute the value exactly or with a calculator instead.
  A["Angle"] --> B{"In degrees?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Convert: t = angle × π/180"]
  B -- no --> D{"Is |t| below about 0.17 (about 10°)?"}
  C --> D
  D -- yes --> E["sin t ≈ t, tan t ≈ t, cos t ≈ 1 − t²/2 (all within 1%)"]
  D -- no --> F["Use exact values or a calculator"]
```

### Example 1

Check the inequality and the areas at $t = 0.5$.

$\sin 0.5 \approx 0.4794$ and $\tan 0.5 \approx 0.5463$, so $0.4794 < 0.5 < 0.5463$. The three areas are
$\tfrac12(0.4794) \approx 0.2397$, $\tfrac12(0.5) = 0.25$ and $\tfrac12(0.5463) \approx 0.2732$, nested as claimed. The
squeeze: $\cos 0.5 \approx 0.8776 < \tfrac{0.4794}{0.5} \approx 0.9589 < 1$.

### Example 2

Estimate $\sin 0.05$, $\tan 0.05$ and $\cos 0.05$ without a calculator, then compare.

$\sin 0.05 \approx 0.05$, $\tan 0.05 \approx 0.05$ and $\cos 0.05 \approx 1 - \tfrac{0.0025}{2} = 0.99875$. The true values are
$0.049979$, $0.050042$ and $0.998750$ (to six decimals). The first two are off by about $0.00002$ and
$0.00004$; the cosine estimate matches to six decimals, since its error is about $\tfrac{0.05^4}{24} \approx 3\times10^{-7}$.

### Example 3

Estimate $\sin 2^\circ$ and $\cos 2^\circ$.

**Step 1: convert.** $t = 2\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{180} = \tfrac{\pi}{90} \approx 0.034907$. (Using 2 itself would claim $\sin 2^\circ \approx 2$,
which is impossible.)

**Step 2: approximate.** $\sin 2^\circ \approx 0.034907$; the true value is $0.034899$ (to six decimals). And
$\cos 2^\circ \approx 1 - \tfrac{0.034907^2}{2} \approx 0.999391$, matching the true value $0.999391$ to six decimals.

### Example 4

Is $\tan t \approx t$ good to 1% at $10^\circ$? Is $\sin t \approx t$?

$t = \tfrac{10\pi}{180} \approx 0.174533$. $\tan 10^\circ \approx 0.176327$, so the relative error is
$\tfrac{0.176327 - 0.174533}{0.176327} \approx 1.02\%$: just over 1%. $\sin 10^\circ \approx 0.173648$, error
$\tfrac{0.174533 - 0.173648}{0.173648} \approx 0.51\%$: comfortably within 1%. The rule of thumb $\tfrac{t^2}{3} \approx 1.02\%$
and $\tfrac{t^2}{6} \approx 0.51\%$ predicts both.

### Example 5

Find $\tfrac{\sin(-0.2)}{-0.2}$ from the table, and estimate $1 - \cos 0.2$.

The ratio is even, so it equals $\tfrac{\sin 0.2}{0.2} \approx 0.9933$. And $1 - \cos 0.2 \approx \tfrac{0.2^2}{2} = 0.02$;
the true value is $0.019933$.

## Beyond small angles

Two of the facts extend to every real number. Since $|\sin t| \le 1 < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, the inequality
$|\sin t| \le |t|$ holds for all $t$ (with equality only at $t = 0$): for $|t| \ge \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ it is automatic,
and for smaller $|t|$ it is the claim above together with oddness. And $\cos t \ge 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$ for all $t$,
because the chord argument used no restriction on $t$. The other inequalities do not extend: $\sin t < t$
fails for negative $t$ (for example $\sin(-1) \approx -0.841 > -1$), and $\tan t > t$ fails past $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$
(for example $\tan 2 \approx -2.185$).

## Common mistakes

- **Using degrees.** $\sin 3^\circ$ is about $0.0524$, not 3. Convert to radians before approximating.
- **Approximating $\cos t$ by $1 - t$.** The correction to $\cos t \approx 1$ is $\tfrac{t^2}{2}$, a square,
  because cosine is even.
- **Using the approximation where it is poor.** At $t = 0.5$, $\tan t \approx t$ is already off by more
  than 8%. Check the size of $t$ (or the error rule) first.
- **Dropping the restriction.** $\sin t < t < \tan t$ is proved for $0 < t < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$; outside that
  interval only $|\sin t| \le |t|$ survives.

## Key points

- For $0 < t < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $\sin t < t < \tan t$, proved by nesting two triangles around a sector.
- Squeeze: $\cos t < \tfrac{\sin t}{t} < 1$, so $\tfrac{\sin t}{t} \to 1$ as $t \to 0$ (radians only).
- Small-angle approximations: $\sin t \approx t$, $\tan t \approx t$, $\cos t \approx 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$.
- Relative errors are about $\tfrac{t^2}{6}$ for sine and $\tfrac{t^2}{3}$ for tangent; under 1% up to about $14^\circ$
  and $10^\circ$.
- $|\sin t| \le |t|$ and $\cos t \ge 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$ for every real $t$.

lessons.title: Graphs of sine and cosine
lessons.body:
## Unrolling the unit circle

The properties from the last lesson (period $2\pi$, range $[-1, 1]$, sine odd and cosine
even) already describe the shape of the graphs. This lesson draws them. Picture a point
moving counterclockwise around the unit circle at one unit of arc per second. Its height
at time $t$ is $\sin t$, and its horizontal position is $\cos t$. Plotting the height
against $t$ "unrolls" the circle into a wave.

The picture shows one moment of that motion. The point has traveled an arc of length $t$, so on
the graph it is plotted at $x = t$, at the same height $\sin t$.

![On the left, the unit circle with a point P at angle t in quadrant I: a blue arc of length t runs from (1, 0) to P, a green horizontal leg of length cos t and a red vertical leg of length sin t form a right triangle. On the right, the graph of y = sin x from 0 to 2π. A dashed line carries the height of P across to the point (t, sin t) on the graph, where a red segment of the same length sin t stands above x = t.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The graph of $y = \sin x$

From the unit circle: the height starts at 0, rises to 1 at a quarter turn, returns to 0
at a half turn, falls to $-1$ at three quarters of a turn, and is back to 0 after a full
turn. Then everything repeats.

```plot
{"x": [-6.6, 6.6], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "functions": [{"f": "sin(x)", "label": "y = sin x"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0]}, {"at": [1.5708, 1], "label": "(π/2, 1)"}, {"at": [3.1416, 0], "label": "(π, 0)"}, {"at": [4.7124, -1], "label": "(3π/2, −1)"}, {"at": [6.2832, 0]}], "caption": "y = sin x; one cycle runs from 0 to 2π"}
```

One complete repetition of the wave is a **[[cycle]]**. For $y = \sin x$, a cycle runs from
$0$ to $2\pi$, and the five **[[key points]]** that split it into quarters are
$$(0, 0),\ \left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 1\right),\ (\pi, 0),\ \left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, -1\right),\ (2\pi, 0).$$
They are the zero, maximum, zero, minimum, zero of one cycle. To sketch, plot those five
points and join them with a smooth curve that is rounded at the peaks and steepest where
it crosses the axis.

Features to read off the graph:

- domain: all reals; range: $[-1, 1]$;
- **[[zeros]]** (x-intercepts) at $x = k\pi$;
- maximum value 1 at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi$, minimum value $-1$ at $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{2} + 2k\pi$;
- symmetric about the origin, because sine is odd.

Any graph with this wavy shape (stretched, shifted or flipped) is called a **[[sinusoid]]**.

## The graph of $y = \cos x$

Cosine is the horizontal coordinate. It starts at 1, drops to 0 at a quarter turn, reaches
$-1$ at a half turn, returns to 0 at three quarters and to 1 at a full turn. Its key points
are
$$(0, 1),\ \left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right),\ (\pi, -1),\ \left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, 0\right),\ (2\pi, 1).$$

```plot
{"x": [-6.6, 6.6], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "functions": [{"f": "cos(x)", "label": "y = cos x"}, {"f": "sin(x)", "dashed": true, "label": "sin x"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 1], "label": "(0, 1)"}, {"at": [3.1416, -1], "label": "(π, −1)"}], "caption": "y = cos x (solid) is y = sin x (dashed) shifted left by π/2"}
```

The cosine graph is the sine graph shifted $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ to the left:
$$\cos x = \sin\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right).$$
It is symmetric about the $y$-axis because cosine is even. Its zeros are at
$x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, its maxima at $x = 2k\pi$ and its minima at $x = \pi + 2k\pi$.

## Stretching vertically: amplitude

Multiplying by a constant $a$ stretches the graph vertically. In $y = a\sin x$ every
$y$-value is multiplied by $a$, so the wave now runs between $-|a|$ and $|a|$. The number
$|a|$ is the **[[amplitude]]**: half the distance from the lowest point to the highest point.

If $a < 0$, the graph is also flipped across the $x$-axis (a **[[reflection]]**): $y = -\sin x$
goes *down* first instead of up.

### Example 1

Sketch one cycle of $y = 3\sin x$ and give its range.

Multiply each key point's $y$-coordinate by 3:
$(0, 0)$, $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 3\right)$, $(\pi, 0)$, $\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, -3\right)$, $(2\pi, 0)$.
Amplitude 3, range $[-3, 3]$. The zeros don't move, because $3 \cdot 0 = 0$.

### Example 2

Sketch one cycle of $y = -2\cos x$ and compare it with $y = \cos x$.

Key points of $\cos x$ times $-2$: $(0, -2)$, $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$, $(\pi, 2)$,
$\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, 0\right)$, $(2\pi, -2)$. Amplitude $|-2| = 2$. The graph starts at its
minimum instead of its maximum: it's the cosine curve stretched by 2 and turned upside down.

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 6.8], "y": [-3.4, 3.4], "functions": [{"f": "3sin(x)", "label": "y = 3 sin x"}, {"f": "-2cos(x)", "label": "y = −2 cos x"}, {"f": "sin(x)", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Amplitude 3 (sin) and amplitude 2 reflected (cos); dashed: y = sin x"}
```

### Example 3

Using the graph, find every $x$ in $[0, 2\pi]$ where $\cos x = 0$, and every $x$ in
$[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ where $\sin x$ has a maximum.

Cosine crosses the axis at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ in $[0, 2\pi]$.
Sine peaks at $\tfrac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi$: in $[-2\pi, 2\pi]$ that's $x = -\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ and $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

## Reading values from the graph

The graph is a picture of the unit-circle values. Between $0$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, sine
increases from 0 to 1 and cosine decreases from 1 to 0; they cross at $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, where
both equal $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} \approx 0.707$. Values at $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($\tfrac12$ and
$\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.866$) show that the curve rises fast near 0 and flattens near the top.

### Example 4: reflecting across the $y$-axis

Compare the graphs of $y = \sin(-x)$ and $y = \cos(-x)$ with the originals.

Replacing $x$ by $-x$ reflects a graph across the $y$-axis. Cosine is even, so $\cos(-x) = \cos x$:
the reflection changes nothing, which is what $y$-axis symmetry means. Sine is odd, so
$\sin(-x) = -\sin x$: reflecting across the $y$-axis gives the same picture as flipping across the
$x$-axis.

## Common mistakes

- **Treating the curve as a zigzag.** The peaks are rounded and the curve is steepest at
  the zeros; straight segments between key points are wrong.
- **Mixing up the starting points.** Sine starts a cycle at 0 going up; cosine starts at
  its maximum.
- **Giving a negative amplitude.** Amplitude is $|a|$. The sign of $a$ means a reflection.
- **Using degrees on the $x$-axis by accident.** Graphs in this course use radians: one
  cycle is $2\pi \approx 6.28$ units long.

## Key points

- $y = \sin x$: key points $(0,0), (\tfrac{\pi}{2},1), (\pi,0), (\tfrac{3\pi}{2},-1), (2\pi,0)$.
- $y = \cos x$: key points $(0,1), (\tfrac{\pi}{2},0), (\pi,-1), (\tfrac{3\pi}{2},0), (2\pi,1)$.
- Both have period $2\pi$ and range $[-1, 1]$; $\cos x = \sin(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2})$.
- $y = a\sin x$ and $y = a\cos x$ have amplitude $|a|$; $a < 0$ reflects across the $x$-axis.

lessons.title: Amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical shift
lessons.body:
## The general sinusoid

Real waves are rarely exactly $\sin x$. A tide might rise 3 m above its average every
12.4 hours; a sound wave might repeat 440 times a second. To describe them we stretch and
slide the basic sine graph. Every such wave can be written in the form

$$y = A\sin\big(B(x - C)\big) + D \qquad\text{or}\qquad y = A\cos\big(B(x - C)\big) + D,$$

with $B > 0$. Each constant does one job, and this lesson takes them one at a time.

## Amplitude: $A$

As in the last lesson, $|A|$ is the **[[amplitude]]**, the vertical distance from the middle of
the wave to a peak. If $A < 0$ the graph is reflected across its middle line.

## Period: $B$

Replacing $x$ by $Bx$ squeezes the graph horizontally. The basic sine completes one cycle
as its input goes from $0$ to $2\pi$. In $\sin(Bx)$ the input is $Bx$, and $Bx$ goes from
$0$ to $2\pi$ while $x$ goes from $0$ to $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$. So

$$\text{period} = \frac{2\pi}{B}.$$

$B > 1$ squeezes (shorter period, more waves); $0 < B < 1$ stretches. The number of cycles
per unit of $x$, $\tfrac{B}{2\pi}$, is called the **[[frequency]]**: it is the reciprocal of the period.

```plot
{"x": [-0.3, 6.6], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "functions": [{"f": "sin(x)", "dashed": true, "label": "sin x"}, {"f": "sin(2x)", "label": "sin 2x"}], "caption": "sin 2x has period π: two cycles fit where sin x has one"}
```

## Phase shift: $C$

Replacing $x$ by $x - C$ slides the graph $C$ units to the right (left if $C < 0$). This
horizontal slide is the **[[phase shift]]**. Because of the factored form, a cycle of
$A\sin(B(x - C)) + D$ starts where $B(x - C) = 0$, at $x = C$.

**Watch the factoring.** In $y = \sin(2x - \tfrac{\pi}{2})$ the phase shift is *not*
$\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Factor out $B$ first: $2x - \tfrac{\pi}{2} = 2\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$, so the
shift is $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ to the right. In general, for $\sin(Bx - c)$ the phase shift is
$\tfrac{c}{B}$.

## Vertical shift: $D$

Adding $D$ moves the whole graph up $D$ units. The horizontal line $y = D$, halfway
between the maximum and minimum values, is the **[[midline]]**. The **[[vertical shift]]** is $D$.
Then
$$\text{max} = D + |A|, \qquad \text{min} = D - |A|.$$

## Graphing in four steps

1. Read $|A|$, the period $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$, the phase shift $C$, and the midline $y = D$.
2. One cycle runs from $x = C$ to $x = C + \tfrac{2\pi}{B}$. Split it into four equal
   quarters; each is $\tfrac14$ of the period.
3. At the five $x$-values, place the key points of the basic shape (for sine: midline, max,
   midline, min, midline; for cosine: max, midline, min, midline, max), measured from the
   midline and using the amplitude. Flip max and min if $A < 0$.
4. Join smoothly and extend periodically.

The same steps as a flowchart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Graphing y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D in order
  accDescr: Start by factoring B out of the argument so it reads B times the quantity x minus C. Then read the amplitude |A|, the period 2 pi over B, the phase shift C and the midline y = D. One cycle runs from x = C to x = C plus one period. Split that cycle into four equal quarters to get five x-values. At those x-values place the basic pattern measured from the midline: for sine midline, max, midline, min, midline; for cosine max, midline, min, midline, max. If A is negative, swap every max and min. Finally join the points with a smooth curve and repeat it every period.
  F["Factor B out: the inside becomes B(x - C)"] --> R["Read amplitude |A|, period 2π/B, phase shift C, midline y = D"]
  R --> CY["One cycle: from x = C to x = C + period"]
  CY --> Q["Split it into 4 quarters: 5 x-values"]
  Q --> P{"Sine or cosine?"}
  P -- sine --> S["midline, max, midline, min, midline"]
  P -- cosine --> K["max, midline, min, midline, max"]
  S --> N{"Is A negative?"}
  K --> N
  N -- yes --> SW["Swap every max and min"]
  N -- no --> J["Join smoothly and repeat every period"]
  SW --> J
```

### Example 1

Graph $y = 3\sin\!\left(2x - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + 1$.

**Step 1.** Factor: $3\sin\!\left(2\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) + 1$. Amplitude 3,
period $\tfrac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$, phase shift $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ right, midline $y = 1$.
Range: $[1 - 3, 1 + 3] = [-2, 4]$.

**Step 2.** The cycle runs from $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{4} + \pi = \tfrac{5\pi}{4}$. A quarter period
is $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, so the key $x$-values are $\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{3\pi}{4}, \pi, \tfrac{5\pi}{4}$.

**Step 3.** Sine pattern from the midline: $y = 1, 4, 1, -2, 1$.

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 5], "y": [-2.6, 4.6], "functions": [{"f": "3sin(2x - pi/2) + 1", "label": "y = 3 sin(2x − π/2) + 1"}, {"f": "1", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0.7854, 1]}, {"at": [1.5708, 4], "label": "max (π/2, 4)"}, {"at": [2.3562, 1]}, {"at": [3.1416, -2], "label": "min (π, −2)"}, {"at": [3.927, 1]}], "caption": "One cycle from π/4 to 5π/4; dashed line is the midline y = 1"}
```

**Check:** at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $3\sin(\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{2}) + 1 = 3\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} + 1 = 4$. ✓

### Example 2

Find the amplitude, period and range of $y = -2\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}x\right) - 1$, and
describe the first cycle starting at $x = 0$.

Amplitude $|-2| = 2$. Period $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/3} = 6$. Midline $y = -1$, so the range is
$[-3, 1]$. No phase shift.

Cycle from 0 to 6, quarter period $1.5$: $x = 0, 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6$. Cosine pattern
(max, mid, min, mid, max) flipped because $A < 0$: $y = -3, -1, 1, -1, -3$.

When $B$ contains $\pi$, the period often comes out a whole number. That's common in
models where $x$ is time in hours or seconds.

### Example 3: from graph to equation

A sinusoid has a maximum at $(1, 5)$ and the next minimum at $(4, -1)$. Write an equation.

**Midline and amplitude.** $D = \tfrac{5 + (-1)}{2} = 2$ and $|A| = \tfrac{5 - (-1)}{2} = 3$.

**Period.** Max to the next min is half a period: $4 - 1 = 3$, so the period is 6 and
$B = \tfrac{2\pi}{6} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$.

**Phase shift.** Cosine starts its cycle at a maximum, so using cosine the shift is the
$x$-value of a maximum: $C = 1$.

$$y = 3\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}(x - 1)\right) + 2.$$

Equations are not unique. A sine version starts a cycle on the midline going up, a quarter
period ($1.5$) before the max: $y = 3\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}(x + 0.5)\right) + 2$ describes the
same graph. Any phase shift can also change by a whole period.

## Summary table

The picture shows where each constant appears on the graph of a sine curve with $A > 0$: the
phase shift is the distance from the $y$-axis to the start of a cycle, the amplitude is measured
from the midline, and a quarter period after the start comes the first maximum.

![A sine-shaped wave with a dashed horizontal midline y = D. A double arrow along the bottom from the y-axis to the point where the cycle starts on the midline is the phase shift; a longer double arrow from that start to the end of the cycle is the period. A double arrow above the curve from the start to the first maximum is the quarter period, and a vertical double arrow from the midline up to that maximum is the amplitude.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| Constant | Effect | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| $A$ | amplitude, reflection if negative | amplitude $= \lvert A\rvert$ |
| $B$ | horizontal stretch or squeeze | period $= \dfrac{2\pi}{B}$ |
| $C$ | horizontal shift | phase shift $= C$ (right if positive) |
| $D$ | vertical shift | midline $y = D$ |

## Common mistakes

- **Not factoring before reading the phase shift.** $\sin(3x + \pi)$ shifts $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ left,
  not $\pi$ left.
- **Using $B$ itself as the period.** The period is $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$.
- **Measuring the amplitude from the $x$-axis** when the graph has been shifted up. Measure
  from the midline: half of (max $-$ min).
- **Sign of the shift.** $x - C$ shifts right by $C$; $x + C$ shifts left.

## Key points

- $y = A\sin(B(x - C)) + D$: amplitude $|A|$, period $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$, phase shift $C$, midline $y = D$.
- Factor $B$ out of the argument before reading the phase shift.
- One cycle runs from $x = C$ to $x = C + \tfrac{2\pi}{B}$; mark quarter points.
- From a graph: $D = \tfrac{\max + \min}{2}$, $|A| = \tfrac{\max - \min}{2}$, period from
  peak-to-peak distance.

lessons.title: Graphs of tangent and cotangent
lessons.body:
## A different kind of periodic graph

Sine and cosine are smooth waves that never leave $[-1, 1]$. Tangent behaves very
differently: it has no maximum or minimum, its graph breaks apart where it is undefined,
and it repeats every $\pi$ instead of every $2\pi$. All three facts follow from
$\tan x = \tfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, so the graph can be predicted from what you already know.

## Building $y = \tan x$

**Where it is undefined.** $\tan x$ is undefined where $\cos x = 0$: at
$x = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, \ldots$ Near those $x$-values the denominator is tiny,
so the quotient is huge. As $x$ approaches $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ from the left, $\sin x \to 1$ and
$\cos x \to 0^+$, so $\tan x \to +\infty$; from the right, $\cos x$ is a small negative
number and $\tan x \to -\infty$. The graph has a **[[vertical asymptote]]**, a vertical line it
approaches but never touches, at each of these points.

**Zeros.** $\tan x = 0$ where $\sin x = 0$: at $x = k\pi$.

**Some values.** $\tan\left(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \pm 1$, $\tan\left(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \pm\sqrt3 \approx \pm1.73$.

**Period $\pi$.** One full branch lives between consecutive asymptotes, from
$-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, and the branches repeat every $\pi$.

```plot
{"x": [-4.8, 4.8], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "tan(x)", "label": "y = tan x"}], "segments": [{"from": [-4.7124, -4], "to": [-4.7124, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [-1.5708, -4], "to": [-1.5708, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [1.5708, -4], "to": [1.5708, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [4.7124, -4], "to": [4.7124, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0.7854, 1], "label": "(π/4, 1)"}, {"at": [-0.7854, -1], "label": "(−π/4, −1)"}, {"at": [0, 0]}], "caption": "y = tan x with asymptotes at x = ±π/2, ±3π/2"}
```

Features of $y = \tan x$:

- domain: $x \ne \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$; range: all real numbers;
- period $\pi$; zeros at $k\pi$; asymptotes at $\tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$;
- increasing on every branch; symmetric about the origin (tangent is odd).

The three points $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{4}, -1\right)$, $(0, 0)$, $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}, 1\right)$ together with the two
asymptotes are the "key points" for sketching one branch.

![One branch of y = tan x between two dashed vertical asymptotes, x = −π/2 on the left and x = π/2 on the right. The curve rises from the bottom near the left asymptote through (−π/4, −1), the origin and (π/4, 1), and climbs toward the top near the right asymptote.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The graph of $y = \cot x$

$\cot x = \tfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ is undefined where $\sin x = 0$, at $x = k\pi$, so its
asymptotes are there. Its zeros are where $\cos x = 0$, at $\tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$. One branch runs
from $0$ to $\pi$, passing through $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{4}, 1\right)$, $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$ and
$\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{4}, -1\right)$. Cotangent is *decreasing* on each branch. Period $\pi$.

```plot
{"x": [-3.5, 6.6], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "1/tan(x)", "label": "y = cot x"}], "segments": [{"from": [-3.1416, -4], "to": [-3.1416, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0, -4], "to": [0, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [3.1416, -4], "to": [3.1416, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [6.2832, -4], "to": [6.2832, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0.7854, 1]}, {"at": [1.5708, 0]}, {"at": [2.3562, -1]}], "caption": "y = cot x: asymptotes at multiples of π, decreasing branches"}
```

## Transformations

The constants work as for sine, with one change: the basic period is $\pi$, so

$$y = A\tan\big(B(x - C)\big) + D \quad\text{has period } \frac{\pi}{B}.$$

There is no amplitude (the graph is unbounded), but $A$ still stretches vertically: the
points where the basic tangent is $\pm1$ now sit at height $D \pm A$. For a branch of
tangent, the asymptotes are where $B(x - C) = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, and the center of the branch,
where $y = D$, is at $x = C$.

The flowchart collects the steps for both functions. (For cotangent, the branch between the
asymptotes where the input is 0 and $\pi$ is centered where the input is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, half a
period after $x = C$.)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Finding the features of a transformed tangent or cotangent graph
  accDescr: For y = A tan(B(x - C)) + D or y = A cot(B(x - C)) + D, first factor B out of the input. The period of both is pi over B. Then ask whether the function is tangent or cotangent. For tangent, the asymptotes of one branch are where the input equals minus pi over 2 and pi over 2, the branch is centered at x = C at height D, and it rises if A is positive. For cotangent, the asymptotes are where the input equals 0 and pi, the center is at x = C plus half a period at height D, and the branch falls if A is positive. In both cases, halfway from the center to each asymptote the graph is at height D plus or minus A.
  F["Factor: input = B(x - C)"] --> P["Period = π/B"]
  P --> W{"Tangent or cotangent?"}
  W -- tangent --> TA["Asymptotes: input = -π/2 and π/2"]
  TA --> TC["Center x = C, height D; rises if A #gt; 0"]
  W -- cotangent --> CA["Asymptotes: input = 0 and π"]
  CA --> CC["Center x = C + half a period, height D; falls if A #gt; 0"]
  TC --> H["Halfway from center to each asymptote: height D ± A"]
  CC --> H
```

### Example 1

Graph one branch of $y = 2\tan\tfrac{x}{2}$.

$B = \tfrac12$, so the period is $\tfrac{\pi}{1/2} = 2\pi$.
Asymptotes: $\tfrac{x}{2} = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ gives $x = \pm\pi$.
The branch passes through $(0, 0)$, and halfway to each asymptote ($x = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$) it
reaches $y = 2\tan\left(\pm\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \pm 2$.

### Example 2

Find the period and the asymptotes of $y = \tan\!\left(2x - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Factor: $\tan\!\left(2\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)$. Period $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, branch centered at
$x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Asymptotes where $2x - \tfrac{\pi}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$:
$x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + \tfrac{k\pi}{2}$, i.e. at every multiple of $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ ($x = 0, \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pm\pi, \ldots$).

```plot
{"x": [-1.8, 3.4], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "tan(2x - pi/2)", "label": "y = tan(2x − π/2)"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -4], "to": [0, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [1.5708, -4], "to": [1.5708, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [3.1416, -4], "to": [3.1416, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [-1.5708, -4], "to": [-1.5708, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0.7854, 0], "label": "(π/4, 0)"}], "caption": "Period π/2; asymptotes at multiples of π/2"}
```

### Example 3

Find the period, asymptotes and zeros of $y = 3\cot(\pi x)$.

Period $\tfrac{\pi}{\pi} = 1$. Cotangent's asymptotes are where its input is a multiple of
$\pi$: $\pi x = k\pi$, so $x = k$ (every integer). Zeros where $\pi x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$:
$x = \tfrac12 + k$. Between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ the branch falls from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$,
passing through $\left(\tfrac14, 3\right)$, $\left(\tfrac12, 0\right)$ and $\left(\tfrac34, -3\right)$.

### Example 4: a reflected, shifted tangent

Describe $y = -\tan\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$.

The period is $\pi$ ($B = 1$). The branch is centered where $x + \tfrac{\pi}{4} = 0$, at $x = -\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, which is
a zero. Asymptotes: $x + \tfrac{\pi}{4} = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $x = -\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ (then every $\pi$). The
minus sign flips the branch, so it *decreases* from $+\infty$ to $-\infty$, like cotangent.

## How fast tangent grows

Near an asymptote tangent grows explosively: $\tan 1.5 \approx 14.1$, while $\tan 1.57 \approx 1256$, and
$\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.5708$. On a sketch, the branch looks nearly vertical well before it reaches the
asymptote. That's also why a small error in an angle near $90^\circ$ makes a big error in its
tangent, something surveyors avoid by not sighting at steep angles.

## Tangent as a slope

Recall from the unit circle that $\tan\theta$ is the slope of the terminal side. As $\theta$ climbs
toward $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ the ray tilts toward vertical and its slope grows without bound; just past
$\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ the ray points up and to the left, with a large negative slope. The asymptote in the
graph is the moment the ray is exactly vertical.

## Common mistakes

- **Using $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$ for the period of tangent or cotangent.** Their period is $\tfrac{\pi}{B}$.
- **Calling $A$ an amplitude.** Tangent has no maximum, so it has no amplitude; $A$ is just
  a vertical stretch.
- **Drawing the graph across an asymptote.** Each branch heads off to $\pm\infty$ and the next
  one comes back from the other end.
- **Mixing up tangent and cotangent asymptotes.** Tangent: where cosine is 0. Cotangent:
  where sine is 0.

## Key points

- $y = \tan x$: period $\pi$, asymptotes $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, zeros $x = k\pi$, increasing.
- $y = \cot x$: period $\pi$, asymptotes $x = k\pi$, zeros $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, decreasing.
- $y = A\tan(B(x - C)) + D$ has period $\tfrac{\pi}{B}$; find asymptotes by setting the input
  equal to $\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (tangent) or $0$ and $\pi$ (cotangent).
- Range of both is all real numbers; there is no amplitude.

lessons.title: Graphs of secant and cosecant
lessons.body:
## Graphs built from reciprocals

Secant and cosecant are $\tfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sin x}$. The easiest way to graph
them is to draw cosine or sine first, lightly, and then take reciprocals of the
$y$-values. Every feature of the reciprocal graph comes from a feature of the original:
zeros become asymptotes, and peaks and valleys stay where they are.

## How a reciprocal behaves

Take $y = \sec x = \tfrac{1}{\cos x}$ and look at what happens to each kind of point on the
cosine graph:

- **Where $\cos x = 0$** the reciprocal is undefined, and nearby, where $\cos x$ is tiny,
  $\sec x$ is huge. So the zeros of cosine become **[[vertical asymptotes]]** of secant:
  $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$.
- **Where $\cos x = 1$**, $\sec x = 1$ too, and since $\cos x \le 1$ nearby, $\sec x \ge 1$
  nearby. A maximum of cosine becomes a **[[local minimum]]** of secant.
- **Where $\cos x = -1$**, $\sec x = -1$, and nearby $\sec x \le -1$: a minimum of cosine
  becomes a **[[local maximum]]** of secant.
- Sign is preserved: secant is positive exactly where cosine is.

The result is a row of U-shaped branches opening up (above the cosine peaks) and down
(below the cosine valleys), separated by asymptotes.

```plot
{"x": [-4.8, 4.8], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "1/cos(x)", "label": "y = sec x"}, {"f": "cos(x)", "dashed": true, "label": "cos x"}], "segments": [{"from": [-4.7124, -4], "to": [-4.7124, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [-1.5708, -4], "to": [-1.5708, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [1.5708, -4], "to": [1.5708, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [4.7124, -4], "to": [4.7124, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0, 1], "label": "(0, 1)"}, {"at": [3.1416, -1], "label": "(π, −1)"}], "caption": "y = sec x (solid) drawn from y = cos x (dashed)"}
```

Features of $y = \sec x$: domain $x \ne \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$; range
$(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$; period $2\pi$; even (symmetric about the $y$-axis); no zeros.

## The graph of $y = \csc x$

The same construction on $y = \sin x$: asymptotes at the zeros of sine, $x = k\pi$; local
minimum $(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 1)$; local maximum $(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, -1)$; period $2\pi$; range
$(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$; odd.

```plot
{"x": [-3.5, 6.6], "y": [-4, 4], "functions": [{"f": "1/sin(x)", "label": "y = csc x"}, {"f": "sin(x)", "dashed": true}], "segments": [{"from": [-3.1416, -4], "to": [-3.1416, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0, -4], "to": [0, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [3.1416, -4], "to": [3.1416, 4], "dashed": true}, {"from": [6.2832, -4], "to": [6.2832, 4], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [1.5708, 1], "label": "(π/2, 1)"}, {"at": [4.7124, -1], "label": "(3π/2, −1)"}], "caption": "y = csc x (solid) drawn from y = sin x (dashed)"}
```

## Transformations

For $y = A\sec(B(x - C)) + D$ or $y = A\csc(B(x - C)) + D$, graph the matching cosine or sine
$y = A\cos(B(x - C)) + D$ first. The reciprocal graph:

- has the same period $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$;
- has asymptotes where the guide graph crosses its midline $y = D$;
- touches the guide graph at its maxima and minima, which become the local minima and
  maxima of the branches;
- has range $(-\infty, D - |A|] \cup [D + |A|, \infty)$.

As a procedure:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Graphing a secant or cosecant from its guide curve
  accDescr: To graph y = A sec(B(x - C)) + D or y = A csc(B(x - C)) + D, first sketch the guide curve lightly, using cosine for secant and sine for cosecant. Draw a vertical asymptote everywhere the guide crosses its midline y = D. Mark each maximum and minimum of the guide; these are the vertices of the branches. Between each pair of neighboring asymptotes draw one U-shaped branch through its vertex. A branch whose vertex is at a maximum of the guide opens up; one whose vertex is at a minimum opens down. The range is y less than or equal to D minus |A| or y greater than or equal to D plus |A|.
  G["Sketch the guide: cos for sec, sin for csc"] --> M["Asymptotes where the guide crosses its midline y = D"]
  M --> V["Mark the guide's maxima and minima: the branch vertices"]
  V --> B["Draw one U between each pair of asymptotes, through its vertex"]
  B --> O{"Vertex at a max or a min of the guide?"}
  O -- max --> U["Branch opens up"]
  O -- min --> DN["Branch opens down"]
  U --> RG["Range: y ≤ D - |A| or y ≥ D + |A|"]
  DN --> RG
```

### Example 1

Describe $y = 2\csc x$: its asymptotes, local extrema and range.

Guide graph: $y = 2\sin x$. Asymptotes at its zeros, $x = k\pi$. The guide's maximum
$\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 2\right)$ is a local minimum of $2\csc x$; its minimum
$\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, -2\right)$ is a local maximum. Range: $(-\infty, -2] \cup [2, \infty)$.

### Example 2

Describe $y = \sec(2x) + 1$.

Guide: $y = \cos(2x) + 1$, period $\pi$, midline $y = 1$, max 2 at $x = 0$, min 0 at
$x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. The guide crosses its midline where $\cos 2x = 0$:
$2x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, so $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4} + \tfrac{k\pi}{2}$. Those are the asymptotes.

Branches: a U opening up with vertex $(0, 2)$, and an upside-down U with vertex
$\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$. Range: $(-\infty, 0] \cup [2, \infty)$.

```plot
{"x": [-2.4, 3.9], "y": [-3, 5], "functions": [{"f": "1/cos(2x) + 1", "label": "y = sec 2x + 1"}, {"f": "cos(2x) + 1", "dashed": true}], "segments": [{"from": [-2.3562, -3], "to": [-2.3562, 5], "dashed": true}, {"from": [-0.7854, -3], "to": [-0.7854, 5], "dashed": true}, {"from": [0.7854, -3], "to": [0.7854, 5], "dashed": true}, {"from": [2.3562, -3], "to": [2.3562, 5], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0, 2], "label": "(0, 2)"}, {"at": [1.5708, 0], "label": "(π/2, 0)"}], "caption": "y = sec 2x + 1 with its guide y = cos 2x + 1"}
```

### Example 3

The graph of $y = -3\csc\!\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$: where are the asymptotes, and what is
the vertex of the branch between the first two positive asymptotes?

Guide: $y = -3\sin\!\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$, which is zero where $x - \tfrac{\pi}{4} = k\pi$, so
the asymptotes are $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4} + k\pi$. The first two positive ones are $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ and
$\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$. Midway, at $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}$, the guide is $-3\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = -3$ (its minimum,
because $A < 0$ flips it), so this branch opens downward with vertex $\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{4}, -3\right)$.

### Example 4: a transformed secant

Find the period, the asymptotes and the range of $y = 3\sec\tfrac{\pi x}{2} - 1$.

Guide: $y = 3\cos\tfrac{\pi x}{2} - 1$, with period $\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi/2} = 4$, midline $y = -1$, maximum 2 and
minimum $-4$. Asymptotes are where $\cos\tfrac{\pi x}{2} = 0$: $\tfrac{\pi x}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, so $x = 1 + 2k$ (the odd
integers). The branches turn at heights 2 and $-4$, so the range is
$(-\infty, -4] \cup [2, \infty)$.

## Where reciprocal graphs appear

The secant graph has a physical meaning: if a lighthouse beam rotates at a steady rate and
shines on a straight wall, the distance from the lighthouse to the lit spot is proportional
to $\sec\theta$, where $\theta$ is the beam's angle from the perpendicular to the wall, which grows without bound as the beam turns parallel to the wall. Reciprocal
trig functions also appear in calculus, as derivatives ($\tfrac{d}{dx}\tan x = \sec^2 x$) and
antiderivatives.

## Reading the graph

Each U-shaped branch sits between two consecutive asymptotes and touches the guide curve at
exactly one point, its vertex. Branches alternate between opening up and opening down, just
as the guide curve alternates between peaks and valleys.

![The graph of y = sec x drawn over its dashed guide curve y = cos x. Dashed vertical asymptotes stand where the cosine crosses the x-axis. Between them, U-shaped branches open upward above each cosine peak, touching it at points such as (0, 1), and open downward below each cosine valley, touching it at points such as (π, −1).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Common mistakes

- **Putting asymptotes at the peaks.** Asymptotes come from the *zeros* (midline crossings)
  of the guide graph; the peaks are where the branches turn.
- **Thinking secant can be between $-1$ and $1$.** A reciprocal of a number in $(-1, 1)$ has
  absolute value greater than 1.
- **Forgetting the guide graph's vertical shift.** With $+D$, asymptotes are where the guide
  crosses $y = D$, not the $x$-axis.
- **Calling the branch vertices maxima and minima of the whole function.** They are only
  local: secant has no overall maximum or minimum.

## Key points

- Graph $\sec$ and $\csc$ from $\cos$ and $\sin$: zeros become asymptotes, peaks become
  turning points of U-shaped branches.
- $\sec x$: asymptotes $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$. $\csc x$: asymptotes $x = k\pi$. Both have period $2\pi$.
- Range of $A\sec(\cdot) + D$ or $A\csc(\cdot) + D$: $(-\infty, D - |A|] \cup [D + |A|, \infty)$.

lessons.title: Modeling periodic data and harmonic motion
lessons.body:
## Why sinusoids model the world

Anything driven by rotation or by a restoring force tends to rise and fall in a
sinusoidal pattern: daylight hours over a year (Earth's orbit and tilt), tides (the Moon's
orbit), a rider's height on a Ferris wheel, a weight bouncing on a spring, alternating
current. This lesson turns the four constants of the last lessons into a recipe for
building such models from a description or from data, and introduces the physics term for
the cleanest case: simple harmonic motion.

## The recipe

To fit $y = A\cos\big(B(t - C)\big) + D$ (or the sine version) to a repeating quantity:

1. **Midline:** $D = \dfrac{\max + \min}{2}$.
2. **Amplitude:** $|A| = \dfrac{\max - \min}{2}$.
3. **Period:** the time for one full cycle (peak to next peak, or twice peak to trough).
   Then $B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\text{period}}$.
4. **Phase shift:** with cosine, $C$ is the time of a maximum (use $-A$ and a minimum if
   that's what you know). With sine, $C$ is a time when the quantity crosses the midline
   going up.

A model built this way assumes the pattern is perfectly sinusoidal. Real data only
approximately are, so treat predictions as estimates.

Step 4 is where most choices are made. This chart sums it up, with $A$ the (positive) amplitude
and $h$ the time of the moment you know:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the form of a sinusoidal model
  accDescr: First compute the midline D as the average of the maximum and minimum, the amplitude A as half their difference, and B as 2 pi divided by the period. Then look at one moment you know, at time h. If the quantity is at a maximum then, use A cos(B(t - h)) + D. If it is at a minimum, use -A cos(B(t - h)) + D. If it is on the midline going up, use A sin(B(t - h)) + D. If it is on the midline going down, use -A sin(B(t - h)) + D.
  S["D = (max + min)/2, A = (max - min)/2, B = 2π/period"] --> K{"What happens at a known time h?"}
  K -- "at a maximum" --> C1["y = A cos(B(t - h)) + D"]
  K -- "at a minimum" --> C2["y = -A cos(B(t - h)) + D"]
  K -- "midline, rising" --> S1["y = A sin(B(t - h)) + D"]
  K -- "midline, falling" --> S2["y = -A sin(B(t - h)) + D"]
```

### Example 1: seasonal temperature

In a certain city the average daily high is lowest in January, $31^\circ$F, and highest in
July, $89^\circ$F. Let $t$ be the month ($t = 1$ for January). Build a model and estimate the
average high in May.

- $D = \tfrac{89 + 31}{2} = 60$ and $A = \tfrac{89 - 31}{2} = 29$.
- The cycle is one year, 12 months: $B = \tfrac{2\pi}{12} = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$.
- The maximum is at $t = 7$, so use cosine with $C = 7$:

$$T(t) = 29\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}(t - 7)\right) + 60.$$

May is $t = 5$: $T(5) = 29\cos\!\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + 60 = 29\cdot\tfrac12 + 60 = 74.5^\circ$F.

```plot
{"x": [0, 13], "y": [20, 100], "functions": [{"f": "29cos(pi/6*(x - 7)) + 60", "label": "T(t)"}], "points": [{"at": [1, 31], "label": "Jan 31°"}, {"at": [7, 89], "label": "Jul 89°"}, {"at": [5, 74.5], "label": "May ≈ 74.5°"}], "xLabel": "month t", "yLabel": "°F", "caption": "A sinusoidal model of average daily highs"}
```

Check: at $t = 1$, $\cos(-\pi) = -1$ gives $T = 31$. ✓

### Example 2: a Ferris wheel

A Ferris wheel 50 m in diameter has its center 30 m above the ground and turns once every
4 minutes. A rider boards at the bottom at $t = 0$. Write the rider's height $h(t)$ in
meters and find when the rider first reaches 42.5 m.

![A Ferris wheel with its center 30 m above the ground and a radius of 25 m drawn straight down to the boarding point at the bottom, 5 m above the ground. A height scale beside the wheel marks 0, 5, 30 and 55 m, with dotted lines from the boarding point, the center and the top of the wheel.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- Midline: the center, $D = 30$. Amplitude: the radius, $25$. Lowest point $5$ m, highest $55$ m.
- Period 4 min, so $B = \tfrac{2\pi}{4} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
- The rider starts at a minimum. A cosine starts at a maximum, so flip it: $A = -25$, $C = 0$.

$$h(t) = 30 - 25\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right).$$

Set $h = 42.5$: $-25\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right) = 12.5$, so $\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right) = -\tfrac12$. The
first positive solution has $\tfrac{\pi}{2}t = \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$, so $t = \tfrac43$ min, 80 seconds.

### Example 3: tides

At a harbor, high tide of 4.2 m occurs at 2:00 AM and the next low tide, 0.6 m, at
8:12 AM. Estimate the depth at noon.

- $D = \tfrac{4.2 + 0.6}{2} = 2.4$, $A = \tfrac{4.2 - 0.6}{2} = 1.8$.
- High to low is half a period: 6 h 12 min $= 6.2$ h, so the period is $12.4$ h and
  $B = \tfrac{2\pi}{12.4}$.
- Cosine with the maximum at $t = 2$ (hours after midnight):

$$h(t) = 1.8\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{12.4}(t - 2)\right) + 2.4.$$

At noon, $t = 12$: $h(12) = 1.8\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi \cdot 10}{12.4}\right) + 2.4 \approx 1.8(0.3473) + 2.4 \approx 3.03$ m.
The tide is coming back in toward the next high at 2:24 PM.

## Simple harmonic motion

A weight on a spring, pulled down and released, bobs up and down. If friction is ignored,
its displacement from the rest position (the **[[equilibrium]]**) is a pure sinusoid in time.
Motion of this kind is called **[[simple harmonic motion]]**:

$$d = a\sin(\omega t) \qquad\text{or}\qquad d = a\cos(\omega t),$$

where $|a|$ is the amplitude (the greatest distance from equilibrium), $\omega > 0$ is the
angular frequency, the period is $\tfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$, and the **[[frequency]]** (cycles per unit
time) is $f = \tfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$. With $t$ in seconds, frequency is measured in hertz (Hz),
cycles per second.

Use cosine when the object starts at its farthest point (released from rest after being
pulled), and sine when it starts at equilibrium with some velocity.

### Example 4

A spring's displacement is $d = 6\sin(3\pi t)$ cm, with $t$ in seconds. Find the amplitude,
period and frequency, and the displacement at $t = 0.25$ s.

Amplitude $6$ cm. Period $\tfrac{2\pi}{3\pi} = \tfrac23$ s. Frequency $\tfrac{3\pi}{2\pi} = 1.5$ Hz.
$d(0.25) = 6\sin(0.75\pi) = 6\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} = 3\sqrt2 \approx 4.24$ cm.

### Example 5

A mass is pulled 4 cm below equilibrium and released; it completes 2 oscillations per
second. Write $d(t)$, taking up as positive.

It starts at its lowest point, so use $-4\cos(\omega t)$. Frequency 2 Hz means
$\omega = 2\pi f = 4\pi$. So $d(t) = -4\cos(4\pi t)$.

In reality friction makes the swings shrink over time. That is **damped harmonic
motion**, modeled by multiplying by a decaying factor, as in $d = 4e^{-0.3t}\cos(4\pi t)$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 4], "y": [-4.5, 4.5], "functions": [{"f": "4exp(-0.3x)cos(4pi*x)", "label": "damped"}, {"f": "4exp(-0.3x)", "dashed": true}, {"f": "-4exp(-0.3x)", "dashed": true}], "xLabel": "t", "yLabel": "d", "caption": "d = 4e^(−0.3t) cos(4πt): the amplitude decays inside an exponential envelope (dashed)"}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Confusing period and frequency.** Period is time per cycle; frequency is cycles per
  unit time. They are reciprocals.
- **Using half a period as the period.** Peak to trough is only half a cycle.
- **Wrong starting point.** A rider boarding at the bottom, or a spring released from its
  lowest point, starts at a minimum: use $-\cos$.
- **Calculator in degree mode** when evaluating a model whose argument is in radians.

## Key points

- $D = \tfrac{\max + \min}{2}$, $|A| = \tfrac{\max - \min}{2}$, $B = \tfrac{2\pi}{\text{period}}$, and $C$
  from a known peak (cosine) or upward midline crossing (sine).
- Simple harmonic motion: $d = a\sin\omega t$ or $a\cos\omega t$, period $\tfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$,
  frequency $\tfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$.
- Start with $\cos$ at a maximum, $-\cos$ at a minimum, $\sin$ at equilibrium moving up.

lessons.title: Sums, products and envelopes: combining trig graphs
lessons.body:
## Beyond a single wave

Every graph in this module so far has been one sinusoid (or one tangent, secant or cosecant),
stretched and shifted. Lesson 17 already hinted that real signals are messier: the damped spring
$d = 4e^{-0.3t}\cos(4\pi t)$ is a cosine *multiplied* by a shrinking exponential. The note of a guitar string or a flute is close to
a *sum* of a main tone and quieter overtones at two, three, four times its frequency. A tide is
closer to a sum of several sinusoids with different periods than to a single one.

This lesson shows how to sketch such combinations without plotting hundreds of points, and
answers two questions that the single-sinusoid lessons never had to ask: when is a sum of
periodic functions periodic, and what controls the height of a product?

## Adding graphs point by point

To graph $y = f(x) + g(x)$, add the two heights at each $x$. This is called **addition of
ordinates** (an *ordinate* is a $y$-coordinate). In practice:

1. Sketch $f$ and $g$ lightly on the same axes.
2. Mark the easy $x$-values: where either graph is 0 (the sum equals the other graph there),
   and where either reaches a maximum or minimum.
3. At each marked $x$, add the two heights and plot the result.
4. Join the points smoothly.

Step 2 is the shortcut that makes the method fast. Wherever $g(x) = 0$, the sum is sitting
exactly on the graph of $f$.

### Example 1: a wave riding on a line

Sketch $y = x + \sin x$ for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$.

Here $f(x) = x$ and $g(x) = \sin x$. Where $\sin x = 0$, at $x = 0, \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi, 4\pi$, the sum is
on the line $y = x$. Where $\sin x = 1$, at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$, the sum is one unit
*above* the line; where $\sin x = -1$, at $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ and $\tfrac{7\pi}{2}$, it is one unit below. So the
graph winds around the line $y = x$, crossing it every $\pi$ units and never straying more than 1
from it.

```plot
{"x": [-0.5, 13.2], "y": [-1.5, 14], "functions": [{"f": "x + sin(x)"}, {"f": "x", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [3.1416, 3.1416]}, {"at": [7.854, 8.854]}], "labels": [{"at": [3.5, 12.5], "text": "y = x + sin x (solid)"}, {"at": [3.5, 11], "text": "y = x (dashed)"}, {"at": [2, 4.2], "text": "(π, π)"}, {"at": [7, 10], "text": "(5π/2, 5π/2 + 1)"}], "caption": "y = x + sin x winds around the line y = x and meets it wherever sin x = 0"}
```

Notice that $y = x + \sin x$ is *not* periodic, even though one of its parts is: the line keeps
climbing while $\sin x$ stays between $-1$ and 1, so the sum grows without bound and can never
repeat its values.

### Example 2: a wave plus its overtone

Sketch $y = \sin x + \sin 2x$ on $[0, 2\pi]$.

The second term has period $\pi$, so it changes twice as fast. Use quarter-points of the faster
term, multiples of $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ | $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ | $\pi$ | $\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$ | $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ | $\tfrac{7\pi}{4}$ | $2\pi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin x$ | 0 | 0.707 | 1 | 0.707 | 0 | −0.707 | −1 | −0.707 | 0 |
| $\sin 2x$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | −1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | −1 | 0 |
| sum | 0 | 1.707 | 1 | −0.293 | 0 | 0.293 | −1 | −1.707 | 0 |

```plot
{"x": [-0.3, 6.6], "y": [-2.2, 2.2], "functions": [{"f": "sin(x) + sin(2x)", "from": 0, "to": 6.2832}, {"f": "sin(x)", "dashed": true, "from": 0, "to": 6.2832}, {"f": "sin(2x)", "dashed": true, "from": 0, "to": 6.2832}], "labels": [{"at": [5, 1.6], "text": "y = sin x + sin 2x (solid)"}], "points": [{"at": [0.7854, 1.7071]}, {"at": [5.4978, -1.7071]}], "caption": "The sum (solid) of sin x and sin 2x (dashed); the pattern repeats every 2π"}
```

The sum is a lopsided wave that repeats every $2\pi$. Its highest point is *not* at $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$:
a finer table (or a graphing tool) puts it near $x \approx 0.936$ with $y \approx 1.760$. Addition of
ordinates gives the shape quickly, but it can miss the exact location of a peak, because the
peaks of the parts generally fall at different places.

## When is a sum periodic?

Suppose $f$ has period $p$ and $g$ has period $q$. If some length $L$ is a whole number of
$p$'s *and* a whole number of $q$'s, both parts repeat after $L$, so the sum does too. The
smallest such $L$ is the **[[least common multiple]]** of the periods.

To find it, divide the periods. If $\tfrac{p}{q} = \tfrac{m}{n}$ in lowest terms, then $np = mq$, and
$L = np$ is the least common multiple.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Deciding whether a sum of sinusoids is periodic and finding a period
  accDescr: Find the period of each term, p and q. Divide one period by the other. If the ratio is irrational, the sum is not periodic at all. If the ratio is a fraction m over n in lowest terms, the least common multiple of the periods is L = n times p, which equals m times q, and the sum repeats after L. Usually L is the smallest period, but check smaller candidates with a graph, because in special cases the sum repeats sooner.
  P["Find each term's period, p and q"] --> R{"Is p/q a fraction?"}
  R -- "no, irrational" --> NP["The sum is not periodic"]
  R -- "yes, p/q = m/n in lowest terms" --> L["Common period L = n·p = m·q"]
  L --> C["Usually the smallest period; check smaller candidates"]
```

### Example 3: two different periods

Find the period of $y = \sin\tfrac{\pi x}{3} + \cos\tfrac{\pi x}{2}$, and of $y = \sin 2x + \cos 3x$.

For the first, the periods are $\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi/3} = 6$ and $\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi/2} = 4$. Then
$\tfrac{6}{4} = \tfrac{3}{2}$, so $L = 2 \cdot 6 = 3 \cdot 4 = 12$. After 12 units the first term has done 2
cycles and the second 3, and both are back where they started.

For the second, the periods are $\pi$ and $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$. Their ratio is $\tfrac{\pi}{2\pi/3} = \tfrac32$, so
$L = 2 \cdot \pi = 3 \cdot \tfrac{2\pi}{3} = 2\pi$. A common slip is to multiply the periods
($\pi \cdot \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$) or add them; neither has anything to do with when the pattern repeats.

For both functions a numerical check confirms that no shorter shift works, so 12 and $2\pi$ are
the smallest periods. When the two terms are sinusoids with *different* frequencies, this is
always so. But in other cases the sum can repeat sooner than the least common multiple. For
example $|\sin x|$ and $|\cos x|$ each have period $\pi$, yet $|\sin x| + |\cos x|$ has period
$\tfrac{\pi}{2}$: shifting by a quarter turn just swaps the two terms. That is why the diagram says
"usually".

### When the ratio is irrational

The function $y = \sin x + \sin(\sqrt2\,x)$ has periods $2\pi$ and $\sqrt2\,\pi$, whose ratio is
$\sqrt2$, an irrational number. No length is a whole number of both periods, and in fact the sum
is not periodic at all: its graph wanders forever without exactly repeating. (A short proof
uses the sum formulas of Module 6; here we state the result.) You can see a symptom: the sum
would equal 2 only if both sines were 1 at the same $x$, which would make $\sqrt2$ a ratio of two
whole numbers. So the graph comes as close to 2 as you like but never gets there.

## Multiplying: envelopes

Now take a product $y = f(x)\sin x$, where $f(x) \ge 0$. Because $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$,

$$-f(x) \le f(x)\sin x \le f(x).$$

The graph is trapped between the curves $y = f(x)$ and $y = -f(x)$, which together are called its
**[[envelope]]**. Three facts make products easy to sketch:

- the graph **touches** the upper envelope where $\sin x = 1$ and the lower one where $\sin x = -1$;
- it is **[[zero]]** where $\sin x = 0$ (and wherever $f(x) = 0$);
- between those points it swings from one envelope to the other.

The same holds with $\cos x$ in place of $\sin x$. The damped spring of Lesson 17 is exactly this
picture with the envelope $\pm 4e^{-0.3t}$.

### Example 4: a growing wave

Sketch $y = x\sin x$ for $0 \le x \le 4\pi$.

The envelope is $y = \pm x$, two lines through the origin. The graph touches $y = x$ at
$x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{5\pi}{2}$ and $y = -x$ at $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}, \tfrac{7\pi}{2}$. It is zero at every multiple
of $\pi$.

![The graph of y = x sin x for x from 0 to 4π, between two dashed lines y = x and y = −x that open out from the origin. The wave grows as it moves right. It touches the upper line at 5π/2, crosses zero at 3π, and touches the lower line at 7π/2.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A subtle point: the touching points are *not* the peaks. At $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ the graph touches the
envelope at height $\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571$, but the first peak comes a little later, near
$x \approx 2.029$, at height about $1.820$. There the curve is below the envelope (which is at
2.029) but higher than at the touching point, because the growing factor $x$ keeps pushing it
up after $\sin x$ has passed its maximum. Further right the difference shrinks: the peak near
$5\pi/2 \approx 7.854$ is at $x \approx 7.979$.

### Example 5: how long a damped wave lasts

A plucked string's displacement is modeled by $y = 3e^{-0.2t}\cos(2\pi t)$ mm, $t$ in seconds. When
has the envelope dropped to 10% of its starting height, and about how many vibrations happen
before then?

The envelope is $3e^{-0.2t}$, which starts at 3. Set $e^{-0.2t} = 0.1$ and take natural logs:
$-0.2t = \ln 0.1$, so $t = \tfrac{\ln 10}{0.2} \approx 11.51$ s. The cosine has period
$\tfrac{2\pi}{2\pi} = 1$ s, so about 11 to 12 full vibrations happen first. The envelope sets *how big*
the swings are; the cosine sets *how often* they happen. The two jobs are separate, which is why
envelopes are so useful.

## A product with a shrinking envelope

The function $y = \dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ is $\sin x$ times $\dfrac{1}{x}$. For $x > 0$ the envelope is
$y = \pm\dfrac{1}{x}$, so the waves die away as $x$ grows, and the zeros are at $x = \pi, 2\pi, 3\pi, \ldots$
At $x = 0$ the formula is undefined ($\tfrac{0}{0}$), yet the values near 0 settle down:

| $x$ | 0.5 | 0.1 | 0.01 | 0.001 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ | 0.95885 | 0.99833 | 0.99998 | 0.9999998 |

The values approach 1. The graph is even (both $\sin x$ and $x$ are odd, and an odd function
divided by an odd one is even), so the same happens from the left. The Module 3 honors lesson on
small angles proves that the limit really is 1, with a picture of the unit circle.

```plot
{"x": [-2, 15.4], "y": [-0.4, 1.2], "functions": [{"f": "sin(x)/x", "from": 0, "to": 14.6}, {"f": "1/x", "dashed": true, "from": 0, "to": 14.6}, {"f": "-1/x", "dashed": true, "from": 0, "to": 14.6}], "points": [{"at": [0, 1], "open": true}], "labels": [{"at": [3.6, 0.97], "text": "← approaches 1"}, {"at": [9, 0.55], "text": "y = sin x / x (solid)"}], "caption": "y = (sin x)/x for x > 0 (the graph is symmetric about the y-axis): undefined at 0 but approaching 1; envelope y = ±1/x (dashed)"}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Multiplying or adding the periods.** The period of a sum comes from the least common
  multiple: periods 6 and 4 give 12, not 24 or 10.
- **Assuming every sum is periodic.** If the ratio of the periods is irrational, the sum never
  repeats; if one part grows without bound (like $x$) while the other stays bounded (like
  $\sin x$), the sum grows without bound too, so it is not periodic.
- **Putting the peaks of a product at the envelope.** A product touches its envelope where the
  sine is $\pm1$, but its local maxima are usually nearby, not exactly there.
- **Forgetting the envelope's sign.** For $f(x)\sin x$ with $f$ sometimes negative, the envelope
  is $y = \pm|f(x)|$.

## Key points

- Addition of ordinates: add heights point by point; where one part is 0, the sum lies on the other.
- A sum of terms with periods $p$ and $q$ repeats after their least common multiple: if
  $\tfrac{p}{q} = \tfrac{m}{n}$ in lowest terms, $L = np = mq$. Usually that is the smallest period.
- If $\tfrac{p}{q}$ is irrational, a sum of two sinusoids is not periodic.
- $y = f(x)\sin x$ lies between $\pm|f(x)|$, touches them where $\sin x = \pm1$, and is zero where
  $\sin x = 0$.
- $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ is undefined at 0 but its values approach 1.

lessons.title: How fast a sinusoid changes: slopes, speeds and the pendulum
lessons.body:
## From shape to speed

Lesson 13 described the sine curve as "rounded at the peaks and steepest where it crosses the
axis". This lesson puts numbers on that sentence. How steep is the steepest part? How fast is a
Ferris-wheel rider rising as she passes the height of the hub? How fast is a spring moving when
it passes its rest position? The answers all come from one fact: the slope of the sine graph at
any point is given by the cosine. We reach that fact with tables first and then with an
argument, and it is the first result of the calculus of trig functions.

## Average rate of change

For any function, the **[[average rate of change]]** from $x = a$ to $x = b$ is

$$\frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a},$$

the change in height divided by the change in input. On the graph it is the slope of the
straight line joining the two points, called a *secant line* of the graph.

### Example 1: sine slows down as it climbs

Find the average rate of change of $y = \sin x$ over $\left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{6}\right]$,
$\left[\tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{\pi}{3}\right]$ and $\left[\tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$.

Each interval has width $\tfrac{\pi}{6} \approx 0.5236$.

- $\dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{6} - \sin 0}{\pi/6} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.5236} \approx 0.955$
- $\dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{3} - \sin\frac{\pi}{6}}{\pi/6} = \dfrac{0.8660 - 0.5}{0.5236} \approx 0.699$
- $\dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{2} - \sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{\pi/6} = \dfrac{1 - 0.8660}{0.5236} \approx 0.256$

Over equal steps the climb shrinks: sine rises fast near 0 and hardly at all near its peak.

## The slope at a point

Now shrink the interval. The average rate of change over $[x, x + h]$ is the
**[[difference quotient]]**

$$\frac{\sin(x + h) - \sin x}{h}.$$

As $h$ gets very small, the secant line pivots into the line that just touches the curve at $x$,
and the difference quotient settles on a single number: the **[[slope of the curve]]** at $x$.

At $x = 0$ the difference quotient is $\tfrac{\sin h}{h}$, which approaches 1 (about 0.9983 at
$h = 0.1$ and 0.99998 at $h = 0.01$; the Module 3 honors lesson on small angles proves it). So the
sine curve leaves the origin with slope exactly 1. Here is the same computation, with
$h = 0.001$, at other points of the first half-cycle:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ | $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ | $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ | $\pi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\dfrac{\sin(x + 0.001) - \sin x}{0.001}$ | 1.0000 | 0.8658 | 0.4996 | −0.0005 | −0.5004 | −1.0000 |
| $\cos x$ | 1 | 0.8660 | 0.5 | 0 | −0.5 | −1 |

The slopes match the values of cosine. That is no accident.

## Why the slope of sine is cosine

Expand $\sin(x + h)$ with the sum formula from Lesson 23 and regroup:

$$\frac{\sin(x + h) - \sin x}{h} = \frac{\sin x\cos h + \cos x\sin h - \sin x}{h} = \sin x\cdot\frac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x\cdot\frac{\sin h}{h}.$$

Now let $h$ shrink toward 0, with $x$ held fixed.

- $\dfrac{\sin h}{h}$ approaches 1, as above.
- $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h}$ approaches 0, because $1 - \cos h$ is about $\tfrac{h^2}{2}$ for small $h$
  (another small-angle fact), so the quotient is about $-\tfrac{h}{2}$.

So the difference quotient approaches $\sin x \cdot 0 + \cos x \cdot 1 = \cos x$:

$$\text{the slope of } y = \sin x \text{ at } x \text{ is } \cos x.$$

In calculus this is written $\tfrac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$. (The argument above leans on two limits
that a calculus course proves carefully; here we have used them as established.) Everything also
depends on measuring $x$ in **[[radians]]**: in degrees the slope would carry an extra factor of
$\tfrac{\pi}{180}$, the same factor that spoils $\tfrac{\sin x}{x} \to 1$.

Cosine follows for free. Since $\cos x = \sin\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, the cosine graph is the
sine graph slid left, and its slope at $x$ is the slope of sine at $x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$\cos\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin x$. So the slope of $y = \cos x$ is $-\sin x$.

```plot
{"x": [-0.3, 6.6], "y": [-1.5, 1.5], "functions": [{"f": "sin(x)", "label": "y = sin x", "from": 0, "to": 6.2832}, {"f": "cos(x)", "dashed": true, "label": "slope of sin x", "from": 0, "to": 6.2832}], "points": [{"at": [0, 1], "label": "slope 1 at x = 0"}, {"at": [1.5708, 0], "label": "slope 0"}, {"at": [3.1416, -1]}], "labels": [{"at": [3.1416, -1.27], "text": "slope −1 at x = π"}], "caption": "The slope of y = sin x (solid) at each x is the height of y = cos x (dashed)"}
```

Read the two graphs together: where sine climbs (from $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$) cosine is
positive; where sine has a peak or a trough, cosine is zero; where sine falls, cosine is
negative.

## Slopes of a transformed sinusoid

Each constant in $y = A\sin\big(B(x - C)\big) + D$ affects slopes in a simple way:

- multiplying heights by $A$ multiplies every slope by $A$;
- replacing $x$ by $Bx$ squeezes the graph horizontally by a factor $B$, which multiplies every
  slope by $B$;
- shifting by $C$ or $D$ moves the graph without tilting it, so slopes just travel with it.

Putting these together, the slope of $y = A\sin\big(B(x - C)\big) + D$ at $x$ is
$AB\cos\big(B(x - C)\big)$. Since cosine runs between $-1$ and $1$, the **[[steepest slope]]** of the
sinusoid is $|A|B$, which can also be written $\dfrac{2\pi|A|}{\text{period}}$. It occurs at every
midline crossing, and the slope is 0 at every peak and trough.

![The graph of y = sin x from just left of 0 to 2π. Red tangent lines touch it at the origin with slope 1, at the peak π/2 with slope 0, at π with slope −1, and at the trough 3π/2 with slope 0. A dashed green secant line joins two points on either side of the trough.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: slope at a point

Find the slope of $y = 3\sin(2x)$ at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$, and check it with a difference quotient.

Here $A = 3$, $B = 2$, so the slope is $3 \cdot 2\cos\left(2 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = 6\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3} = 3$. Check with
$h = 0.001$: $\dfrac{3\sin(2(\frac{\pi}{6} + 0.001)) - 3\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{0.001} \approx 2.9948$, very close to 3.

### Example 3: the Ferris wheel rider

In Lesson 17 a rider's height was $h(t) = 30 - 25\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right)$ m, $t$ in minutes.
How fast is the rider rising, at most, and when?

Amplitude 25, $B = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. The fastest rise is $25 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 39.27$ m/min, at the upward
midline crossing: the rider is at the hub's height, 30 m, on the way up, at $t = 1$ min (and
every 4 minutes after).

There is a satisfying check. The rim moves at linear speed $v = r\omega = 25 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ m/min
(Lesson 4). At the side of the wheel the rim is moving straight up, so all of that speed is
vertical: the two methods agree.

### Example 4: the rule of twelfths

In Lesson 17's tide model, $h(t) = 1.8\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{12.4}(t - 2)\right) + 2.4$, the water falls from
4.2 m to 0.6 m in about 6 hours. Sailors estimate the fall hour by hour with the **rule of
twelfths**: 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1 twelfths of the range in the six hours. Compare with the model.

Over half a period the cosine goes from 1 to $-1$, so after $k$ sixths of that half-period the
fraction of the range covered is $\tfrac{1 - \cos(k\pi/6)}{2}$. Taking differences gives
0.067, 0.183, 0.250, 0.250, 0.183, 0.067, while the rule uses $\tfrac{1}{12} \approx 0.083$,
$\tfrac{2}{12} \approx 0.167$ and $\tfrac{3}{12} = 0.25$. The rule is a rough version of the sinusoid: slow
near high and low water, fastest in the middle. The fastest fall is
$1.8 \cdot \tfrac{2\pi}{12.4} \approx 0.91$ m per hour, at the midline crossing $t = 2 + 3.1 = 5.1$, about
5:06 AM. (Real tides are only roughly sinusoidal, so treat both as estimates.)

## Speed in simple harmonic motion

For an object in simple harmonic motion, $d = a\sin(\omega t)$, the slope of the graph is the
**[[velocity]]**: the rate at which the displacement changes. By the rule above it is
$a\omega\cos(\omega t)$. So the object moves fastest, at speed $|a|\omega$, as it passes through
equilibrium, and it is momentarily at rest at the turning points, where $|d| = |a|$.

### Example 5: the spring again

Lesson 17's spring has $d = 6\sin(3\pi t)$ cm, $t$ in seconds. Find its greatest speed and its
velocity at $t = 0.25$ s.

The greatest speed is $|a|\omega = 6 \cdot 3\pi = 18\pi \approx 56.5$ cm/s, reached every time it passes
equilibrium. At $t = 0.25$: $18\pi\cos(0.75\pi) = 18\pi\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right) \approx -40.0$ cm/s. The
negative sign means it is moving in the negative direction (down, if up is positive), even though
its displacement there ($3\sqrt2 \approx 4.24$ cm) is still positive: it is on its way back toward
equilibrium.

## The pendulum

A pendulum is the classic place where a small-angle approximation turns into a physical law.
Physics shows that the force pulling a pendulum bob back toward the bottom is proportional to
$\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is its angle from vertical. For small swings $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ (in radians),
so the pull is proportional to the displacement itself, and that is exactly the condition for
simple harmonic motion. The result, which we take from physics without deriving it, is the
period

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}},$$

where $L$ is the length and $g \approx 9.81$ m/s² is the acceleration due to gravity. For small swings
the period depends on neither the mass nor how far the bob swings.

### Example 6: a seconds pendulum

Find the period of a 1 m pendulum, and the length whose period is exactly 2 s (one second per
swing, the length used in many pendulum clocks).

$T = 2\pi\sqrt{1/9.81} \approx 2.006$ s. For $T = 2$: square both sides of $2 = 2\pi\sqrt{L/9.81}$ to get
$\tfrac{L}{9.81} = \tfrac{1}{\pi^2}$, so $L = \tfrac{9.81}{\pi^2} \approx 0.994$ m.

For larger swings the formula slowly fails, because $\sin\theta$ is noticeably smaller than $\theta$.
The true period is longer: by about 0.2% for a swing of $10^\circ$ to each side, about 1.7% for
$30^\circ$, and about 18% for $90^\circ$. Clocks keep their swings small for this reason.

## Common mistakes

- **Taking the amplitude as the steepest slope.** The steepest slope is $|A|B$; the same amplitude
  with a shorter period makes a steeper wave.
- **Looking for the fastest change at a peak.** At a maximum or minimum the slope is 0; the
  fastest change is at the midline.
- **Confusing average and instantaneous rates.** An average rate over an interval is a secant
  slope; it equals the slope at a point only in the limit of tiny intervals.
- **Using degrees.** "The slope of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$" is true only with $x$ in radians.

## Key points

- Average rate of change: $\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$, the slope of a secant line.
- The slope of $y = \sin x$ at $x$ is $\cos x$, and the slope of $y = \cos x$ is $-\sin x$ (radians).
- The slope of $A\sin(B(x - C)) + D$ is $AB\cos(B(x - C))$; the steepest slope, $|A|B$, comes at
  the midline crossings, and the slope is 0 at peaks and troughs.
- In simple harmonic motion $d = a\sin\omega t$, the greatest speed is $|a|\omega$, at equilibrium.
- Small-swing pendulum: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$.

lessons.title: Inverse sine, cosine and tangent
lessons.body:
## Running trig backward

So far we have gone from an angle to a ratio: given $\theta$, find $\sin\theta$. Many problems
run the other way: a ramp rises 1 m over 12 m, so what is its angle? You have already
used the $\sin^{-1}$ and $\tan^{-1}$ keys for acute angles in right triangles. This lesson
makes those keys into honest functions and pins down exactly which angle they return.

## The problem: too many answers

For a function to have an inverse, each output must come from only one input; such a
function is called **[[one-to-one]]**. Sine is not: $\sin\theta = \tfrac12$ for
$\theta = \tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}, \tfrac{13\pi}{6}, \ldots$, infinitely many angles. A horizontal
line crosses the sine graph infinitely often.

The fix is to **[[restrict the domain]]** to a piece of the graph that

- takes every value in the range exactly once, and
- includes the acute angles $0$ to $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so right-triangle answers come out naturally.

The plot shows the piece of the sine graph that is kept for the inverse sine. The dashed line
$y = \tfrac12$ crosses the full sine curve over and over (open dots), but it crosses the solid
piece exactly once.

```plot
{"x": [-6.4, 6.4], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "functions": [{"f": "sin(x)", "dashed": true}, {"f": "sin(x)", "from": -1.5708, "to": 1.5708}, {"f": "0.5", "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [-2.4, -1.35], "text": "kept piece"}, {"at": [1.0, 0.2], "text": "π/6"}], "points": [{"at": [0.5236, 0.5]}, {"at": [2.618, 0.5], "open": true}, {"at": [-3.6652, 0.5], "open": true}, {"at": [-5.7596, 0.5], "open": true}], "caption": "sin x = 1/2 has infinitely many solutions, but only π/6 lies on the kept piece from −π/2 to π/2"}
```

## Inverse sine

Restrict sine to $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. On that interval it increases from $-1$ to 1
and hits each value once. The **[[inverse sine]]** (or **[[arcsine]]**) is

$$y = \sin^{-1}x = \arcsin x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sin y = x \text{ and } -\tfrac{\pi}{2} \le y \le \tfrac{\pi}{2}.$$

Domain $[-1, 1]$, range $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. In words: $\sin^{-1}x$ is *the angle between
$-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ whose sine is $x$*. On the unit circle those angles are quadrants I and
IV, the right half.

The $-1$ in $\sin^{-1}$ means inverse function, not reciprocal: $\sin^{-1}x \ne \tfrac{1}{\sin x}$.
The reciprocal is $\csc x$. Writing $\arcsin x$ avoids the confusion.

## Inverse cosine

Cosine is not one-to-one on $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ (it's even), so a different piece is
used: $[0, \pi]$, where cosine decreases from 1 to $-1$. The **[[inverse cosine]]**
(**[[arccosine]]**) is

$$y = \cos^{-1}x = \arccos x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \cos y = x \text{ and } 0 \le y \le \pi.$$

Domain $[-1, 1]$, range $[0, \pi]$: the upper half of the unit circle, quadrants I and II.

## Inverse tangent

Restrict tangent to the open interval $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, one full branch. The
**[[inverse tangent]]** (**[[arctangent]]**) is

$$y = \tan^{-1}x = \arctan x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tan y = x \text{ and } -\tfrac{\pi}{2} < y < \tfrac{\pi}{2}.$$

Domain all reals, range $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. The endpoints are excluded because tangent is
undefined there; the graph of $\tan^{-1}x$ has horizontal asymptotes $y = \pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

```plot
{"x": [-4, 4], "y": [-2, 3.6], "equal": true, "functions": [{"f": "asin(x)", "label": "sin⁻¹ x"}, {"f": "acos(x)", "label": "cos⁻¹ x"}, {"f": "atan(x)", "label": "tan⁻¹ x"}, {"f": "1.5708", "dashed": true}, {"f": "-1.5708", "dashed": true}], "caption": "The three inverse functions; tan⁻¹ x approaches ±π/2 (dashed)"}
```

| Function | Domain | Range | Quadrants of the answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin^{-1}x$ | $[-1, 1]$ | $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ | I, IV |
| $\cos^{-1}x$ | $[-1, 1]$ | $[0, \pi]$ | I, II |
| $\tan^{-1}x$ | all reals | $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ | I, IV |

On the unit circle the three ranges look like this. The shaded half of each circle holds every
angle the function can return; an open dot marks an endpoint that is not included.

![Three unit circles. For inverse sine, the right half of the circle is highlighted from −π/2 to π/2 with solid endpoint dots. For inverse cosine, the upper half is highlighted from 0 to π with solid dots. For inverse tangent, the right half is highlighted from −π/2 to π/2 with open endpoint dots.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Exact values

To evaluate exactly: identify the reference angle from the special values, then pick the
angle *in the range* with the right sign.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Evaluating an inverse trig function exactly
  accDescr: For inverse sine or cosine, first check that the input is between −1 and 1; if not, the value is undefined. Inverse tangent accepts any input. Next find the reference angle from the special values. If the input is not negative, the answer is the reference angle. If it is negative, inverse sine and inverse tangent give minus the reference angle (quadrant IV), and inverse cosine gives π minus the reference angle (quadrant II).
  A["Inverse sine or cosine: is the input between −1 and 1?"] -- no --> U["Undefined"]
  A -- yes --> R["Find the reference angle from the special values"]
  T["Inverse tangent: any input is allowed"] --> R
  R --> S{"Is the input negative?"}
  S -- no --> P["Answer: the reference angle"]
  S -- yes --> W{"Which function?"}
  W -- "inverse sine or tangent" --> N["Answer: minus the reference angle (quadrant IV)"]
  W -- "inverse cosine" --> C["Answer: π minus the reference angle (quadrant II)"]
```

### Example 1

Find $\sin^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac12\right)$, $\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$ and $\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt3)$.
