Angle $BAC$ is the exterior angle at $A$, which equals the sum of those two remote interior angles, so each is half of it. Triangle $BCD$ is not similar to $BCA$ (its angles are different), $CD$ is not $2\,CA$ in general, and angle $ABD$ is one of the two equal base angles, $\tfrac{\theta}{2}$, not a right angle.

questions.stem: In the golden triangle with legs 1 and apex angle $36^\circ$, the base $x$ satisfies $x^2 + x - 1 = 0$. What is $\sin 18^\circ$?
questions.explanation: $x = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2}$. The altitude from the apex splits the triangle into right triangles with an $18^\circ$ angle, hypotenuse 1 and opposite side $\tfrac{x}{2}$, so $\sin 18^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4} \approx 0.309$. ($\tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2}$ is $x$ itself, $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{4}$ is $\cos 36^\circ$, and $\tfrac{\sqrt{10 - 2\sqrt5}}{4}$ is $\sin 36^\circ$.)

questions.stem: A regular decagon (10 sides) has circumradius 4. What is its exact side length?
questions.explanation: $s = 2R\sin\tfrac{180^\circ}{10} = 8\sin 18^\circ = 8\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4} = 2(\sqrt5 - 1) \approx 2.47$. ($\sqrt5 - 1$ is half a side; $4\sin 36^\circ \approx 2.35$ uses the full central angle without the 2; $2(\sqrt5 + 1) = 8\cos 36^\circ$ uses the wrong value.)

questions.stem: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12 and hypotenuse 13, and $\theta$ is the angle opposite the leg of length 5. Using $\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj} + \text{hyp}}$, $\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} =$ ___. Give an exact fraction.
questions.explanation: $\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \tfrac{5}{12 + 13} = \tfrac{5}{25} = \tfrac15$. Check: $\theta = \tan^{-1}\tfrac{5}{12} \approx 22.62^\circ$, and $\tan 11.31^\circ \approx 0.2$.

questions.stem: The segment from the center of a regular polygon to the midpoint of a side, perpendicular to that side, is called the ___.
questions.explanation: The apothem is a leg of the polygon's right triangle; the circumradius, which goes to a vertex, is the hypotenuse.

questions.stem: The angle at the center of the small right triangle in a regular polygon is $\dfrac{180^\circ}{n}$. Match each angle to its polygon.
questions.explanation: Solve $\tfrac{180^\circ}{n} = \text{angle}$: $n = 12, 10, 8, 6, 5$. A regular nonagon ($n = 9$) gives $20^\circ$, which is not listed.

questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ has $AB = AC = 1$, apex angle $A = 36^\circ$ and base $BC = x$. Put the steps of the derivation of $x$ in order.
choices: Bisect the $72^\circ$ angle at $B$, meeting $AC$ at $D$
Triangle $BCD$ has angles $36^\circ, 72^\circ, 72^\circ$, so $BD = BC = x$
Triangle $ABD$ has two $36^\circ$ angles, so $AD = BD = x$ and $DC = 1 - x$
questions.explanation: The point $D$ must exist before anything about it can be said; $BD = x$ is needed before $AD = BD$ tells you $AD = x$; the proportion needs $DC = 1 - x$; and the quadratic comes from the proportion.

questions.stem: Let $\varphi = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2}$ be the golden ratio. Which are exactly equal to $\dfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\sin 18^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$, and $\cos 72^\circ = \sin 18^\circ$ by the cofunction identity. Also $\tfrac{1}{\varphi} = \tfrac{2}{1 + \sqrt5} = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2}$, so $\tfrac{1}{2\varphi} = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$. But $\cos 36^\circ = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{4} \approx 0.809$ and $\sin 36^\circ \approx 0.588$.

questions.stem: A regular pentagon with the right triangle used to find its side and apothem. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A regular pentagon with a dot at its center. A solid segment runs from the center to the lower right vertex, and a dashed segment runs straight down from the center to the midpoint of the bottom side, meeting it at a right angle. The small angle at the center between them is shaded. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The segment to a vertex is the circumradius $R$ (the hypotenuse); the dashed segment to the midpoint of a side is the apothem $a$; the part of the bottom side between them is $\tfrac{s}{2}$. The shaded angle lies between the radius and the apothem, so it is half of the $72^\circ$ central angle: $36^\circ$.

questions.stem: From 40 m away on level ground, the angle of elevation to the top of a pole (at eye level) is $50^\circ \pm 1^\circ$. Between what heights above eye level is the top?
questions.explanation: Compute both ends: $40\tan 49^\circ \approx 46.0$ m and $40\tan 51^\circ \approx 49.4$ m (the middle value is $40\tan 50^\circ \approx 47.7$ m). Adding $\pm 1$ m to 47.7 confuses degrees with meters; $30.2$ to $31.1$ uses sine; $32.4$ to $34.8$ divides by tangent.

questions.stem: A height is reported as $12.0 \pm 0.3$ m. What is the relative error?
questions.explanation: Relative error is absolute error divided by the value: $\tfrac{0.3}{12.0} = 0.025 = 2.5\%$. ($0.3\%$ treats the absolute error as a percent; $0.025\%$ forgets to multiply the decimal by 100; $25\%$ slips a decimal place.)

questions.stem: You measure a height with $h = d\tan\theta$ and can choose where to stand. Your angle reading has a fixed uncertainty. Which angle of elevation gives the smallest relative error in $h$?
questions.explanation: The relative error is about $\tfrac{\Delta\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$, and $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ is largest, $\tfrac12$, at $45^\circ$ (because $(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 \ge 0$). Very shallow and very steep angles are the worst.

questions.stem: With $d = 200$ m and $\theta = 30^\circ$, an angle error of $\pm 0.2^\circ$ changes $h = d\tan\theta$ by about how much? Use $\Delta h \approx \dfrac{d\,\Delta\theta}{\cos^2\theta}$.
questions.explanation: Convert to radians: $0.2^\circ = 0.2\cdot\tfrac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.003491$. Then $\Delta h \approx \tfrac{200(0.003491)}{\cos^2 30^\circ} = \tfrac{0.6981}{0.75} \approx 0.93$ m. ($53.3$ m uses degrees; $0.81$ m divides by $\cos 30^\circ$ only once; $0.52$ m multiplies by $\cos^2 30^\circ$.)

questions.stem: Which angle of elevation gives the same relative error in $h = d\tan\theta$ as $20^\circ$ does?
questions.explanation: The relative error depends on $\sin\theta\cos\theta$, which is unchanged when $\theta$ is replaced by its complement: $\sin 70^\circ\cos 70^\circ = \cos 20^\circ\sin 20^\circ$. An angle of elevation of $160^\circ$ makes no sense.

questions.stem: Your eyes are 25 m above the sea. Using $R = 6371$ km and ignoring refraction, about how far away is the horizon?
questions.explanation: $d \approx \sqrt{2Rh} = \sqrt{2(6\,371\,000)(25)} \approx 17\,848$ m $\approx 17.8$ km (or $3.57\sqrt{25} \approx 17.8$ km). $12.6$ km forgets the 2; $89.3$ km is $3.57 \times 25$ without the square root; $564$ km mixes kilometers for $R$ with meters for $h$.

questions.stem: In the triangle formed by the Earth's center $O$, an observer $P$ and the horizon point $T$, why is the right angle at $T$?
choices: The observer stands straight up, so $OP$ is perpendicular to the ground
The line of sight just touches the Earth at $T$, and a tangent line is perpendicular to the radius there
Light travels in straight lines, so every angle at the surface is $90^\circ$
The horizontal at $P$ is parallel to $OT$
questions.explanation: The line of sight to the horizon grazes the Earth, so it is tangent at $T$, and a tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. The horizontal at $P$ is perpendicular to $OP$, which is why the dip angle at $P$ equals the angle at $O$, but it is not parallel to $OT$.

questions.stem: From 200 m above sea level, the dip of the horizon is $0.454^\circ$. Estimate the Earth's radius with $R = \dfrac{h\cos\alpha}{1 - \cos\alpha}$.
questions.explanation: $\cos 0.454^\circ \approx 0.99996861$ (keep all the digits), so $R \approx \tfrac{200(0.99996861)}{0.00003139} \approx 6.37\times 10^6$ m, about 6400 km. About 25 km is $\tfrac{h}{\tan\alpha}$, the wrong formula; 3200 km is half the radius; 12,700 km is the diameter.

questions.stem: The angle between the horizontal at an observer and the line of sight to the sea horizon is called the ___ of the horizon.
questions.explanation: It is the dip of the horizon, $\alpha$, with $\cos\alpha = \tfrac{R}{R + h}$. It is tiny: under a degree even from a 500 m hill.

questions.stem: From 4 m above the sea, with $R = 6371$ km and ignoring refraction, the horizon is about ___ km away. Round to the nearest tenth.
questions.explanation: $d \approx \sqrt{2(6\,371\,000)(4)} \approx 7139$ m $\approx 7.1$ km. The rule $3.57\sqrt{h} = 3.57 \times 2 = 7.14$ km agrees.

questions.stem: The same instrument (fixed angle uncertainty) is used to measure a height with $h = d\tan\theta$. Put these angles of elevation in order from the smallest relative error in $h$ to the largest.
questions.explanation: Relative error is about $\tfrac{\Delta\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$. The values of $\tfrac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$ are $2.00$ at $45^\circ$, $2.13$ at $35^\circ$, $3.11$ at $20^\circ$ and $7.26$ at $8^\circ$: the farther from $45^\circ$, the worse.

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its formula ($R$ is the Earth's radius, $h$ the height, $\alpha$ the dip, $d$ the horizontal distance, $\theta$ the angle of elevation).
choices: h cos α divided by (1 − cos α)
d Δθ divided by cos² θ
Δθ divided by (sin θ cos θ)
questions.explanation: $d = \sqrt{(R + h)^2 - R^2} = \sqrt{2Rh + h^2}$; $\cos\alpha = \tfrac{R}{R + h}$ solves to $R = \tfrac{h\cos\alpha}{1 - \cos\alpha}$; $\Delta h \approx \tfrac{d\,\Delta\theta}{\cos^2\theta}$, and dividing by $h = d\tan\theta$ gives $\tfrac{\Delta\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$. $\tfrac{d}{\tan\theta}$ is not any of these.

questions.stem: Which statements about measuring a height with $h = d\tan\theta$ are true? Select all that apply.
choices: A 1% error in $d$ gives about a 1% error in $h$
At $45^\circ$ the relative error is about $2\,\Delta\theta$, with $\Delta\theta$ in radians
Standing very close, so the angle is steep, reduces the relative error
In $\Delta h \approx \dfrac{d\,\Delta\theta}{\cos^2\theta}$, $\Delta\theta$ must be in radians
The relative error at $10^\circ$ is much smaller than at $80^\circ$
questions.explanation: $h$ is proportional to $d$, so relative errors in $d$ pass straight through. At $45^\circ$, $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \tfrac12$, giving $2\,\Delta\theta$. The formula comes from arc length, which needs radians. Steep angles increase the error, and $10^\circ$ and $80^\circ$ are complements, so their relative errors are about the same.

questions.stem: An observer above the sea looks at the horizon (not to scale). Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A large circle for the Earth with a dot at its center. A point above the circle has a vertical segment down through the surface to the center, a dashed horizontal line to the right, and a line down to a point where it touches the circle, which is joined to the center. The angle between the dashed horizontal and the touching line is shaded, and so is the angle at the center. Five parts are numbered.

choices: Line of sight to the horizon
questions.explanation: The line of sight touches the Earth at the horizon point, where it is perpendicular to the radius. The shaded angle at the observer, down from the horizontal to the line of sight, is the dip of the horizon; it equals the shaded angle at the center. The short vertical segment above the surface is the height $h$. The dip is measured downward, so it is not an angle of elevation.

questions.stem: An angle $\theta$ is in standard position, with a point on its terminal side in quadrant II. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Coordinate axes with origin O. A thick green segment runs along the positive x-axis from O. A thick blue segment runs from O up and to the left to a dot in quadrant II, with a dashed vertical segment from that dot down to the x-axis. A curved arrow goes counterclockwise from the positive x-axis around to the blue segment. Five numbered markers: on the blue segment, on the green segment, on the dot, on the dashed segment, and on the curved arrow.

questions.explanation: The initial side lies on the positive $x$-axis (2) and the angle $\theta$ is the counterclockwise turn from it (5) to the terminal side (1). The point $(x, y)$ on the terminal side (3) is at distance $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ from the origin, and the dashed segment (4) is its distance $|y|$ from the $x$-axis. The vertex is the origin, which has no marker, and the reference angle would be the acute angle between the terminal side and the negative $x$-axis, not the big arc.

questions.stem: The point $(-5, -12)$ is on the terminal side of $\theta$. Then $r =$ ___ and $\cos\theta =$ ___. (Give exact numbers, such as fractions.)
questions.explanation: $r = \sqrt{(-5)^2 + (-12)^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13$, always positive. Then $\cos\theta = \tfrac{x}{r} = -\tfrac{5}{13}$, negative because $x < 0$ (quadrant III, where only tangent and cotangent are positive).

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding $\sin\theta$ from $\tan\theta = -\tfrac{5}{12}$ and $\cos\theta > 0$ in order.
choices: Find the quadrant where both conditions hold: quadrant IV
Choose $x = 12$ and $y = -5$, with the signs of quadrant IV
questions.explanation: The quadrant has to come first, because it decides the signs of $x$ and $y$; $r$ needs both coordinates; and $\sin\theta = \tfrac{y}{r}$ needs $r$. Tangent is negative in II and IV and cosine positive in I and IV, so the quadrant is IV.

questions.stem: Which of these values are undefined? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Undefined" means a zero denominator. At $90^\circ$ the point is $(0, 1)$, so $\tan 90^\circ = \tfrac{1}{0}$ is undefined, but $\csc 90^\circ = \tfrac{1}{1} = 1$. At $180^\circ$ the point is $(-1, 0)$, so $\cot 180^\circ = \tfrac{-1}{0}$ is undefined. At $270^\circ$ the point is $(0, -1)$, so $\sec 270^\circ = \tfrac{1}{0}$ is undefined.

questions.stem: Match each quadrant to the trig functions that are positive there.
questions.explanation: ASTC (All Students Take Calculus), counterclockwise from quadrant I. Sine has the sign of $y$ (positive in I, II), cosine the sign of $x$ (positive in I, IV), and tangent is positive where $x$ and $y$ agree (I, III). Each reciprocal shares its partner's sign. Sine and cosine are both positive only in quadrant I, where all six are.

questions.stem: Each panel shows an angle $\theta$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, with its reference angle $\theta'$ shaded. Give the formula for each numbered reference angle.

image.alt: Four panels, each with coordinate axes and an angle theta drawn as a counterclockwise arc from the positive x-axis to a terminal side. The terminal side is in quadrant I in the top-left panel, quadrant II in the top-right, quadrant III in the bottom-left and quadrant IV in the bottom-right. In each panel a shaded wedge between the terminal side and the nearest part of the x-axis is numbered 1 to 4.

questions.explanation: The reference angle is measured to the nearest part of the $x$-axis, never the $y$-axis. In quadrant I it is $\theta$ itself (1). In quadrant II the terminal side is $180^\circ - \theta$ short of the negative $x$-axis (2). In quadrant III it is $\theta - 180^\circ$ past it (3). In quadrant IV it is $360^\circ - \theta$ short of a full turn (4). Formulas with $90^\circ$ measure to the $y$-axis.

questions.stem: The reference angle of $520^\circ$ is ___ degrees. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Reduce first: $520^\circ - 360^\circ = 160^\circ$, in quadrant II. The reference angle is $180^\circ - 160^\circ = 20^\circ$. Applying a formula to $520^\circ$ directly (for example $520 - 360 = 160$, stopping there) skips the quadrant step.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding $\cos(-240^\circ)$ exactly in order.
choices: It is in quadrant II, so the reference angle is $60^\circ$
Cosine is negative in quadrant II, so $\cos(-240^\circ) = -\tfrac12$
questions.explanation: Reduce to $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$, find the quadrant and the reference angle, evaluate, and attach the sign last. Each step uses the result of the one before.

questions.stem: Which angles have a reference angle of $40^\circ$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $140^\circ$ is in quadrant II: $180^\circ - 140^\circ = 40^\circ$. $220^\circ$ is in quadrant III: $220^\circ - 180^\circ = 40^\circ$. $-320^\circ + 360^\circ = 40^\circ$, in quadrant I, so it is its own reference angle. $130^\circ$ has reference angle $180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ$; $40^\circ$ would be its distance to the $y$-axis.

questions.stem: Match each angle to its reference angle.
questions.explanation: $150^\circ$: $180 - 150 = 30$. $225^\circ$: $225 - 180 = 45$. $300^\circ$: $360 - 300 = 60$. $-100^\circ$ is coterminal with $260^\circ$, in quadrant III: $260 - 180 = 80$. ($10^\circ$ is the distance from $-100^\circ$ to the negative $y$-axis, which is the wrong axis.)

questions.stem: The dots are the special points on the unit circle. Give the angle $t$ in $[0, 2\pi)$ for each numbered point.

image.alt: The unit circle with sixteen unlabeled dots at the axis points and at every multiple of 30 and 45 degrees, each joined to the center by a thin line. Five dots are numbered: one in quadrant I close to the y-axis, one in quadrant II on the diagonal, one in quadrant III close to the x-axis, one in quadrant IV close to the y-axis, and the dot at the top of the circle.

questions.explanation: Point 1 is in quadrant I near the $y$-axis: $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($60^\circ$). Point 2 is on the quadrant II diagonal: $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ ($135^\circ$). Point 3 is in quadrant III near the $x$-axis: $\tfrac{7\pi}{6}$ ($210^\circ$). Point 4 is in quadrant IV near the $y$-axis: $\tfrac{5\pi}{3}$ ($300^\circ$). Point 5 is the top of the circle, $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Denominator 6 is near the $x$-axis, 3 near the $y$-axis, 4 on a diagonal.

questions.stem: The terminal point of $t = \tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is $(x, y)$ with $x =$ ___ and $y =$ ___. (Type square roots as sqrt, for example sqrt(2)/2.)
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{5\pi}{6} = \pi - \tfrac{\pi}{6}$ is in quadrant II, near the $x$-axis (denominator 6), so $|x| = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the big coordinate and $|y| = \tfrac12$ the small one. In quadrant II, $x < 0$ and $y > 0$: the point is $\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tfrac12\right)$.

questions.stem: Match each number $t$ to its terminal point on the unit circle.
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{7\pi}{4} = 2\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{4}$: quadrant IV diagonal. $\tfrac{2\pi}{3} = \pi - \tfrac{\pi}{3}$: quadrant II near the $y$-axis, so $|x| = \tfrac12$. $\tfrac{11\pi}{6} = 2\pi - \tfrac{\pi}{6}$: quadrant IV near the $x$-axis, so $|y| = \tfrac12$. $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is the bottom of the circle. The extra point $\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\right)$ belongs to $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every real number $t$ where the expressions are defined? Select all that apply.
choices: $\tan t$ is the slope of the line through the origin and the terminal point of $t$
The terminal point of $-t$ is $(\cos t, \sin t)$
questions.explanation: The terminal point $(\cos t, \sin t)$ is on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$, which gives the identity, and both coordinates of a point on the unit circle lie between $-1$ and $1$. The slope of the line through $(0, 0)$ and $(x, y)$ is $\tfrac{y}{x} = \tan t$. Walking $t$ in the opposite direction reflects the point across the $x$-axis, so the terminal point of $-t$ is $(\cos t, -\sin t)$.

questions.stem: Put these values in order from least to greatest.
questions.explanation: Read each from the circle: $\cos\pi = -1$, $\sin\tfrac{7\pi}{6} = -\tfrac12$, $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac12$, $\cos\tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} \approx 0.866$ and $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = 1$. All five values are different, so there is only one order.

questions.stem: Match each function to its period.
questions.explanation: Sine, cosine, secant and cosecant repeat after a full turn, $2\pi$. Tangent and cotangent repeat after half a turn, $\pi$: the point at $t + \pi$ is $(-x, -y)$, and the ratios $\tfrac{y}{x}$ and $\tfrac{x}{y}$ don't change.

questions.stem: Which of these functions are odd? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The points for $t$ and $-t$ are $(x, y)$ and $(x, -y)$. Sine ($y$) changes sign, so it is odd, and so is cotangent ($\tfrac{x}{y}$). Cosine ($x$) does not change, so it is even, and so is its reciprocal, secant. Only cosine and secant are even.

questions.stem: $\sin\left(-\tfrac{17\pi}{6}\right) =$ ___ (exact value).
questions.explanation: Strip whole periods: $-\tfrac{17\pi}{6} + 4\pi = \tfrac{7\pi}{6}$, in quadrant III near the $x$-axis, so $\sin\tfrac{7\pi}{6} = -\tfrac12$. (Or use oddness first: $-\sin\tfrac{17\pi}{6} = -\sin\tfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\tfrac12$. Both routes agree.)

questions.stem: Match each function to its range.
questions.explanation: Sine and cosine are coordinates of points on the unit circle, so they take every value in $[-1, 1]$. Tangent is a slope and takes every real value. Secant is $\tfrac{1}{\cos t}$, the reciprocal of a number between $-1$ and $1$ (not 0), so its absolute value is at least 1: the range is $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$.

questions.stem: Is $f(x) = \sin x \tan x$ even, odd or neither?
questions.explanation: $f(-x) = \sin(-x)\tan(-x) = (-\sin x)(-\tan x) = \sin x\tan x = f(x)$, so $f$ is even. A product of two odd functions is even, just as $(-1)(-1) = 1$. Only the zero function is both even and odd.

questions.stem: In this unit-circle picture, $\theta$ is the angle at $O$, $P$ is on the circle, and the dashed lines are the tangent lines $x = 1$ and $y = 1$. Name the length of each numbered segment.

image.alt: A quarter of the unit circle with angle theta at the origin O. P is on the circle and M directly below it on the x-axis. The ray from O through P meets the dashed vertical line x = 1 at T (above A) and the dashed horizontal line y = 1 at C (right of B). Numbered segments: 1 is PM, 2 is OM, 3 is AT, 4 is BC, 5 is a bracket beside the ray from O to T on its upper-left side, 6 is a bracket beside the ray from O to C on its lower-right side.

questions.explanation: Triangle $OMP$ has hypotenuse 1, so $MP = \sin\theta$ (1) and $OM = \cos\theta$ (2). On the tangent line $x = 1$, triangle $OAT$ with $OA = 1$ gives $AT = \tan\theta$ (3) and $OT = \sec\theta$ (5). On the tangent line $y = 1$, triangle $OBC$ with $OB = 1$ gives $BC = \cot\theta$ (4) and $OC = \csc\theta$ (6). The versine would be $MA$ and the exsecant $PT$; neither is marked.

questions.stem: Why is the tangent function called the "tangent"?
choices: Because it measures how steeply the graph of sine rises
Because it is the ratio of the two legs of a right triangle
Because $\tan\theta$ is the length of a segment on the line tangent to the unit circle at $(1, 0)$
Because it is the cofunction of the cotangent
questions.explanation: The ray at angle $\theta$ meets the line $x = 1$, which touches the unit circle only at $A = (1, 0)$, at the point $T = (1, \tan\theta)$. The segment $AT$ on that tangent line has length $\tan\theta$, and the name comes from it. Similarly, $OT = \sec\theta$ lies on a line that cuts the circle (Latin secare, "to cut").

questions.stem: For $\theta = 30^\circ$, the ray from the origin at angle $\theta$ meets the line $x = 1$ at $T$. What are the coordinates of $T$?
questions.explanation: $T = (1, \tan\theta)$ and $\tan 30^\circ = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$. The height $\tfrac12$ is $\sin 30^\circ$, the height of $P$ on the circle, not of $T$; $\sqrt3 = \tan 60^\circ$; and $\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}, \tfrac12\right)$ is $P$ itself.

questions.stem: In the unit-circle picture with $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$, the tangent segment is $AT = \tfrac34$. Then the secant segment is $OT =$ ___.
questions.explanation: Triangle $OAT$ is right-angled at $A$ with legs $OA = 1$ and $AT = \tfrac34$, so $OT = \sqrt{1 + \tfrac{9}{16}} = \sqrt{\tfrac{25}{16}} = \tfrac54$. This is $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$ in action.

questions.stem: Applying the Pythagorean theorem to which triangle in the picture gives $1 + \cot^2\theta = \csc^2\theta$?
questions.explanation: Triangle $OBC$ has a right angle at $B$, legs $OB = 1$ and $BC = \cot\theta$, and hypotenuse $OC = \csc\theta$. Triangle $OMP$ gives $\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1$, triangle $OAT$ gives $1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$, and triangle $OAP$ has no right angle.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every $\theta$ strictly between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Triangle $OAT$ is triangle $OMP$ enlarged by the factor $\tfrac{1}{\cos\theta} > 1$, so $AT = \tan\theta$ is longer than $MP = \sin\theta$. $OT = \sec\theta$ is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with a leg of length 1, so it is more than 1. But $\tan\theta < 1$ and $\sin\theta < \cos\theta$ both fail for angles above $45^\circ$ (for example $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt3$).

questions.stem: For $\theta = 120^\circ$, where does the line through the origin and $P = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ meet the line $x = 1$?
choices: At $(1, \sqrt3)$, above the $x$-axis, on the ray through $P$
At $(1, -\sqrt3)$, on the ray extended backward through the origin, away from $P$
At $(1, -\sqrt3)$, on the ray through $P$, beyond $P$
At $(-1, \sqrt3)$, on the ray through $P$, beyond $P$
questions.explanation: The meeting point is $T = (1, \tan 120^\circ) = (1, -\sqrt3)$. $P = \left(-\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$ is to the left of the origin, and $T$ is to the right of it, so $T$ is on the backward extension. That is why $\sec 120^\circ = -2$ is negative: $T = \sec\theta\cdot P = -2P$. A point with $x = -1$ is not on the line $x = 1$ at all.

questions.stem: In the unit-circle picture, what is the geometric reason that $\tan 90^\circ$ is undefined?
choices: At $90^\circ$ the point $P$ is not on the unit circle
At $90^\circ$ the tangent segment has length 0
At $90^\circ$ the triangle $OMP$ has no hypotenuse
At $90^\circ$ the ray is vertical, parallel to the line $x = 1$, so it never meets it
questions.explanation: $T$ is where the ray meets the tangent line $x = 1$. As $\theta$ approaches $90^\circ$, $T$ climbs without bound; at $90^\circ$ the ray points straight up along the $y$-axis, parallel to $x = 1$, and there is no point $T$. The point $P = (0, 1)$ is still on the circle, and $\tan 0^\circ = 0$ is the case of a zero-length segment.

questions.stem: In a circle of radius 10, the chord cut off by a central angle of $120^\circ$ has length ___ (exact, or to 2 decimal places; type square roots as sqrt).
questions.explanation: A chord of central angle $\theta$ in a circle of radius $R$ has length $2R\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}$, so this one is $20\sin 60^\circ = 20\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$. Using $2R\sin\theta$ instead gives the same number here only by coincidence ($\sin 120^\circ = \sin 60^\circ$); the half-angle is what the geometry calls for.

questions.stem: Ptolemy's chord table used a circle of radius 60. In that circle, the chord of a central angle $2x$ equals:
questions.explanation: The chord of central angle $\theta$ in radius $R$ is $2R\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}$. With $R = 60$ and $\theta = 2x$, that is $120\sin x$. So a chord table is a sine table in disguise: $\sin x = \tfrac{\text{crd}\,2x}{120}$. For example, the chord of $60^\circ$ is 60 (an equilateral triangle), and $\tfrac{60}{120} = \tfrac12 = \sin 30^\circ$.

questions.stem: Match each older trig function (for a unit circle) to its formula.
left: Jya of θ (half the chord of 2θ)
questions.explanation: The versine is the segment $MA$ from the foot of the sine to the circle, $1 - \cos\theta$. The exsecant is the part $PT$ of the secant outside the circle, $\sec\theta - 1$. The chord of $\theta$ splits into two half-chords, each $\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}$, so it is $2\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}$. The Indian jya of an angle $\theta$ is half the chord of the doubled angle $2\theta$, which is $\sin\theta$: the sine itself.

questions.stem: Put these steps in the history of the trig functions in chronological order.
choices: Hipparchus compiles a table of chords
Ptolemy's Almagest gives chords in half-degree steps
Latin translators turn the Arabic jiba into sinus
Thomas Fincke names the tangent and the secant
questions.explanation: Hipparchus worked in the 2nd century BC and Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD. Indian half-chord tables appear by about 500 AD (Aryabhata wrote in 499). The Latin word sinus comes from 12th-century translations of Arabic works. Fincke introduced "tangent" and "secant" in his book Geometria rotundi (1583).

questions.stem: In the unit-circle picture ($O$ the origin, $P$ on the circle at angle $\theta$, $M$ below $P$ on the $x$-axis, $A = (1, 0)$, $T$ where ray $OP$ meets $x = 1$), which segment has length $\text{exsec}\,\theta = \sec\theta - 1$?
questions.explanation: $OT = \sec\theta$ and $OP = 1$, so the part of the ray between $P$ and $T$, outside the circle, is $\sec\theta - 1$. $MA = 1 - \cos\theta$ is the versine, $AT$ is the tangent and $OT$ the whole secant.

questions.stem: A circular arch has radius 5 m and spans a central angle of $40^\circ$. How high does the middle of the arch rise above the chord joining its ends (to the nearest hundredth)?
questions.explanation: The center is $5\cos 20^\circ \approx 4.70$ m from the chord (half the angle, since the radius to the middle of the arch bisects it). The rise is the rest of the radius: $5 - 5\cos 20^\circ = 5\,\text{versin}\,20^\circ \approx 0.30$ m. $1.71$ m is $5\sin 20^\circ$, half the chord, and $1.17$ m comes from using the full $40^\circ$ instead of $20^\circ$.

questions.stem: Which inequality holds for every $t$ with $0 < t < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$?
questions.explanation: The triangle $OAP$ (area $\tfrac12\sin t$) lies inside the sector of angle $t$ (area $\tfrac12 t$), which lies inside triangle $OAT$ (area $\tfrac12\tan t$). Doubling gives $\sin t < t < \tan t$. For example, at $t = 0.5$: $0.479 < 0.5 < 0.546$.

questions.stem: For $0 < t < \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, with $O$ the origin, $A = (1, 0)$, $P = (\cos t, \sin t)$ and $T = (1, \tan t)$, put these regions in order from smallest area to largest.
questions.explanation: Their areas are $\tfrac12\sin t$, $\tfrac12 t$ and $\tfrac12\tan t$, and each region lies inside the next. This nesting is the proof that $\sin t < t < \tan t$.

questions.stem: With $t$ in radians, as $t$ approaches 0 the ratio $\tfrac{\sin t}{t}$ approaches ___.
questions.explanation: From $\sin t < t < \tan t$, dividing by $\sin t$ and taking reciprocals gives $\cos t < \tfrac{\sin t}{t} < 1$. As $t \to 0$, $\cos t \to 1$, so the ratio is squeezed to 1.

questions.stem: If $x$ is measured in degrees, what does $\dfrac{\sin x^\circ}{x}$ approach as $x$ approaches 0?
questions.explanation: $\sin x^\circ = \sin\tfrac{\pi x}{180}$, and for small angles that is about $\tfrac{\pi x}{180}$. Dividing by $x$ leaves $\tfrac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.01745$. The limit is 1 only in radians, which is a main reason calculus uses radians.

questions.stem: Use $\cos t \approx 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$ to estimate $\cos 0.1$: ___ (give the estimate exactly as a decimal).
questions.explanation: $1 - \tfrac{0.1^2}{2} = 1 - \tfrac{0.01}{2} = 1 - 0.005 = 0.995$. The true value is $0.995004\ldots$, a little above the estimate, as it always is.

questions.stem: Which approximations have a relative error under 1%? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\sin 0.1 \approx 0.09983$: relative error about 0.17%. $\sin 10^\circ \approx 0.17365$ and $10^\circ \approx 0.17453$ radians: about 0.51%. But $\tan 0.3 \approx 0.30934$: about 3.0%. And $\sin 1 \approx 0.841$: about 19%, because 1 radian (about $57^\circ$) is not a small angle.

questions.stem: What is the relative error of the approximation $\tan t \approx t$ at $t = 0.2$, to the nearest hundredth of a percent? ($\tan 0.2 \approx 0.20271$.)
questions.explanation: The error is $0.20271 - 0.2 = 0.00271$, and dividing by the true value gives $\tfrac{0.00271}{0.20271} \approx 0.0134 = 1.34\%$. The rule of thumb $\tfrac{t^2}{3} = \tfrac{0.04}{3} \approx 1.33\%$ agrees. 0.27% treats the absolute error 0.0027 as a percent, and 0.67% is the error of $\sin t \approx t$ at the same $t$.

questions.stem: Why is the small-angle approximation for cosine $\cos t \approx 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$, with a square, rather than something like $1 - t$?
choices: Because cosine is an odd function
Because $1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2\tfrac{t}{2}$, the square of a small number, which is about $\tfrac{t^2}{2}$
Because $\cos t$ is always less than $1 - t$
Because the chord from $(1, 0)$ to $(\cos t, \sin t)$ has length $\tfrac{t^2}{2}$
questions.explanation: The chord from $A$ to $P$ has squared length $2 - 2\cos t$ and length $2\sin\tfrac{t}{2}$, so $1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2\tfrac{t}{2} \approx 2\left(\tfrac{t}{2}\right)^2 = \tfrac{t^2}{2}$. Cosine is even, not odd, which is another way to see that no $t$ term can appear. $\cos t < 1 - t$ is false (at $t = 0.5$, $0.878 > 0.5$), and the chord's length is about $t$, not $\tfrac{t^2}{2}$.

questions.stem: Calculus shows how big the error of each small-angle approximation is. Match each approximation to the approximate size of its error.
questions.explanation: The sine and tangent errors are cubes, with tangent's twice sine's (so tangent's relative error, about $\tfrac{t^2}{3}$, is twice sine's, about $\tfrac{t^2}{6}$). The cosine estimate already includes the $\tfrac{t^2}{2}$ term, so what is left is much smaller, about $\tfrac{t^4}{24}$.

questions.stem: Use a small-angle approximation to estimate $\sin 3^\circ$.
questions.explanation: Convert first: $3^\circ = \tfrac{3\pi}{180} \approx 0.05236$ radians, so $\sin 3^\circ \approx 0.0524$ (the true value is $0.05234$). The answer 3 forgets to convert (a sine can't exceed 1), $0.1411$ is $\sin 3$ with 3 in radians, and $0.0167$ is $\tfrac{3}{180}$, which drops the factor $\pi$.

questions.stem: Given $\sin 0.2 \approx 0.19867$, find $\dfrac{\sin(-0.2)}{-0.2}$.
questions.explanation: Sine is odd, so $\sin(-0.2) = -0.19867$, and $\tfrac{-0.19867}{-0.2} = 0.9933$. The ratio $\tfrac{\sin t}{t}$ is even, so it has the same value at $0.2$ and $-0.2$, and it is close to 1 as the squeeze predicts.

questions.stem: Because $\sin t$ and $t$ are both odd functions, the ratio $\dfrac{\sin t}{t}$ is an ___ function.
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{\sin(-t)}{-t} = \tfrac{-\sin t}{-t} = \tfrac{\sin t}{t}$: the minus signs cancel, so the ratio is even (its graph is symmetric about the vertical axis). That is why the squeeze for positive $t$ also covers negative $t$.

questions.stem: Which statement is true for every real number $t$?
questions.explanation: For $|t| \ge \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $|\sin t| \le 1 < |t|$; for smaller $|t|$ it follows from $\sin t < t$ on $\left(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and oddness. The others fail: $\sin(-1) \approx -0.841 > -1$; $\tan 2 \approx -2.185 < 2$; and $\cos t \ge 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$, not $\le$ (at $t = 0.5$, $0.878 > 0.875$).

questions.stem: Estimate $1 - \cos 0.2$ without a calculator.
questions.explanation: $1 - \cos t \approx \tfrac{t^2}{2} = \tfrac{0.04}{2} = 0.02$ (true value $0.01993$). $0.2$ treats $1 - \cos t$ like $t$, $0.04$ forgets to halve, and $0.01$ halves twice.

questions.stem: The picture shows how the unit circle unrolls into the graph of $y = \sin x$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: On the left, the unit circle with a point in quadrant I, a thick arc from (1, 0) to the point, and a right triangle with a horizontal leg and a vertical leg. On the right, one cycle of the sine graph, with a dashed line carrying the height of the circle point across to a point on the graph. Five parts are numbered.

choices: Point (t, sin t) on the graph
Point (cos t, t) on the graph
questions.explanation: The point on the circle is $(\cos t, \sin t)$: its horizontal leg has length $\cos t$ and its vertical leg (its height) has length $\sin t$. It got there by traveling an arc of length $t$ from $(1, 0)$, because on the unit circle arc length equals the angle in radians. On the graph the input is that arc length, so the matching point is $(t, \sin t)$, at the same height as the circle point. Swapping sine and cosine is the usual mistake: sine is the vertical one.

questions.stem: On $[0, 2\pi]$, the graph of $y = \cos x$ reaches its minimum value ___ at $x =$ ___. (Type pi for $\pi$.)
questions.explanation: Cosine is the horizontal coordinate of the unit-circle point. It is smallest, $-1$, when the point is at $(-1, 0)$, a half turn: $x = \pi$. The key points of one cycle are $(0, 1), (\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0), (\pi, -1), (\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, 0), (2\pi, 1)$. ($\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is where sine has its minimum.)

questions.stem: Follow the graph of $y = -2\cos x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\pi$. Put the points it passes through in order.
choices: A zero where it is rising
A zero where it is falling
questions.explanation: Multiply the cosine key points by $-2$: $(0, -2)$, $(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 0)$, $(\pi, 2)$, $(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, 0)$, $(2\pi, -2)$. The graph starts at its minimum because the negative factor flips cosine upside down, rises through the zero at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ to the maximum at $\pi$, falls through the zero at $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, and is back at the minimum at $2\pi$.

questions.stem: Which statements about the graph of $y = \sin x$ are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its zeros are at $x = k\pi$ for every integer $k$
questions.explanation: Sine's values run from $-1$ to $1$, it is zero at every multiple of $\pi$, and it peaks at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and every full turn after that. It is not symmetric about the $y$-axis: sine is odd, so its graph is symmetric about the origin (cosine is the even one). Its period is $2\pi$, not $\pi$: after $\pi$ units the graph is upside down.

questions.stem: Match each function to how its graph starts at $x = 0$.
questions.explanation: Sine starts on the axis going up; a negative factor makes it go down first. Cosine starts at its maximum; a negative factor turns that into a minimum. All four have amplitude 3 (amplitude is never negative), so "maximum −3" describes none of them.

questions.stem: The picture shows $y = A\sin\big(B(x - C)\big) + D$ with $A > 0$ and $C > 0$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A sine-shaped wave with a dashed horizontal line through its middle. Five parts are numbered: a short double arrow from the y-axis to where a cycle starts, the dashed line, a vertical double arrow from the dashed line up to a peak, a long double arrow along the bottom covering one full cycle, and a double arrow above the curve from the start of the cycle to the first peak.

questions.explanation: The phase shift $C$ is the horizontal distance from the $y$-axis to the start of a cycle, where the curve crosses the midline going up. The midline is the line $y = D$ through the middle of the wave. The amplitude $|A|$ is measured from the midline up to a peak. The period $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$ is the length of one full cycle, and a quarter of it takes the curve from the start to the first maximum. Frequency is a number (cycles per unit), not a length on the picture, and a sinusoid has no asymptotes.

questions.stem: For $y = 4\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{5}x - \pi\right) - 2$: the amplitude is ___, the period is ___, the phase shift is ___ units to the right, and the midline is $y =$ ___. Give numbers only.
questions.explanation: Factor $B = \tfrac{\pi}{5}$ out of the argument: $\tfrac{\pi}{5}x - \pi = \tfrac{\pi}{5}(x - 5)$. So the amplitude is $|4| = 4$, the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/5} = 10$, the phase shift is 5 to the right, and the midline is $y = -2$. Reading the shift as $\pi$ from the unfactored form is the classic mistake.

questions.stem: Put the steps for graphing $y = 2\sin(4x + \pi) + 1$ in order.
choices: Read amplitude 2, period $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, phase shift $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ left, midline $y = 1$
Split that cycle into quarters of length $\tfrac{\pi}{8}$
Plot midline, max, midline, min, midline at the five $x$-values and join smoothly
questions.explanation: Each step needs the one before it. The phase shift can only be read after factoring. The cycle runs from the phase shift $-\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ to $-\tfrac{\pi}{4} + \tfrac{\pi}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$, so you need the shift and the period first. The quarter points split that cycle, and the sine pattern (heights $1, 3, 1, -1, 1$) is placed at those five $x$-values last.

questions.stem: Which functions have period $\pi$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The period is $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$, so period $\pi$ means $B = 2$. That is true of $\sin 2x$, $3\cos(2x - 1)$ and $-\sin(2x) + 5$; the amplitude, the phase shift and the vertical shift don't change the period. $\sin(x + \pi)$ has $B = 1$ and period $2\pi$ (the $+\pi$ is a shift), and $\cos\tfrac{x}{2}$ has period $\tfrac{2\pi}{1/2} = 4\pi$.

questions.stem: Match each function to its phase shift.
questions.explanation: Factor out $B$ and read $C$ from $B(x - C)$. $x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}$: $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ right. $2x + \tfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$: $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$ left. $2x - \pi = 2\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$: $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ right. $3x + \pi = 3\left(x + \tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$: $\tfrac{\pi}{3}$ left. "$\pi$ to the left" is what you get for the last one if you forget to factor.

questions.stem: The picture shows one branch of $y = \tan x$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: One rising branch of the tangent graph between two dashed vertical lines, one on each side of the y-axis. Five parts are numbered: the left dashed line, the right dashed line, the point where the curve crosses the origin, a point on the curve to the right of the origin, and a point on the curve to the left of it.

questions.explanation: Tangent is undefined where $\cos x = 0$, so the branch is fenced in by asymptotes at $x = -\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (left) and $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (right). It crosses the origin because $\tan 0 = 0$, and halfway to each asymptote it passes through $(\tfrac{\pi}{4}, 1)$ and $(-\tfrac{\pi}{4}, -1)$. $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ is $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, not $\tan\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, and the branch has no maximum: it rises without bound.

questions.stem: For $y = \tan\tfrac{\pi x}{4}$, the period is ___, and the first vertical asymptote to the right of the origin is $x =$ ___. Give numbers only.
questions.explanation: Tangent's period is $\tfrac{\pi}{B} = \dfrac{\pi}{\pi/4} = 4$. The branch through the origin has its asymptotes where the input is $\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$: $\tfrac{\pi x}{4} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ gives $x = 2$. (Using $\tfrac{2\pi}{B}$ would give the wrong period 8.)

questions.stem: Match each feature to the function it describes.
questions.explanation: $\tan x = \tfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is zero where $\sin x = 0$ (at $k\pi$) and has asymptotes where $\cos x = 0$ (at $\tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$). $\cot x = \tfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ swaps those roles, so its asymptotes are at $k\pi$. Tangent rises on every branch and cotangent falls on every branch.

questions.stem: Which statements about $y = 3\tan(2x)$ are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It has a vertical asymptote at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$
Its range is all real numbers
questions.explanation: Period: $\tfrac{\pi}{B} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Asymptotes where $2x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, so $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$ is one. Like every tangent graph its range is all real numbers. It has no amplitude (3 only stretches it), and it cannot pass through a point at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$, since it is undefined there. (It passes through $\left(\tfrac{\pi}{8}, 3\right)$.)

questions.stem: Put these values in order from smallest to largest (angles in radians).
questions.explanation: $0.5$ and $1.4$ are in $(0, \tfrac{\pi}{2})$, where tangent is positive and increasing, so $\tan 0.5 \approx 0.546 < \tan 1.4 \approx 5.80$. $2$ and $3$ are in $(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi)$, quadrant II, where tangent is negative. That piece of the next branch is also increasing, so $\tan 2 \approx -2.19 < \tan 3 \approx -0.14$. The two negative values come first.

questions.stem: The picture shows $y = \sec x$ drawn from $y = \cos x$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A dashed wave and a set of U-shaped solid branches separated by dashed vertical lines. Five parts are numbered: a point on the dashed wave, one dashed vertical line, a branch opening upward, a branch opening downward, and a point where a branch touches the dashed wave.

questions.explanation: The dashed wave is the guide $y = \cos x$. Where it crosses the axis, $\sec x = \tfrac{1}{\cos x}$ is undefined, giving vertical asymptotes. Above each cosine peak a branch opens up, and below each valley a branch opens down; each branch touches the guide at its vertex, such as $(0, 1)$, where $\cos x = \sec x = \pm1$. Secant has no zeros (a reciprocal is never 0) and no horizontal asymptote.

questions.stem: The range of $y = 2\sec x - 1$ is $(-\infty,$ ___ $] \cup [$ ___ $, \infty)$. Give numbers only.
questions.explanation: The guide $y = 2\cos x - 1$ has midline $y = -1$ and amplitude 2, so its maximum is 1 and its minimum is $-3$. The secant branches turn at those heights and head away from the midline: $(-\infty, -3] \cup [1, \infty)$.

questions.stem: Move along the graph of $y = \csc x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 2\pi$. Put the features in the order you meet them.
questions.explanation: $\csc x = \tfrac{1}{\sin x}$ has asymptotes where $\sin x = 0$: at $0$, $\pi$ and $2\pi$. Between $0$ and $\pi$ sine is positive with peak 1 at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so cosecant has an upward branch with local minimum $(\tfrac{\pi}{2}, 1)$. Between $\pi$ and $2\pi$ sine is negative with valley $-1$ at $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$, giving a downward branch with local maximum $(\tfrac{3\pi}{2}, -1)$.

questions.stem: Which values can $\sec x$ take? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $\sec x = \tfrac{1}{\cos x}$ with $\cos x$ in $[-1, 1]$ and never 0, so $|\sec x| \ge 1$: the range is $(-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)$. $-3$ (when $\cos x = -\tfrac13$), $1$ (at $x = 0$) and $-1$ (at $x = \pi$) all occur. $0.5$ would need $\cos x = 2$, and $0$ would need $\tfrac{1}{\cos x} = 0$, which never happens.

questions.stem: Match each function to its range.
questions.explanation: For $A\sec(\cdot) + D$ or $A\csc(\cdot) + D$ the range is $(-\infty, D - |A|] \cup [D + |A|, \infty)$. $\sec x$: $D = 0$, $|A| = 1$. $3\csc x$: $\pm3$. $\sec x + 2$: $2 \pm 1$, so 1 and 3. $2\csc x - 1$: $-1 \pm 2$, so $-3$ and 1. $[-1, 1]$ is the range of sine and cosine, the one set of values secant and cosecant mostly avoid.

questions.stem: A rider's height on this Ferris wheel is modeled by $h(t) = 30 - 25\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right)$. Name the numbered parts by the role each plays in the model.

image.alt: A Ferris wheel beside a height scale marked 0, 5, 30 and 55 m. Five parts are numbered: the hub, the red spoke from the hub down to the rider, the rider at the bottom of the wheel, the top of the wheel, and the ground.

questions.explanation: The hub's height, 30 m, is the midline $D$, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. The radius, 25 m, is the amplitude: the farthest the rider gets from the hub's height. The rider boards at the bottom, the minimum $30 - 25 = 5$ m, which is why the model uses $-\cos$; the top is the maximum $30 + 25 = 55$ m. Heights are measured from the ground. The period (4 minutes) is a time, not a length on the wheel.

questions.stem: A buoy rides the waves between 1.2 m and 3.6 m above the sea floor. In a sinusoidal model of its height, the midline is $y =$ ___ and the amplitude is ___. Give numbers only.
questions.explanation: Midline: $\dfrac{\max + \min}{2} = \dfrac{3.6 + 1.2}{2} = 2.4$. Amplitude: $\dfrac{\max - \min}{2} = \dfrac{3.6 - 1.2}{2} = 1.2$. (2.4 is also the full max-to-min distance; the amplitude is half of it.)

questions.stem: A mass on a spring moves 5 cm from equilibrium at most, with up positive and angular frequency $\omega$. Match each start at $t = 0$ to its model.
left: Released from rest 5 cm above equilibrium
Released from rest 5 cm below equilibrium
questions.explanation: Cosine starts at its maximum, so it fits a release from the highest point; $-\cos$ starts at the minimum, a release from below. Sine starts at 0 heading up, so it fits a mass passing equilibrium on the way up; $-\sin$ starts at 0 heading down. Displacement is measured from equilibrium, so no $+5$ shift belongs in any of these models.

questions.stem: A model of average monthly highs is $T(t) = 12\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{6}(t - 7)\right) + 60$, with $t = 1$ for January. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The lowest average high comes at $t = 1$
questions.explanation: The midline is $T = 60$ and the amplitude is 12, so the maximum is $60 + 12 = 72$ and the minimum is 48. The period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6} = 12$. The cosine peaks at $t = 7$ (July), and the minimum is half a period away, at $t = 7 - 6 = 1$ (January). 24 is the max-to-min distance, twice the amplitude, and 12 is the amplitude, not the midline.

questions.stem: A rider boards a Ferris wheel at the bottom at $t = 0$, and the wheel turns once every 8 minutes. Put the rider's positions in order of time during the first ride around.
choices: At the height of the hub, rising
At the height of the hub, descending
questions.explanation: The height is $h(t) = D - r\cos\!\left(\tfrac{2\pi}{8}t\right)$: minimum at $t = 0$, the midline (hub height) going up at $t = 2$, the maximum at $t = 4$, the midline going down at $t = 6$, and the minimum again at $t = 8$. Each step is a quarter of the 8-minute period.

questions.stem: What is the smallest period of $y = \sin\tfrac{\pi x}{2} + \cos\tfrac{\pi x}{3}$?
questions.explanation: The periods are $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/2} = 4$ and $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/3} = 6$. Their ratio is $\tfrac46 = \tfrac23$, so the least common multiple is $3 \cdot 4 = 2 \cdot 6 = 12$. After 12 units the first term has done 3 cycles and the second 2. The two terms have different frequencies, so nothing shorter works. (24 is the product of the periods and 10 their sum; neither is how periods combine.)

questions.stem: What is the smallest period of $y = \sin 3x + \cos 2x$?
questions.explanation: The periods are $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\pi$. Their ratio is $\dfrac{2\pi/3}{\pi} = \tfrac23$, so $L = 3 \cdot \tfrac{2\pi}{3} = 2 \cdot \pi = 2\pi$. $\tfrac{2\pi^2}{3}$ multiplies the periods and $\tfrac{5\pi}{3}$ adds them. After only $\pi$ the $\sin 3x$ term is half a cycle off, so $\pi$ is not a period.

questions.stem: Which function is not periodic?
questions.explanation: $\sin x$ has period $2\pi$ and $\sin(\pi x)$ has period $\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi} = 2$. Their ratio, $\pi$, is irrational, so no length is a whole number of both periods and the sum never repeats. The others are periodic: $\sin x + \cos 2x$ and $\sin 2x + \cos 3x$ both repeat every $2\pi$, and $|\sin x|$ repeats every $\pi$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $y = x + \sin x$ at $x = \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$?
questions.explanation: Add the ordinates: the line gives $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ and $\sin\tfrac{3\pi}{2} = -1$, so $y = \tfrac{3\pi}{2} - 1 \approx 3.71$. The graph is one unit below the line $y = x$ there, its farthest point below the line. ($-1$ forgets the line; $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ is where $\sin x = 0$ would put it.)

questions.stem: On $[0, 2\pi]$, where does the graph of $y = \sin x + \sin 2x$ meet the graph of $y = \sin x$?
choices: Nowhere, because the two graphs are different
questions.explanation: The two graphs meet exactly where the added term $\sin 2x$ is zero: $2x = k\pi$, so $x = \tfrac{k\pi}{2}$. On $[0, 2\pi]$ that is $0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}, 2\pi$. Only $0, \pi, 2\pi$ are the zeros of $\sin x$, which is a different question. At $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, $\sin 2x = 1$, so the sum is a full unit above $\sin x$ there.

questions.stem: Which pair of curves is the envelope of $y = e^{-0.5x}\sin(4x)$, the curves its graph stays between and touches?
questions.explanation: Since $-1 \le \sin(4x) \le 1$ and $e^{-0.5x} > 0$, the product stays between $-e^{-0.5x}$ and $e^{-0.5x}$, and it touches them wherever $\sin(4x) = \pm1$: that is its envelope. The 4 inside the sine changes how fast the graph swings, not how high, so $\pm4e^{-0.5x}$ is too wide (never touched) and $\pm4$ makes no sense. $\pm1$ does not shrink with the swings, and for $x < 0$ the graph goes beyond it.

questions.stem: For $x > 0$, where does the graph of $y = x\sin x$ touch the line $y = x$? ($k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$)
questions.explanation: $x\sin x = x$ with $x > 0$ means $\sin x = 1$, so $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + 2k\pi$. At $\tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$ with $k$ odd, $\sin x = -1$, and the graph touches the lower envelope $y = -x$ instead. At $k\pi$ the graph is zero, crossing the axis.

questions.stem: The graph of $y = x\sin x$ touches $y = x$ at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Where is its first local maximum for $x > 0$?
choices: Exactly at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, since that is where $\sin x = 1$
A little to the left, near $x \approx 1.2$
A little to the right, near $x \approx 2.03$
At $x = \pi$, where the graph meets the axis
questions.explanation: After $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$, $\sin x$ starts to decrease, but slowly at first, while the factor $x$ keeps growing, so the product keeps rising for a while. The first peak is near $x \approx 2.029$, height about $1.820$, which is above the touching point's height $\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.571$ but still below the envelope there. At $\pi$ the graph is 0.

questions.stem: A damped vibration is $y = 5e^{-0.1t}\cos(\pi t)$. When has its envelope fallen to half its starting height?
questions.explanation: The envelope is $5e^{-0.1t}$, starting at 5. Set $e^{-0.1t} = \tfrac12$: $-0.1t = \ln\tfrac12$, so $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.1} \approx 6.93$. $0.69$ forgets to divide by 0.1, and $3.47$ uses 0.2. The cosine factor doesn't affect when the envelope halves.

questions.stem: As $x$ gets closer and closer to 0 (in radians), what happens to $\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$?
questions.explanation: The formula is undefined at 0, but the values settle down: about 0.9983 at $x = 0.1$ and 0.99998 at $x = 0.01$. They approach 1 (the Module 3 honors lesson on small angles proves it). The value $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$ would appear if $x$ were measured in degrees.

questions.stem: The function $y = \sin\tfrac{\pi x}{5} + \cos\tfrac{\pi x}{2}$ has smallest period ___. Give a number.
questions.explanation: The periods are $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/5} = 10$ and $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/2} = 4$. Their ratio is $\tfrac{10}{4} = \tfrac52$, so $L = 2 \cdot 10 = 5 \cdot 4 = 20$. The terms have different frequencies, so 20 is the smallest period.

questions.stem: Match each function to its smallest period.
questions.explanation: Periods 2 and 4 give 4. Periods 1 and $\tfrac23$ have ratio $\tfrac32$, giving $2 \cdot 1 = 3 \cdot \tfrac23 = 2$. $|\sin x|$ and $|\cos x|$ each have period $\pi$, but shifting by $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ swaps them, so the sum repeats every $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (the special case). Periods $\pi$ and $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$ give $2\pi$. Periods $2\pi$ and $\sqrt2\,\pi$ have an irrational ratio, so that sum is not periodic.

questions.stem: Which statements about $y = e^{-0.3t}\cos(2\pi t)$, for $t \ge 0$, are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its graph stays between $y = e^{-0.3t}$ and $y = -e^{-0.3t}$
Its zeros are evenly spaced, 0.5 apart
It touches its upper envelope at $t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$
Its local maxima get higher as $t$ grows
questions.explanation: The envelope is $\pm e^{-0.3t}$. The zeros are the zeros of $\cos(2\pi t)$, at $t = \tfrac14, \tfrac34, \tfrac54, \ldots$, which are 0.5 apart, and the graph touches the upper envelope where $\cos(2\pi t) = 1$, at whole numbers. But the function is not periodic: the swings shrink, so the values never repeat a full cycle. For the same reason its peaks get lower, not higher.

questions.stem: The picture shows $y = x\sin x$ with its envelope. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A wave that grows as it moves right, drawn between two dashed lines opening out from the origin. Five parts are numbered: a point on the upper dashed line, a point on the lower dashed line, a point where the wave touches the upper line, a point where it touches the lower line, and a point where it crosses the x-axis.

questions.explanation: Because $-1 \le \sin x \le 1$, the product $x\sin x$ stays between the lines $y = x$ and $y = -x$ (for $x > 0$). It touches the upper line where $\sin x = 1$ (the marked point is at $\tfrac{5\pi}{2}$), touches the lower line where $\sin x = -1$ (at $\tfrac{7\pi}{2}$), and crosses the axis where $\sin x = 0$ (at $3\pi$). The graph has no asymptotes, and it has no horizontal midline.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the period of $y = \sin\tfrac{\pi x}{4} + \cos\tfrac{\pi x}{6}$ in order.
choices: Confirm that no shorter shift works: the period is 24
questions.explanation: The periods are $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/4} = 8$ and $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/6} = 12$. Their ratio in lowest terms, $\tfrac23$, tells you that 3 of the first period equal 2 of the second: $L = 24$. The last step is the check; here the terms have different frequencies, so 24 is the smallest period.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of change of $y = \cos x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{\cos\frac{\pi}{2} - \cos 0}{\frac{\pi}{2} - 0} = \dfrac{0 - 1}{\pi/2} = -\dfrac{2}{\pi} \approx -0.637$. It is negative because cosine falls on this interval. $-1$ forgets to divide by the width, and $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ divides the wrong way.

questions.stem: Over which interval does $y = \sin x$ have the greatest average rate of change?
questions.explanation: All four intervals have width $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, so compare the rises: $0.5$ on $[0, \tfrac{\pi}{6}]$, $0.366$ on $[\tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{\pi}{3}]$, $0.134$ on $[\tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, and $-0.134$ on $[\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3}]$ (sine is falling there). The rates are about $0.955$, $0.699$, $0.256$ and $-0.256$: sine climbs fastest near its zero.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the graph of $y = \sin x$ at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$?
questions.explanation: The slope of $y = \sin x$ at $x$ is $\cos x$, and $\cos\tfrac{\pi}{3} = \tfrac12$. A difference quotient agrees: $\dfrac{\sin(\frac{\pi}{3} + 0.001) - \sin\frac{\pi}{3}}{0.001} \approx 0.4996$. $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the height $\sin\tfrac{\pi}{3}$, not the slope.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the graph of $y = \cos x$ at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$?
questions.explanation: The slope of $y = \cos x$ is $-\sin x$, and $-\sin\tfrac{\pi}{2} = -1$. On the graph, cosine is crossing the axis on its way down at $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, as steeply as it ever falls. $0$ is the height there, not the slope, and $+1$ forgets the minus sign.

questions.stem: In the argument that the slope of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$, what does $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h}$ approach as $h$ shrinks to 0?
questions.explanation: For small $h$, $1 - \cos h \approx \tfrac{h^2}{2}$, so $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} \approx -\dfrac{h}{2}$, which goes to 0. (For example, at $h = 0.1$ it is about $-0.04996$.) $-\tfrac12$ is the limit of $\dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h^2}$, with $h^2$ in the denominator, and 1 is the limit of the other quotient, $\dfrac{\sin h}{h}$.

questions.stem: What is the steepest slope of the graph of $y = 3\sin(2x) + 1$?
questions.explanation: The slope is $AB\cos(Bx) = 3 \cdot 2\cos(2x) = 6\cos(2x)$, which is largest, 6, where $\cos(2x) = 1$: at the upward midline crossings. The amplitude 3 alone ignores how fast the wave repeats, and the $+1$ shift does not change any slope.

questions.stem: A rider's height is $h(t) = 20 - 15\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)$ m, $t$ in minutes. What is the fastest rate at which the rider rises?
questions.explanation: The steepest slope of a sinusoid is $|A|B = 15 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{3} = 5\pi \approx 15.7$ m/min, reached at the hub's height on the way up. It matches the rim's linear speed $r\omega = 15 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{3}$, since at the side of the wheel the rider moves straight up. 15 is the amplitude alone, and 20 is the hub height.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring has displacement $d = 4\cos(5t)$ cm, $t$ in seconds. What is its greatest speed?
questions.explanation: The velocity is the slope of the displacement graph, $-4 \cdot 5\sin(5t) = -20\sin(5t)$, so the greatest speed is $|a|\omega = 4 \cdot 5 = 20$ cm/s, reached as the mass passes equilibrium. 4 cm is the amplitude (a distance, not a speed), and 5 is the angular frequency.

questions.stem: For small swings a pendulum's period is $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. If the length is made 4 times as long, what happens to the period?
questions.explanation: $T$ is proportional to $\sqrt{L}$, and $\sqrt{4L} = 2\sqrt{L}$, so the period doubles. For example, a 0.25 m pendulum has $T \approx 1.00$ s and a 1 m pendulum has $T \approx 2.01$ s.

questions.stem: Where is the slope of the graph of $y = 2\sin x + 5$ equal to 0?
questions.explanation: The slope is $2\cos x$, which is 0 where $\cos x = 0$: at $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + k\pi$, the peaks ($y = 7$) and troughs ($y = 3$). At $x = k\pi$ the graph is on its midline $y = 5$, where it is steepest, not level.

questions.stem: The slope of the graph of $y = 4\sin\tfrac{x}{2}$ at $x = 0$ is ___. Give a number.
questions.explanation: With $A = 4$ and $B = \tfrac12$ the slope is $AB\cos(Bx) = 2\cos\tfrac{x}{2}$, which is 2 at $x = 0$. Stretching the graph up by 4 multiplies slopes by 4, and stretching it sideways by 2 (period $4\pi$) halves them.

questions.stem: Match each function to the slope of its graph at $x = 0$.
questions.explanation: The slope of $A\sin(Bx)$ at 0 is $AB\cos 0 = AB$: $1 \cdot 1 = 1$, $5 \cdot 3 = 15$ and $-2 \cdot \tfrac12 = -1$. Cosine is at its peak at 0, so its slope there is $-\sin 0 = 0$. 5 and $-2$ are amplitudes (with sign), which forget the factor $B$.

questions.stem: Which statements about $y = 4\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right)$ are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its slope is 0 at its maxima
It is steepest at $t = 0$ and at $t = 2$
questions.explanation: The slope is $4 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{2}\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right) = 2\pi\cos\!\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2}t\right)$. Its size is greatest, $2\pi \approx 6.28$, at the midline crossings $t = 0, 2, 4, \ldots$ (rising at 0, falling at 2). At $t = 1$ the graph is at its maximum 4, where the slope is 0. The amplitude 4 alone is not a slope.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the argument that the slope of $y = \sin x$ is $\cos x$ in order.
choices: Write the difference quotient $\dfrac{\sin(x + h) - \sin x}{h}$
Expand $\sin(x + h)$ with the sum formula
Regroup as $\sin x \cdot \dfrac{\cos h - 1}{h} + \cos x \cdot \dfrac{\sin h}{h}$
Conclude that the slope at $x$ is $\cos x$
questions.explanation: The slope is the limit of a difference quotient, so that comes first. The sum formula $\sin(x + h) = \sin x\cos h + \cos x\sin h$ turns it into something that can be regrouped around the two small-angle quotients. Only after regrouping can you let $h$ shrink and use their limits, which leaves $\sin x \cdot 0 + \cos x \cdot 1 = \cos x$.

questions.stem: The picture shows $y = \sin x$ with four tangent lines and one secant line. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: One cycle of the sine graph with short straight lines touching it at four points: the origin, the peak, the zero at the middle of the cycle, and the trough. A dashed line joins two points on either side of the trough. Five parts are numbered.

choices: Secant line: average rate of change
questions.explanation: The slope of $\sin x$ is $\cos x$. At the origin that is $\cos 0 = 1$, the steepest rise; at the peak $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ and the trough $\tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ it is 0 (level tangent lines); at $\pi$ it is $\cos\pi = -1$, the steepest fall. The dashed line joins two points of the curve, so it is a secant line, and its slope is the average rate of change between them.

questions.stem: In degrees, $\sin^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac12\right) =$ ___. Give only the number of degrees.
questions.explanation: The reference angle is $30^\circ$ ($\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$). The range of $\sin^{-1}$ is $[-90^\circ, 90^\circ]$, and a negative input puts the answer in quadrant IV: $-30^\circ$. ($330^\circ$ and $210^\circ$ also have sine $-\tfrac12$, but they are outside the range.)

questions.stem: Match each inverse function to its range.
choices: From −π/2 to π/2, both endpoints included
From 0 to π, both endpoints included
questions.explanation: Sine is restricted to $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ and cosine to $[0, \pi]$, so those are the ranges of their inverses. Tangent is undefined at $\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $\tan^{-1}$ never reaches those values. $[-1, 1]$ is the domain of $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$, not a range, and no inverse function returns a full turn of angles.

questions.stem: Which of these are undefined? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Sine and cosine stay between $-1$ and 1, so $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ only accept inputs in $[-1, 1]$: $1.2$ and $-1.01$ are outside. $\cos^{-1}(-1) = \pi$ is fine (the endpoint is allowed), and $\tan^{-1}$ accepts every real number: $\tan^{-1}50 \approx 1.5508$.

questions.stem: Each circle shows the range of one inverse function: the shaded half holds every angle the function can return, and an open dot marks an endpoint that is not included. Name the function for each numbered range.

image.alt: Three unit circles. On the first, the right half is highlighted from −π/2 to π/2 with solid endpoint dots. On the second, the upper half is highlighted from 0 to π with solid dots. On the third, the right half is highlighted from −π/2 to π/2 with open endpoint dots.

questions.explanation: Inverse sine and inverse tangent both return angles in the right half of the circle, but $\tan^{-1}$ never reaches $\pm\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (tangent is undefined there), so its endpoints are open. Inverse cosine returns the upper half, $[0, \pi]$, endpoints included. Inverse cotangent also covers the upper half but with open endpoints, $(0, \pi)$, which matches none of the pictures.

questions.stem: Put these values in order from smallest to largest.
questions.explanation: $\sin^{-1}(-1) = -\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx -1.5708$, $\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\tfrac{\pi}{4} \approx -0.7854$, $\cos^{-1}1 = 0$, $\tan^{-1}100 \approx 1.5608$ (just under $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, which $\tan^{-1}$ never reaches), and $\cos^{-1}(-1) = \pi \approx 3.1416$, the largest value any of the three inverse functions returns.

questions.stem: Evaluate exactly: $\sin\!\left(\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac{8}{17}\right)\right) =$ ___. Give a fraction.
questions.explanation: Let $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac{8}{17}\right)$. It lies in $[0, \pi]$ with a negative cosine, so it is in quadrant II. Take $x = -8$ and $r = 17$; then $y = \sqrt{17^2 - 8^2} = \sqrt{225} = 15$, positive in quadrant II. So $\sin\theta = \tfrac{15}{17}$. A negative answer would come from copying the sign of the input, but sine is positive in quadrant II.

questions.stem: Match each expression to its value.
questions.explanation: None of the inner angles is in its inverse's range, so evaluate the inside first. $\sin\tfrac{2\pi}{3} = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\sin^{-1}\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \tfrac{\pi}{3}$. $\cos\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$, giving $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ (not $-\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, which is outside $[0, \pi]$). $\tan\tfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$, giving $-\tfrac{\pi}{6}$. $\cos\tfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\tfrac12$, giving $\tfrac{2\pi}{3}$. $\tfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is what blind cancelling would give for the tangent.

questions.stem: For which values of $x$ (in radians) is $\sin^{-1}(\sin x) = x$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The cancellation works exactly when $x$ is in the range of $\sin^{-1}$, $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right] \approx [-1.5708, 1.5708]$. $-1.5$ and $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ are in it. $1.6$ and $-2$ are not: $\sin^{-1}(\sin 1.6) = \pi - 1.6 \approx 1.5416$ and $\sin^{-1}(\sin(-2)) = -\pi + 2 \approx -1.1416$.

questions.stem: The picture shows $\theta = \cos^{-1}\!\left(-\tfrac{5}{13}\right)$ with its reference triangle. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A coordinate plane with a point in quadrant II joined to the origin. A right triangle hangs from the point down to the negative x-axis. Two angles are marked at the origin: a large one from the positive x-axis, and a smaller one between the terminal side and the negative x-axis.

questions.explanation: $\cos\theta = \tfrac{x}{r} = -\tfrac{5}{13}$, so $x = -5$ (the horizontal leg points left) and $r = 13$ (the hypotenuse, always positive). Then $y = \sqrt{169 - 25} = 12$, positive because $\theta$ is in quadrant II. $\theta$ is measured from the positive $x$-axis; the reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the negative $x$-axis.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\cos^{-1}(\cos 5)$, where 5 is in radians.
questions.explanation: 5 is outside $[0, \pi]$, so it can't be the answer. Cosine has period $2\pi$ and is even, so $\cos 5 = \cos(5 - 2\pi) = \cos(2\pi - 5)$, and $2\pi - 5 \approx 1.2832$ lies in $[0, \pi]$. That is the answer. $5 - \pi$ has the opposite cosine ($\cos(5 - \pi) = -\cos 5$), and $\pi - 5$ is negative, outside the range.

questions.stem: How many solutions does $\sin 3x = \tfrac12$ have in $[0, 2\pi)$? ___
questions.explanation: Let $u = 3x$. As $x$ runs over $[0, 2\pi)$, $u$ runs over $[0, 6\pi)$: three full turns, with two solutions of $\sin u = \tfrac12$ in each. That makes 6: $x = \tfrac{\pi}{18}, \tfrac{5\pi}{18}, \tfrac{13\pi}{18}, \tfrac{17\pi}{18}, \tfrac{25\pi}{18}, \tfrac{29\pi}{18}$. Dividing too early gives only 2.

questions.stem: Match each equation to the number of solutions it has in $[0, 2\pi)$.
questions.explanation: A sine or cosine equation with $-1 < c < 1$ has two solutions per turn. At $c = \pm1$ the two points merge into one ($\cos x = -1$ only at $\pi$), and $|c| > 1$ gives none. $\sin 2x = 0.4$ covers two turns of $2x$, so 4 solutions. Tangent has one solution per period $\pi$, so 2 in $[0, 2\pi)$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving $\sin 2x = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ on $[0, 2\pi)$ in order.
choices: Find the solutions in the first turn: $u = \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{2\pi}{3}$
Add $2\pi$ to get the second turn: $u = \tfrac{7\pi}{3}, \tfrac{8\pi}{3}$
questions.explanation: Substitute first so you know how far $u$ runs, solve for $u$ over that whole interval (the second turn comes from adding $2\pi$ to the first), and divide by 2 only at the end. Dividing earlier loses the solutions from the second turn.

questions.stem: Which of these are solutions of $\tan x = -1$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The general solution is $x = \tan^{-1}(-1) + k\pi = -\tfrac{\pi}{4} + k\pi$: $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ ($k = 1$) and $\tfrac{7\pi}{4}$ ($k = 2$) are in it. $\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$ and $-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ are in quadrant III, where tangent is positive: $\tan\tfrac{5\pi}{4} = \tan\left(-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = 1$.

questions.stem: The picture shows how $\cos x = c$ is solved on the unit circle. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A unit circle with a dashed vertical line crossing it at an upper and a lower point, each joined to the center. A small angle is marked from the positive x-axis up to the upper radius.

questions.explanation: Cosine is the $x$-coordinate, so $\cos x = c$ picks out the points where the vertical line $x = c$ meets the circle. The upper one is at $\beta = \cos^{-1}c$; the lower one is its mirror image across the $x$-axis, at $-\beta$, which is the same point as $2\pi - \beta$. The angle $\pi - \beta$ belongs to sine equations (a horizontal line).

questions.stem: Evaluate $\tan^{-1}\tfrac12 + \tan^{-1}\tfrac13$.
questions.explanation: $ab = \tfrac16 < 1$, so the sum is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tfrac12 + \tfrac13}{1 - \tfrac16} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{5/6}{5/6} = \tan^{-1}1 = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. $\tan^{-1}\tfrac56 \approx 0.6947$ comes from adding the inputs, which is not how arctangents add.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\tan^{-1}2 + \tan^{-1}3$.
questions.explanation: $\tfrac{a + b}{1 - ab} = \tfrac{5}{-5} = -1$, but $ab = 6 > 1$: the point $(1 - ab, a + b) = (-5, 5)$ is in quadrant II, so add $\pi$ to $\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\tfrac{\pi}{4}$, giving $\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ ($\approx 1.1071 + 1.2490 = 2.3562$). $-\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ is the uncorrected formula; $\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$ is too big, since each arctangent is less than $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

questions.stem: The angle $\tan^{-1}a + \tan^{-1}b$ is the direction angle of which point?
questions.explanation: Start at $B = (1, a)$, which is at angle $\tan^{-1}a$. Turning $(1, a)$ a quarter turn counterclockwise gives $(-a, 1)$; stepping $b$ of those from $B$ turns the direction by $\tan^{-1}b$ more and lands at $(1, a) + b(-a, 1) = (1 - ab, a + b)$. Swapping the coordinates would give the complementary angle.

questions.stem: If $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\tfrac13$ and $\beta = \tan^{-1}\tfrac14$, then $\tan(\alpha + \beta) =$ ___. Give a fraction.
questions.explanation: $\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \dfrac{a + b}{1 - ab} = \dfrac{\tfrac13 + \tfrac14}{1 - \tfrac{1}{12}} = \dfrac{7/12}{11/12} = \dfrac{7}{11}$.

questions.stem: Which expression equals $2\tan^{-1}\tfrac13$?
questions.explanation: The doubling rule (valid since $\tfrac13 < 1$) gives $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2 \cdot \tfrac13}{1 - \tfrac19} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2/3}{8/9} = \tan^{-1}\tfrac34$. $\tan^{-1}\tfrac23$ doubles the input, $\tfrac35$ uses $1 + a^2$ in the denominator, and $\tfrac19$ squares the input.

questions.stem: For $x = -3$, what is $\tan^{-1}x + \tan^{-1}\tfrac1x$?
questions.explanation: The product of the inputs is 1, so the point $(1 - ab, a + b) = \left(0, -\tfrac{10}{3}\right)$ is on the negative $y$-axis and the sum is $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. Both arctangents are negative here, so the sum can't be $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$; that value is for $x > 0$.

questions.stem: Which of these equal $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: First: $\tfrac{5/6}{5/6} = 1$, so $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Third: the difference formula ($ab = \tfrac32 > -1$) gives $\tfrac{3 - 1/2}{1 + 3/2} = \tfrac{5/2}{5/2} = 1$, so $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Second: doubling gives $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{3/4} = \tan^{-1}\tfrac43 \approx 0.9273$. Fourth: $\tfrac{1}{1 - 3/16} = \tfrac{16}{13}$, so $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{16}{13} \approx 0.8885$.

questions.stem: Match each sum to its value.
questions.explanation: $\tan^{-1}2 + \tan^{-1}3 = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ (the point $(-5, 5)$ is in quadrant II), and adding $\tan^{-1}1 = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$ gives $\pi$. $\tan^{-1}\tfrac12 + \tan^{-1}\tfrac13 = \tan^{-1}1 = \tfrac{\pi}{4}$. Reciprocal inputs have product 1: the sum is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ for positive inputs and $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ for negative ones.

questions.stem: Put the steps of checking Machin's formula $\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 4\tan^{-1}\tfrac15 - \tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{239}$ in order, with $\theta = \tan^{-1}\tfrac15$.
choices: Subtract $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{239}$ with the difference formula: the tangent comes out as $1$
questions.explanation: $\tan 2\theta = \tfrac{2/5}{24/25} = \tfrac{5}{12}$, then $\tan 4\theta = \tfrac{5/6}{119/144} = \tfrac{120}{119}$. The difference formula gives $\tfrac{120 \cdot 239 - 119}{119 \cdot 239 + 120} = \tfrac{28561}{28561} = 1$, and every step stayed in the range where no $\pi$ correction is needed.

questions.stem: The picture shows the construction for adding $\alpha = \tan^{-1}a$ and $\beta = \tan^{-1}b$. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two right triangles stacked at the origin O. The lower one has a side of length 1 along the x-axis to A and a vertical side a up to a point. The upper one has a right angle at that point and goes up to a second point. Two angles are marked at O, one inside each triangle.

questions.explanation: The lower triangle has adjacent side 1 and opposite side $a$, so it ends at $B = (1, a)$ and its angle at $O$ is $\tan^{-1}a$. The upper triangle has a right angle at $B$ and $\tfrac{BC}{OB} = b$, so its angle at $O$ is $\tan^{-1}b$, and $C = (1, a) + b(-a, 1) = (1 - ab, a + b)$. The whole angle from the $x$-axis to $OC$ is the sum.

questions.stem: Why does Machin's formula give $\pi$ much faster than the series $\tfrac{\pi}{4} = \tan^{-1}1 = 1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \cdots$?
choices: It avoids the arctangent series altogether
Its inputs are small, so the terms of the arctangent series shrink quickly
It works in degrees instead of radians
Its series have only positive terms
questions.explanation: The series for $\tan^{-1}x$ has terms $\tfrac{x^{2k+1}}{2k+1}$. With $x = 1$ they shrink very slowly (1,000 terms still give $\pi \approx 3.1406$); with $x = \tfrac15$ each term is less than $\tfrac{1}{25}$ of the one before, and with $x = \tfrac{1}{239}$ far less still. Machin's formula still uses the series, in radians, and its terms still alternate in sign.

questions.stem: To four decimal places, what is $\tan^{-1}3 + \tan^{-1}4$?
questions.explanation: $ab = 12 > 1$ with $a > 0$: the point $(1 - 12, 7) = (-11, 7)$ is in quadrant II. $\tan^{-1}\tfrac{7}{-11} \approx -0.5667$, plus $\pi$ gives $2.5749$ (check: $1.2490 + 1.3258 = 2.5748$ to rounding). $-0.5667$ forgets the correction, $0.5667$ also drops the sign, and $3.7083 = \pi + 0.5667$ adds $\pi$ to the wrong angle.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\tan^{-1}\tfrac12 - \tan^{-1}\tfrac13$.
questions.explanation: With $ab = \tfrac16 > -1$, the difference formula gives $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tfrac12 - \tfrac13}{1 + \tfrac16} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{1/6}{7/6} = \tan^{-1}\tfrac17$. $\tfrac16$ forgets the denominator, $\tfrac15$ uses $1 - ab$ (the sum's denominator), and $\tan^{-1}1$ is the sum, not the difference.

$\tan^{-1}b = \tfrac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1}4$, the complement of $\tan^{-1}4$. In a right triangle with legs 4 and 1 the two acute angles are $\tan^{-1}4$ and $\tan^{-1}\tfrac14$, so $b = \tfrac14$. (Product of the inputs is 1, as the formula requires.)

questions.stem: Using the first two terms of the arctangent series, what is the approximation of $\tan^{-1}0.1$?
questions.explanation: $\tan^{-1}x \approx x - \tfrac{x^3}{3} = 0.1 - \tfrac{0.001}{3} = 0.099667$ (the true value is $0.0996687$). $0.1$ is one term, $0.100333$ adds the second term instead of subtracting it, and $0.099833$ divides by 6 as in the sine series.

questions.stem: Which describes every solution of $\sin A = \sin B$?
questions.explanation: Equal sines mean equal heights on the unit circle: the angle $B$ and its mirror image across the $y$-axis, $\pi - B$, plus full turns. $\pm B + 2k\pi$ is the rule for equal cosines (mirror across the $x$-axis), and $B + k\pi$ is the rule for equal tangents.

questions.stem: Solve $\sin 3x = \sin x$ on $[0, 2\pi)$.
questions.explanation: $3x = x + 2k\pi$ gives $x = k\pi$: $0, \pi$. $3x = \pi - x + 2k\pi$ gives $x = \tfrac{\pi}{4} + \tfrac{k\pi}{2}$: $\tfrac{\pi}{4}, \tfrac{3\pi}{4}, \tfrac{5\pi}{4}, \tfrac{7\pi}{4}$. Both families together give six solutions; each of the first and third choices is only one family, and $0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$ solves $\cos 3x = \cos x$.

questions.stem: How many solutions does $\cos 3x = \cos x$ have in $[0, 2\pi)$? ___
questions.explanation: $3x = x + 2k\pi$ gives $x = k\pi$: $0, \pi$. $3x = -x + 2k\pi$ gives $x = \tfrac{k\pi}{2}$: $0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}, \pi, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$. The families overlap at $0$ and $\pi$, so there are 4 different solutions. Counting 6 double-counts the overlap.

questions.stem: Solve $\sin 2x = \cos x$ on $[0, 2\pi)$.
questions.explanation: Write $\cos x = \sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$. Family 1: $2x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} - x + 2k\pi$, so $x = \tfrac{\pi}{6} + \tfrac{2k\pi}{3}$: $\tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}$. Family 2: $2x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} + x + 2k\pi$, so $x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$. All four together; the other choices each miss part of a family.
