glossary.definition: The square array of the four numbers $\cos\theta$, $-\sin\theta$ (first row) and $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ (second row) that encodes a rotation by $\theta$; multiplying it by a point's coordinates applies the rotation formulas.
A simple robot arm moving in a plane: a fixed shoulder joint, a link of length $L_1$ to an elbow joint, and a second link of length $L_2$ to the end effector.
The tool at the tip of a robot arm, such as a gripper or a welding torch; its position is what kinematics computes.
The angles that describe a robot arm's pose. For a two-link arm, $\theta_1$ is measured from the positive $x$-axis and $\theta_2$ from the direction of link 1.

Finding the position of a robot arm's end effector from its joint angles; for a two-link arm, $x = L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ and $y = L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.
Finding the joint angles that put a robot arm's end effector at a given point; for a two-link arm it uses the law of cosines and usually has two solutions.
The two mirror-image solutions of a two-link arm's inverse kinematics, with elbow angles $\theta_2$ and $-\theta_2$, one on each side of the line from the shoulder to the target.
The set of points a robot arm's end effector can reach. For a two-link arm with free joints it is the ring $|L_1 - L_2| \le d \le L_1 + L_2$ around the shoulder.
The arrow (or complex number) $A\angle\varphi$ of length $A$ at angle $\varphi$ that represents the sinusoid $A\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$; sinusoids of one frequency add by adding their phasors.
The difference $\Delta = \varphi_2 - \varphi_1$ between the phases of two sinusoids with the same frequency; it is the angle between their phasors.
Two waves of the same frequency adding in phase (phase difference $0^\circ$), so the amplitude of the sum is the sum of the amplitudes.
Two waves of the same frequency adding half a cycle apart (phase difference $180^\circ$), so the amplitude of the sum is the difference of the amplitudes; equal waves cancel completely.
Electric current (and voltage) that reverses direction periodically, usually as a sinusoid; household electricity in North America alternates at 60 Hz.

The opposition of an inductor, $X_L = \omega L$, or a capacitor, $X_C = \tfrac{1}{\omega C}$, to alternating current, measured in ohms. An inductor's voltage leads the current by $90^\circ$; a capacitor's lags it by $90^\circ$.
A circuit with a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor in one loop, so the same current flows through all three and the source voltage is the phasor sum of their voltages.
A circuit's total opposition to alternating current, in ohms; for a series RLC circuit $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, the modulus of the complex number $R + j(X_L - X_C)$.
The condition $X_L = X_C$ in a series RLC circuit, where the impedance is smallest and the current largest; it happens at $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$.
$\cos\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the phase angle between voltage and current; the average power is $\tfrac12 VI\cos\varphi$ for peak values $V$ and $I$.
In optics, the line perpendicular to a surface at the point where a ray hits it; angles of incidence, reflection and refraction are measured from it.
A ray of light arriving at a boundary between two materials.
The angle between an incident ray and the normal to the surface it strikes.
A reflected ray leaves a surface at the same angle from the normal as the incident ray arrived, on the other side of the normal.
The angle between a refracted ray and the normal, on the far side of the boundary.
The bending of light (or any wave) as it crosses from one material into another in which it travels at a different speed.
The ratio $n = \tfrac{c}{v}$ of the speed of light in a vacuum to its speed in a material; about 1.00 for air, 1.33 for water and 1.5 for glass.
$n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2$: the law of refraction, with both angles measured from the normal.
Complete reflection of light at a boundary into a material of smaller index of refraction, which happens when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
The angle of incidence beyond which total internal reflection occurs, going from index $n_1$ to a smaller index $n_2$: $\sin\theta_c = \tfrac{n_2}{n_1}$.
The central glass strand of an optical fiber, which carries the light; it has a slightly larger index of refraction than the cladding around it.
The layer of glass around an optical fiber's core, with a slightly smaller index of refraction, so light in the core is trapped by total internal reflection.
For an optical fiber with core index $n_1$ and cladding index $n_2$, the number $\sqrt{n_1^2 - n_2^2}$; it equals the sine of the acceptance angle in air.
The largest angle from an optical fiber's axis at which light entering its end is still trapped and carried along the fiber.
The shortest distance between two points along the surface of a sphere, $d = Rc$, where $c$ is the central angle between them in radians.
Three points on a sphere joined by arcs of great circles; its sides are measured by the central angles they span, and its angles add up to more than $180^\circ$.
The angular distance of a point from the North Pole, $90^\circ$ minus its latitude.
For a spherical triangle with sides $a$, $b$, $c$ (as central angles) and angle $C$ opposite $c$: $\cos c = \cos a\cos b + \sin a\sin b\cos C$.
The direction, clockwise from north, in which a great-circle route starts; the bearing changes along the route.
A path on the Earth that keeps one fixed compass bearing; except along a meridian or the equator it is longer than the great-circle route.
A form of the great-circle distance formula, $\sin^2\tfrac{c}{2} = \sin^2\tfrac{\Delta\varphi}{2} + \cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\sin^2\tfrac{\Delta\lambda}{2}$, that stays accurate for nearby points.
The amount $E = A + B + C - 180^\circ$ by which a spherical triangle's angles exceed $180^\circ$; its area is $R^2E$ with $E$ in radians.
A vertical stick or pillar whose shadow is used to measure the Sun's angle, as on a sundial or in Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth.
The central angle between a place and the equator, measured north or south along the place's meridian, from $0^\circ$ at the equator to $90^\circ$ at a pole.
A north–south line on the Earth's surface running from pole to pole. Places on the same meridian differ only in latitude.
A circle on a sphere whose center is the center of the sphere, such as the equator. The shortest path between two points on a sphere's surface is an arc of a great circle.
A unit of distance at sea and in the air, defined as exactly 1852 m; it is about the length of one minute of latitude.
A speed of one nautical mile per hour.
The angle an object covers as seen from a given point. For an object of width $D$ at a much larger distance $d$, it is about $D/d$ radians.

For a small angle $t$ in radians, $\sin t \approx t$, $\tan t \approx t$ and $\cos t \approx 1 - \tfrac{t^2}{2}$. In particular an object of width $D$ at a much larger distance $d$ has angular size $\theta \approx \tfrac{D}{d}$ radians.
A second of angle, $\tfrac{1}{60}$ of an arcminute or $\tfrac{1}{3600}$ of a degree; one radian is about $206{,}265$ arcseconds.
One thousandth of a radian. An object covering 1 mrad is about $\tfrac{1}{1000}$ of its distance across, such as 1 m at 1 km.
The apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when it is viewed from two different places.
For a star, the angle that one astronomical unit subtends as seen from the star; with the angle $p$ in arcseconds, the distance is $1/p$ parsecs.
The average distance from the Earth to the Sun, defined as exactly 149,597,870.7 km.
The distance at which one astronomical unit subtends one arcsecond: $\tfrac{648{,}000}{\pi}$ au, about $3.086 \times 10^{13}$ km or 3.26 light-years.
The rate at which the angle between two rotating objects changes. For two rotations about the same center in the same direction, it is $\omega_1 - \omega_2$.
The time from one noon to the next, when the Sun returns to the same place in the sky; its average defines the 24-hour day.
The time for the Earth to turn once relative to the distant stars, about 23 h 56 min 4 s.

The time for one orbiting body to come back into the same position relative to another, for example new Moon to new Moon (about 29.5 days). For two bodies circling the same way with periods $T_1 < T_2$, it satisfies $\tfrac{1}{T} = \tfrac{1}{T_1} - \tfrac{1}{T_2}$.
A chain of gears that pass rotation from a driver to an output. Each mesh satisfies $N_1\omega_1 = N_2\omega_2$ and reverses the direction.
A gear placed between two others. It reverses the direction of the output but does not change the speed ratio.
Two or more gears fixed on one shaft, so they turn with the same angular speed.
The curve traced by a point on the rim of a wheel rolling along a straight line without slipping: a series of arches, one per turn.
A polygon whose sides all have the same length and whose angles all have the same size, such as an equilateral triangle, a square or a regular pentagon.
The radius $R$ of the circle through all the vertices of a regular polygon: the distance from its center to any vertex.
The segment from the center of a regular polygon to the midpoint of a side, perpendicular to that side; its length is $R\cos\tfrac{180^\circ}{n}$ for an $n$-gon with circumradius $R$.
An isosceles triangle with apex angle $36^\circ$ and base angles $72^\circ$. Bisecting a base angle cuts off a smaller golden triangle, which leads to $\sin 18^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt5 - 1}{4}$.

The number $\varphi = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2} \approx 1.618$, the positive solution of $\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1$. A regular pentagon's diagonal is $\varphi$ times its side, and $\cos 36^\circ = \tfrac{\varphi}{2}$.
How far a measured value could be from the true value, written with $\pm$, as in $38^\circ \pm 0.5^\circ$.
The size of the possible error in a result, in the result's own units (for example $\pm 0.7$ m).
The absolute error divided by the value, often written as a percent; it lets you compare the accuracy of measurements of different sizes.
The slight bending of light as it passes through air of changing density; near the ground it usually makes the visible horizon a little farther than the purely geometric one.
The angle from the horizontal at an observer down to the line of sight to the sea horizon. From height $h$ above a sphere of radius $R$, $\cos\alpha = \tfrac{R}{R + h}$.
A line that touches a circle at exactly one point. It is perpendicular to the radius at that point; the line $x = 1$ is tangent to the unit circle at $(1, 0)$.
A line that cuts through a circle at two points (Latin secare, "to cut"). The segment $OT$ that measures $\sec\theta$ lies on one.

A length with a sign that records direction: positive one way along a line and negative the other. Read this way, $\tan\theta$ and $\sec\theta$ are lengths in the unit-circle picture in every quadrant.
An older trig function, $\text{versin}\,\theta = 1 - \cos\theta$: on the unit circle, the distance from the foot of the sine to the point $(1, 0)$. Half of it is the haversine.
An older trig function, $\text{exsec}\,\theta = \sec\theta - 1$: the part of the secant segment that lies outside the unit circle.

If a quantity always lies between two others, and those two approach the same number, then it approaches that number too. It shows that $\tfrac{\sin t}{t} \to 1$ as $t \to 0$, because $\cos t < \tfrac{\sin t}{t} < 1$.
Replacing a function near a point by a straight line that matches it there, such as $\sin t \approx t$ and $\tan t \approx t$ for small $t$ in radians.
Graphing a sum $y = f(x) + g(x)$ by adding the heights (ordinates, or $y$-coordinates) of the two graphs at each $x$. Where one part is 0, the sum lies on the other graph.

The smallest positive number that is a whole-number multiple of each of two given numbers. A sum of terms with periods $p$ and $q$ repeats after their least common multiple: if $\tfrac{p}{q} = \tfrac{m}{n}$ in lowest terms, it is $np = mq$.
For a product such as $y = f(x)\sin x$, the pair of curves $y = \pm|f(x)|$ that the graph stays between and touches (where $\sin x = \pm1$). It controls how big the swings are.
The change in a function divided by the change in its input, $\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$: the slope of the straight line joining two points of its graph.
The average rate of change over a short interval $[x, x + h]$: $\dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$. As $h$ shrinks it approaches the slope of the curve at $x$.
The number that difference quotients at a point approach as the interval shrinks: the slope of the line that just touches the graph there. The slope of $y = \sin x$ at $x$ is $\cos x$ (radians).
For $y = A\sin(B(x - C)) + D$, the largest size of the slope, $|A|B = \tfrac{2\pi|A|}{\text{period}}$. It occurs at every midline crossing; at peaks and troughs the slope is 0.
A sailors' rule of thumb for a tide between high and low water (about 6 hours): the level changes by 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the range in successive hours. It roughly matches a sinusoid.

The rate at which a position or displacement changes, with a sign for direction. In simple harmonic motion $d = a\sin(\omega t)$ it is $a\omega\cos(\omega t)$, largest in size ($|a|\omega$) at equilibrium.

$\tan^{-1}a + \tan^{-1}b = \tan^{-1}\tfrac{a + b}{1 - ab}$ when $ab < 1$; add $\pi$ when $ab > 1$ and $a > 0$, subtract $\pi$ when $ab > 1$ and $a < 0$. The sum is the direction angle of the point $(1 - ab, a + b)$.
$\tfrac{\pi}{4} = 4\tan^{-1}\tfrac15 - \tan^{-1}\tfrac{1}{239}$, found by John Machin in 1706 and used by him to compute $\pi$ to 100 decimal places.
Any formula that writes $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ as a combination of arctangents of small numbers, such as $\tan^{-1}\tfrac12 + \tan^{-1}\tfrac13$; small inputs make the arctangent series converge quickly.
$\tan^{-1}x = x - \tfrac{x^3}{3} + \tfrac{x^5}{5} - \tfrac{x^7}{7} + \cdots$ for $-1 \le x \le 1$ (proved in calculus); it converges fast when $|x|$ is small and very slowly at $x = 1$.

An equation involving trig, exponential or logarithmic functions. The term matters most for equations that mix such a function with a polynomial, such as $\cos x = x$: no algebraic steps can isolate $x$, so they are solved numerically.
A way to find a root of $f(x) = 0$: start with an interval where $f$ changes sign, test the midpoint, keep the half where the sign still changes, and repeat. Each step halves the interval.
A way to solve an equation written as $x = g(x)$: from a guess $x_0$, compute $x_1 = g(x_0)$, $x_2 = g(x_1)$, and so on. If the values settle down, they settle on a solution.

$M = E - e\sin E$, linking the mean anomaly $M$ (an angle that grows steadily with time) to the eccentric anomaly $E$ (which locates an orbiting body on its ellipse); $e$ is the eccentricity. It has no algebraic solution for $E$.

The change of variable $t = \tan\tfrac{x}{2}$, which gives $\sin x = \tfrac{2t}{1 + t^2}$, $\cos x = \tfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}$ and $\tan x = \tfrac{2t}{1 - t^2}$ with no square roots. It works for every $x$ except $\pi + 2k\pi$.

A description of a curve in which both coordinates are fractions of polynomials in one parameter. The unit circle has one: $\left(\tfrac{1 - t^2}{1 + t^2}, \tfrac{2t}{1 + t^2}\right)$, which reaches every point except $(-1, 0)$.
The polynomials $T_n$ with $T_n(\cos x) = \cos nx$: $T_0 = 1$, $T_1 = c$, and $T_{n+1} = 2cT_n - T_{n-1}$, so $T_2 = 2c^2 - 1$, $T_3 = 4c^3 - 3c$. Named for Pafnuty Chebyshev.
Solving $4c^3 - 3c = k$ (with $|k| \le 1$) by setting $c = \cos\theta$, so that $\cos 3\theta = k$; the three roots are the cosines of three angles $120^\circ$ apart. Worked out by Viète around 1600.
A sum whose terms are differences $a_k - a_{k+1}$, so that neighboring pieces cancel and only the first and last remain: $\sum_{k=1}^{n}(a_k - a_{k+1}) = a_1 - a_{n+1}$.

The chord function of Greek astronomy: $\text{crd}\,\theta$ is the length of the chord cut off by a central angle $\theta$, so $\text{crd}\,\theta = 2R\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}$ in a circle of radius $R$.
Written in base 60. Ptolemy's $84;51,10$ means $84 + \tfrac{51}{60} + \tfrac{10}{60^2}$, the same system as degrees, minutes and seconds.
A quadrilateral whose four vertices lie on one circle. Its opposite angles add to $180^\circ$.
For a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ (vertices in order), $AC \cdot BD = AB \cdot CD + AD \cdot BC$: the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides.
The circle through all three vertices of a triangle. Its radius is written $R$.

The center $O$ of a triangle's circumcircle, where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet. Inside an acute triangle, at the midpoint of the hypotenuse of a right triangle, outside an obtuse one.
$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C} = 2R$, where $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle.

An angle with its vertex on a circle and chords as its sides equals half the central angle on the same arc. So inscribed angles on the same arc (same side) are equal, and an angle inscribed in a semicircle is $90^\circ$.
The circle inside a triangle that touches all three sides. Its radius is the inradius $r$.
The center $I$ of a triangle's incircle, where the three angle bisectors meet; it is the same distance $r$ from every side.
The radius $r$ of a triangle's incircle: $r = \tfrac{K}{s}$, the area divided by the semiperimeter.
For every triangle, the circumradius is at least twice the inradius: $R \ge 2r$, with equality only for an equilateral triangle.
Describes a calculation in which small errors in the inputs (such as rounding) cause large errors in the result, for example finding a very small angle from its cosine.
$\dfrac{a - b}{a + b} = \dfrac{\tan\frac{A - B}{2}}{\tan\frac{A + B}{2}}$ in any triangle; with the included angle $C$ known, $\tan\frac{A - B}{2} = \frac{a - b}{a + b}\cot\frac{C}{2}$ solves SAS.
$\dfrac{a + b}{c} = \dfrac{\cos\frac{A - B}{2}}{\sin\frac{C}{2}}$ and $\dfrac{a - b}{c} = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A - B}{2}}{\cos\frac{C}{2}}$; each uses all six parts, so it checks a solved triangle.
The push of a surface on an object resting against it, directed perpendicular to the surface. On a ramp at angle $\theta$ with no other forces across the ramp, it equals $W\cos\theta$.
Rotating $\langle a, b\rangle$ counterclockwise by $\theta$ gives $\langle a\cos\theta - b\sin\theta,\ a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta\rangle$; it comes from the sum formulas for sine and cosine.

For two plane vectors, $\det(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = u_1v_2 - u_2v_1 = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\sin\varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the signed angle from $\mathbf{u}$ to $\mathbf{v}$. Its absolute value is the area of the parallelogram the vectors span.

The angle you turn through to go from $\mathbf{u}$ to $\mathbf{v}$: positive counterclockwise, negative clockwise, between $-180^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. Its cosine and sine are in the ratio (dot product) : (determinant).
In the plane, $(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 + \det(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})^2 = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2$, the vector form of $\cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi = 1$.
Area with a sign that records orientation: $\det(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v})$ is positive when $\mathbf{v}$ is counterclockwise from $\mathbf{u}$ and negative when clockwise.

The area of a polygon with vertices $(x_k, y_k)$ listed in order around the boundary: $\tfrac12\left|\sum (x_k y_{k+1} - x_{k+1} y_k)\right|$, wrapping around to the first vertex. The polygon must not cross itself.

The sign of $\det(\overrightarrow{AB}, \overrightarrow{BC})$: positive means the path $A \to B \to C$ turns left (counterclockwise), negative means it turns right, zero means the points are collinear.
The vector from the origin to a point; the point $(a, b)$ has position vector $\langle a, b\rangle$.
The point $P$ dividing segment $AB$ so that $AP : PB = m : n$ is $P = \dfrac{nA + mB}{m + n}$.
A segment from a vertex of a triangle to the midpoint of the opposite side.
The point where the three medians of a triangle meet, $G = \tfrac{A + B + C}{3}$; it lies two thirds of the way from each vertex to the opposite midpoint.
A nonzero vector parallel to a line; the line through $P_0$ with direction $\mathbf{d}$ is $P = P_0 + t\mathbf{d}$.
A nonzero vector perpendicular to a line. For the line $ax + by = c$, $\langle a, b\rangle$ is a normal vector.
The point on a line closest to a given point $Q$, where the perpendicular from $Q$ meets the line.
If $AB$ is a diameter of a circle and $P$ is any other point on the circle, then $\angle APB = 90^\circ$.

For any vectors, $\lVert\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\rVert^2 = 2\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2 + 2\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2$: the squares of a parallelogram's diagonals add up to the squares of its four sides.
$|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \le \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert$, with equality exactly when one vector is a scalar multiple of the other.

A fixed point used to define a conic: the conic is the set of points whose distance to the focus is $e$ times their distance to the directrix. In the polar form $r = \tfrac{ed}{1 + e\cos\theta}$ the focus is at the pole.
A fixed line used with a focus to define a conic; for every point $P$ of the conic, $PF = e \cdot PD$, where $PD$ is the distance from $P$ to the directrix.
The constant ratio $e = \tfrac{PF}{PD}$ in the focus–directrix definition of a conic: $0 < e < 1$ for an ellipse, $e = 1$ for a parabola, $e > 1$ for a hyperbola. For an ellipse, $e = \tfrac{c}{a}$.

An ellipse, parabola or hyperbola (originally, a curve cut from a double cone by a plane). With a focus at the pole, every conic has a polar equation $r = \tfrac{ed}{1 \pm e\cos\theta}$ or $r = \tfrac{ed}{1 \pm e\sin\theta}$.
The point of an orbit around the Sun closest to the Sun, at distance $a(1 - e)$ for an elliptical orbit with semi-major axis $a$ and eccentricity $e$.
The point of an elliptical orbit around the Sun farthest from the Sun, at distance $a(1 + e)$.
A sharp point on a curve where the tracing point stops for an instant and reverses direction, such as where a cycloid touches the ground.

The path of a point at distance $b$ from the center of a circle of radius $a$ rolling along a line: $x = at - b\sin t$, $y = a - b\cos t$. It is wavy if $b < a$, a cycloid if $b = a$, and looped if $b > a$.
The path of a point on a circle of radius $b$ rolling around the outside of a fixed circle of radius $a$; it has $\tfrac ab$ cusps when that is a whole number. The cardioid is the case $a = b$.
The path of a point on a circle of radius $b$ rolling around the inside of a fixed circle of radius $a$; it has $\tfrac ab$ cusps when that is a whole number of at least 3.
The four-cusped hypocycloid ($a = 4b$): $x = a\cos^3 t$, $y = a\sin^3 t$, or $x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = a^{2/3}$.
The three-cusped hypocycloid, traced by a point on a circle rolling inside a circle three times its radius.
A curve on which a bead sliding without friction reaches the lowest point in the same time from any starting point. An upside-down cycloid arch has this property (Huygens, 1659).
The curve of fastest descent between two points for a bead sliding without friction under gravity: an arch of an upside-down cycloid. The problem was posed by Johann Bernoulli in 1696.
An $n$th root of unity whose powers give all $n$ of them, such as $\omega = \operatorname{cis}\tfrac{2\pi}{n}$: the roots are $1, \omega, \omega^2, \ldots, \omega^{n-1}$.
Two complex numbers $a + bi$ and $a - bi$, mirror images across the real axis. Their sum $2a$ and product $a^2 + b^2$ are real, so $(z - (a + bi))(z - (a - bi))$ is a real quadratic.
A rotation of a ray about its endpoint, from an initial side to a terminal side. Counterclockwise rotations are positive.
The starting position of the ray that forms an angle; in standard position it lies along the positive $x$-axis.
The final position of the ray that forms an angle.
The common endpoint of the two sides of an angle; also a corner of a triangle or polygon.
An angle formed by a counterclockwise rotation.
An angle formed by a clockwise rotation.
An angle with its vertex at the origin and its initial side on the positive $x$-axis.
An angle in standard position whose terminal side lies on an axis, such as $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.
A unit of angle measure equal to $\tfrac{1}{360}$ of a full rotation.
An angle between $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.
An angle of exactly $90^\circ$ (a quarter turn).
An angle between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.
An angle of exactly $180^\circ$ (a half turn).
Two positive angles are complementary if their measures add to $90^\circ$.
Two positive angles are supplementary if their measures add to $180^\circ$.
One sixtieth of a degree: $1^\circ = 60'$.
One sixtieth of a minute of angle: $1' = 60''$, so $1^\circ = 3600''$.
Degrees–minutes–seconds notation for angles, such as $47^\circ\,21'\,36''$.
Angles in standard position with the same terminal side; they differ by a multiple of $360^\circ$ ($2\pi$).
An angle whose vertex is at the center of a circle.
The central angle that subtends an arc equal in length to the radius. $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$.
The part of a circle between two points on it.
The length of an arc: $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians.
The straight segment joining two points of a circle; always shorter than the arc between them.
The pie-shaped region bounded by two radii and the arc between them; area $\tfrac12 r^2\theta$.
Angle swept per unit time, $\omega = \theta/t$, usually in radians per second or per minute.
Distance traveled along a path per unit time, $v = s/t$. For circular motion $v = r\omega$.
Revolutions per minute, an angular speed. Multiply by $2\pi$ to get radians per minute.
Triangles with equal corresponding angles; their corresponding sides are proportional.
The side of a right triangle opposite the right angle; the longest side.
In a right triangle, the leg across from the acute angle being considered.
In a right triangle, the leg that forms the acute angle being considered (not the hypotenuse).
In a right triangle, opposite over hypotenuse. For any angle, $y/r$; on the unit circle, the $y$-coordinate.
In a right triangle, adjacent over hypotenuse. For any angle, $x/r$; on the unit circle, the $x$-coordinate.
In a right triangle, opposite over adjacent; in general $\tan\theta = \tfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tfrac{y}{x}$.
The reciprocal of sine: $\csc\theta = \tfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ (hypotenuse over opposite).
The reciprocal of cosine: $\sec\theta = \tfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ (hypotenuse over adjacent).
The reciprocal of tangent: $\cot\theta = \tfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \tfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ (adjacent over opposite).
Mnemonic: Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent.
The reciprocal of a nonzero number $x$ is $\tfrac1x$. Cosecant, secant and cotangent are the reciprocals of sine, cosine and tangent.
In a right triangle with legs $a$, $b$ and hypotenuse $c$: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.
Three whole numbers that satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, such as 3, 4, 5 or 5, 12, 13.
A value written with integers, fractions, radicals and $\pi$, not rounded, such as $\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
An isosceles right triangle; its sides are in the ratio $1 : 1 : \sqrt2$.
Half of an equilateral triangle; sides in the ratio $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$ (short leg : long leg : hypotenuse).
Pairs of functions related by complementary angles: sine and cosine, tangent and cotangent, secant and cosecant.
A function of $\theta$ equals its cofunction of the complement: $\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ - \theta)$, $\tan\theta = \cot(90^\circ - \theta)$, $\sec\theta = \csc(90^\circ - \theta)$.
Find all three sides and all three angles of a triangle from the parts that are given.
Functions such as $\sin^{-1}$, $\cos^{-1}$, $\tan^{-1}$ that take a ratio and return an angle.
The straight line from an observer's eye to the object being viewed.
The angle from the horizontal up to the line of sight of an object above the observer.
The angle from the horizontal down to the line of sight of an object below the observer.
A direction given relative to north or south: either clockwise from north in three digits ($125^\circ$) or as N/S, an acute angle, then E/W (S $55^\circ$ E).
A bearing measured clockwise from north and written with three digits, such as $040^\circ$ or $200^\circ$.
A bearing written as N or S, an acute angle, then E or W, such as N $35^\circ$ E.
Mnemonic for signs: All functions positive in quadrant I, Sine in II, Tangent in III, Cosine in IV (with their reciprocals).
One of the four regions of the plane cut out by the axes, numbered I to IV counterclockwise from the upper right.
The acute angle between the terminal side of an angle and the $x$-axis.
The circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. The point at angle $t$ is $(\cos t, \sin t)$.
Sine, cosine and the others viewed as functions of a real number $t$, the arc length along the unit circle.
The point on the unit circle reached by traveling a distance $t$ from $(1, 0)$; its coordinates are $(\cos t, \sin t)$. For a vector, the head (ending point) of the arrow.
The set of inputs for which a function is defined.
The set of output values a function takes.
A function is periodic if $f(t + p) = f(t)$ for some $p > 0$ and all $t$ in its domain.
The smallest positive $p$ with $f(t + p) = f(t)$; $2\pi$ for sine and cosine, $\pi$ for tangent. For $\sin Bx$ it is $\tfrac{2\pi}{|B|}$.
A function with $f(-x) = f(x)$; its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. Cosine and secant are even.
A function with $f(-x) = -f(x)$; its graph is symmetric about the origin. Sine, tangent, cosecant and cotangent are odd.
One complete repetition of a periodic graph, spanning one period.
The five points that divide one cycle of a sinusoid into quarters: the midline crossings, the maximum and the minimum.
Inputs where a function equals 0; where its graph crosses the $x$-axis.
Any graph of the form $y = A\sin(B(x - C)) + D$ or the cosine version: a stretched, shifted sine wave.
For a sinusoid, $|A|$: half the distance from the minimum to the maximum.
A flip of a graph across a line; a negative $A$ reflects a sinusoid across its midline.
Number of cycles per unit of the input variable; the reciprocal of the period. In hertz (Hz) when time is in seconds.
The horizontal shift $C$ of $y = A\sin(B(x - C)) + D$; for $\sin(Bx - c)$ it is $\tfrac{c}{B}$.
The horizontal line $y = D$ halfway between the maximum and minimum of a sinusoid.
The constant $D$ added to a sinusoid, moving the graph up or down.
A vertical line $x = a$ that a graph approaches but never reaches, with the function growing without bound.
A point where a function is lower than at all nearby points (not necessarily lowest overall).
A point where a function is higher than at all nearby points (not necessarily highest overall).
The rest position of an oscillating object; for forces, the state in which the forces on an object sum to zero.
Oscillation described by $d = a\sin\omega t$ or $d = a\cos\omega t$, with amplitude $|a|$ and period $\tfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$.
Oscillation whose amplitude shrinks over time, such as $d = ae^{-kt}\cos\omega t$.
Unit of frequency: one cycle per second.
A function in which each output comes from exactly one input; only one-to-one functions have inverses.
Use only part of a function's domain so that the function becomes one-to-one and has an inverse.
$\sin^{-1}x$: the angle in $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ whose sine is $x$; domain $[-1, 1]$.
$\cos^{-1}x$: the angle in $[0, \pi]$ whose cosine is $x$; domain $[-1, 1]$.
$\tan^{-1}x$: the angle in $\left(-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ whose tangent is $x$; domain all reals.

$\sec^{-1}x = \cos^{-1}\tfrac1x$ for $|x| \ge 1$; range $[0, \pi]$ excluding $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ (some calculus texts use $\left[0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left[\pi, \tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)$ instead).
$\csc^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\tfrac1x$ for $|x| \ge 1$; range $\left[-\tfrac{\pi}{2}, \tfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ excluding 0.
$\cot^{-1}x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} - \tan^{-1}x$, with range $(0, \pi)$.
Having no value; for trig functions, the result of a zero denominator (as in $\tan 90^\circ$) or an input outside the domain (as in $\sin^{-1}2$).
An equation involving trig functions of an unknown angle, true only for certain values.
A formula listing every solution of a trig equation, such as $x = \tfrac{\pi}{6} + 2k\pi$ or $\tfrac{5\pi}{6} + 2k\pi$.
An equation that is true for every value of the variable for which both sides are defined.
$\csc x = \tfrac{1}{\sin x}$, $\sec x = \tfrac{1}{\cos x}$, $\cot x = \tfrac{1}{\tan x}$.
$\tan x = \tfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and $\cot x = \tfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$.
$\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$, $1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x$, $1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x$.
$\cos(-x) = \cos x$ and $\sec(-x) = \sec x$; $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$, $\tan(-x) = -\tan x$, and likewise for $\csc$ and $\cot$.
Rewrite a trig expression with fewer terms or functions, using identities and algebra.
Show that an identity holds by transforming one side step by step into the other.
For an expression $a + b$, the expression $a - b$; multiplying $1 - \sin x$ by its conjugate $1 + \sin x$ gives $\cos^2 x$. For a complex number $a + bi$, the conjugate is $a - bi$.
$\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta$, $\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta$, and the tangent version.
$\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta$, $\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta$, and the tangent version.
$\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x$, $\cos 2x = \cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$, $\tan 2x = \tfrac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x}$.
$\sin^2 x = \tfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$ and $\cos^2 x = \tfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$.

$\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\tfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{2}}$, $\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \pm\sqrt{\tfrac{1 + \cos\theta}{2}}$, $\tan\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \tfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$; sign from the quadrant of $\tfrac{\theta}{2}$.
Formulas rewriting products like $\sin\alpha\cos\beta$ as $\tfrac12[\sin(\alpha + \beta) + \sin(\alpha - \beta)]$.
Formulas rewriting sums like $\sin u + \sin v$ as $2\sin\tfrac{u + v}{2}\cos\tfrac{u - v}{2}$.
The pulsing loudness heard when two tones of nearly equal frequency combine; the beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies.
A value that solves a transformed equation (for example after squaring) but not the original equation.
A triangle with no right angle.
Angle–angle–side: two angles and a side not between them are known.
Angle–side–angle: two angles and the side between them are known.
Side–side–angle: two sides and an angle opposite one of them are known; may give 0, 1 or 2 triangles.
Side–angle–side: two sides and the angle between them are known; solve with the law of cosines.
Side–side–side: all three sides are known; solve with the law of cosines.
$\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$ in any triangle.
The SSA situation, in which the given data may fit no triangle, one triangle or two triangles.
The perpendicular distance from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension). In SSA problems, $h = b\sin A$.
$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$ (and its rotations) in any triangle.
Half the perimeter of a triangle: $s = \tfrac{a + b + c}{2}$.
Area of a triangle from its sides: $\sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}$, where $s$ is the semiperimeter.
A quantity described by a single number (size only), such as mass or temperature.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, drawn as an arrow and written $\langle a, b\rangle$.
The tail (starting point) of a vector arrow.
The head (ending point) of a vector arrow. Components are terminal minus initial.
The length of a vector: $\lVert\langle a, b\rangle\rVert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
Vectors with the same magnitude and direction, wherever they are drawn.
Writing a vector as $\langle a, b\rangle$, its horizontal and vertical components.
The angle from the positive $x$-axis, counterclockwise, to a vector.
The sum of two or more vectors, such as the combined effect of several forces.
Multiplying a vector by a number: $k\langle a, b\rangle = \langle ka, kb\rangle$; stretches by $|k|$ and reverses if $k < 0$.
The vector $\langle 0, 0\rangle$, with magnitude 0 and no direction.
A vector of magnitude 1; $\tfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{v}$.
$\mathbf{i} = \langle 1, 0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{j} = \langle 0, 1\rangle$; every vector is $a\mathbf{i} + b\mathbf{j}$.
$\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\cos\theta$, a scalar.
Perpendicular; two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is 0.
$\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2}\mathbf{v}$, the part of $\mathbf{u}$ along $\mathbf{v}$.
The signed length $\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert} = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\cos\theta$ of the projection of $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$.
The direction in which a plane or ship is pointed, usually given as a bearing.
A plane's speed relative to the air around it.
The magnitude of a plane's velocity relative to the ground: air velocity plus wind velocity.
The actual direction of travel over the ground, usually given as a bearing.
Force times distance along the motion: $W = \mathbf{F}\cdot\mathbf{D} = \lVert\mathbf{F}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{D}\rVert\cos\theta$; in joules for newtons and meters.
The origin of a polar coordinate system.
The ray from the pole (the positive $x$-axis) from which polar angles are measured.
A pair $(r, \theta)$ locating a point by rotating through $\theta$ and moving a directed distance $r$; $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$.
An equation in $r$ and $\theta$, usually $r = f(\theta)$.
The heart-shaped limaçon $r = a(1 \pm \cos\theta)$ or $r = a(1 \pm \sin\theta)$.
A polar curve $r = a + b\cos\theta$ or $r = a + b\sin\theta$: inner loop if $a < b$, cardioid if $a = b$, dimpled or convex if $a > b$.
$r = a\cos n\theta$ or $r = a\sin n\theta$: $n$ petals if $n$ is odd, $2n$ if $n$ is even, each of length $|a|$.
A figure-eight polar curve such as $r^2 = a^2\cos 2\theta$.
The plane in which $a + bi$ is drawn as the point $(a, b)$: real part horizontal, imaginary part vertical.
The horizontal axis of the complex plane.
The vertical axis of the complex plane.

aliases: absolute value of a complex number
glossary.definition: The distance from $a + bi$ to the origin: $|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$.
An angle $\theta$ from the positive real axis to the point $z$ in the complex plane; $\tan\theta = \tfrac{b}{a}$ with the quadrant checked.
Writing a complex number as $r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$, with modulus $r$ and argument $\theta$.
Shorthand for "$\cos + i\sin$": $\operatorname{cis}\theta = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$.
A number $a + bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real and $i^2 = -1$.
$\left[r\operatorname{cis}\theta\right]^n = r^n\operatorname{cis}(n\theta)$ for every positive integer $n$.
A number $w$ with $w^n = z$. A nonzero complex number has $n$ of them: $\sqrt[n]{r}\operatorname{cis}\tfrac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}$, $k = 0, \ldots, n - 1$.
The $n$th roots of 1, $\operatorname{cis}\tfrac{2\pi k}{n}$; they form a regular $n$-gon on the unit circle.
Turning about a fixed point; an angle measures a rotation, and multiplying by $\operatorname{cis}\theta$ rotates a complex number by $\theta$.
The constant $\omega$ in $\sin\omega t$, in radians per unit time; the frequency is $\tfrac{\omega}{2\pi}$.
In any triangle each side is shorter than the sum of the other two; also $\lVert\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\rVert \le \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert + \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert$ for vectors.
A pair of equations $x = f(t)$, $y = g(t)$ that give both coordinates of a point in terms of a third variable, the parameter.
The independent variable (often $t$, for time) in parametric equations; each value of it gives one point $(f(t), g(t))$.
The set of points $(f(t), g(t))$ traced as the parameter $t$ runs through an interval.
The direction in which a parametric curve is traced as the parameter increases, shown with arrows on a graph.

Removing $t$ from parametric equations to get an equation in $x$ and $y$, by solving for $t$ and substituting or by an identity such as $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$. Restrictions on $x$ and $y$ must be carried over, and the orientation is lost.
A set of parametric equations that traces a given curve; a curve has many, differing in start, direction and speed. Example: $x = h + r\cos t$, $y = k + r\sin t$ for a circle.
Motion under gravity alone after launch: $x = (v_0\cos\theta)t$, $y = h + (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 gt^2$, with $g \approx 9.8$ m/s² or 32 ft/s².
How long a projectile is in the air: the positive solution of $y(t) = 0$; on level ground, $\tfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$.

references.title: Trigonometric identities
references.body:
## Fundamental identities

| Type | Identities |
|---|---|
| Reciprocal | $\csc x = \dfrac{1}{\sin x}$, $\sec x = \dfrac{1}{\cos x}$, $\cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}$ |
| Quotient | $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, $\cot x = \dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$ |
| Pythagorean | $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$, $1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x$, $1 + \cot^2 x = \csc^2 x$ |
| Even–odd | $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$, $\cos(-x) = \cos x$, $\tan(-x) = -\tan x$ |
| Cofunction | $\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cos x$, $\tan\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cot x$, $\sec\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \csc x$ |
| Periodicity | $\sin(x + 2\pi) = \sin x$, $\cos(x + 2\pi) = \cos x$, $\tan(x + \pi) = \tan x$ |

## Sum and difference

| Formula | |
|---|---|
| $\sin(\alpha \pm \beta)$ | $\sin\alpha\cos\beta \pm \cos\alpha\sin\beta$ |
| $\cos(\alpha \pm \beta)$ | $\cos\alpha\cos\beta \mp \sin\alpha\sin\beta$ |
| $\tan(\alpha \pm \beta)$ | $\dfrac{\tan\alpha \pm \tan\beta}{1 \mp \tan\alpha\tan\beta}$ |
| $a\sin x + b\cos x$ | $R\sin(x + \varphi)$, $R = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, $\cos\varphi = \tfrac{a}{R}$, $\sin\varphi = \tfrac{b}{R}$ |

## Double angle and power reducing

| Formula | |
|---|---|
| $\sin 2x$ | $2\sin x\cos x$ |
| $\cos 2x$ | $\cos^2 x - \sin^2 x = 2\cos^2 x - 1 = 1 - 2\sin^2 x$ |
| $\tan 2x$ | $\dfrac{2\tan x}{1 - \tan^2 x}$ |
| $\sin^2 x$ | $\dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}$ |
| $\cos^2 x$ | $\dfrac{1 + \cos 2x}{2}$ |
| $\tan^2 x$ | $\dfrac{1 - \cos 2x}{1 + \cos 2x}$ |

## Half angle

Sign of $\pm$: the quadrant of $\tfrac{\theta}{2}$.

| Formula | |
|---|---|
| $\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ | $\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{2}}$ |
| $\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ | $\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1 + \cos\theta}{2}}$ |
| $\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ | $\dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{1 + \cos\theta}$ |

## Product to sum

| Product | Sum |
|---|---|
| $\sin\alpha\cos\beta$ | $\tfrac12[\sin(\alpha + \beta) + \sin(\alpha - \beta)]$ |
| $\cos\alpha\sin\beta$ | $\tfrac12[\sin(\alpha + \beta) - \sin(\alpha - \beta)]$ |
| $\cos\alpha\cos\beta$ | $\tfrac12[\cos(\alpha - \beta) + \cos(\alpha + \beta)]$ |
| $\sin\alpha\sin\beta$ | $\tfrac12[\cos(\alpha - \beta) - \cos(\alpha + \beta)]$ |

## Sum to product

| Sum | Product |
|---|---|
| $\sin u + \sin v$ | $2\sin\dfrac{u + v}{2}\cos\dfrac{u - v}{2}$ |
| $\sin u - \sin v$ | $2\cos\dfrac{u + v}{2}\sin\dfrac{u - v}{2}$ |
| $\cos u + \cos v$ | $2\cos\dfrac{u + v}{2}\cos\dfrac{u - v}{2}$ |
| $\cos u - \cos v$ | $-2\sin\dfrac{u + v}{2}\sin\dfrac{u - v}{2}$ |

## Solving equations

| Equation | General solution |
|---|---|
| $\sin x = c$ | $x = \sin^{-1}c + 2k\pi$ or $x = \pi - \sin^{-1}c + 2k\pi$ |
| $\cos x = c$ | $x = \pm\cos^{-1}c + 2k\pi$ |
| $\tan x = c$ | $x = \tan^{-1}c + k\pi$ |

Strategy: one angle, one function, set to zero, factor, solve each factor, check (especially
after squaring).

references.title: Triangles, vectors, polar, parametric and complex
references.body:
## Right triangles

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| SOH-CAH-TOA | $\sin\theta = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos\theta = \tfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan\theta = \tfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$ |
| Pythagorean theorem | $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ |
| Acute angles | $A + B = 90^\circ$ |
| Bearing $\theta$ (clockwise from north), distance $d$ | north $= d\cos\theta$, east $= d\sin\theta$ |

## Oblique triangles

| Case | Method |
|---|---|
| AAS, ASA | third angle, then law of sines |
| SSA | law of sines; 0, 1 or 2 triangles |
| SAS | law of cosines for the third side |
| SSS | law of cosines for the largest angle |

| Law | Formula |
|---|---|
| Law of sines | $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$ |
| Law of cosines | $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$ |
| Angle from sides | $\cos C = \dfrac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2ab}$ |
| SSA height | $h = b\sin A$: acute $A$ gives 0 ($a < h$), 1 ($a = h$ or $a \ge b$), 2 ($h < a < b$) |

## Area

| Known | Area |
|---|---|
| SAS | $\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ |
| SSS (Heron) | $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}$, $s = \tfrac{a + b + c}{2}$ |
| AAS / ASA | $\dfrac{a^2\sin B\sin C}{2\sin A}$ |

## Vectors in the plane

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| Component form | $\mathbf{v} = \langle a, b\rangle = a\mathbf{i} + b\mathbf{j}$ |
| From $P(x_1, y_1)$ to $Q(x_2, y_2)$ | $\langle x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1\rangle$ |
| Magnitude | $\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ |
| From magnitude and direction | $\mathbf{v} = \langle \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\cos\theta, \lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\sin\theta\rangle$ |
| Direction angle | $\tan\theta = \tfrac{b}{a}$, quadrant from the signs of $a$, $b$ |
| Unit vector | $\dfrac{\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}$ |
| Dot product | $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert\cos\theta$ |
| Angle between | $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert}$ |
| Orthogonal | $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0$ |
| Projection of $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$ | $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2}\mathbf{v}$ |
| Work | $W = \mathbf{F}\cdot\overrightarrow{PQ} = \lVert\mathbf{F}\rVert\lVert\overrightarrow{PQ}\rVert\cos\theta$ |

## Polar coordinates

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| Polar to rectangular | $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ |
| Rectangular to polar | $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$, $\tan\theta = \tfrac{y}{x}$ (check the quadrant) |
| Same point | $(r, \theta) = (r, \theta + 2k\pi) = (-r, \theta + \pi)$ |
| Circles | $r = a$; $r = 2a\cos\theta$; $r = 2a\sin\theta$ |
| Rose $r = a\cos n\theta$ or $a\sin n\theta$ | $n$ petals if $n$ odd, $2n$ if $n$ even |
| Limaçon $r = a \pm b\cos\theta$ | inner loop if $a < b$; cardioid if $a = b$ |
| Lemniscate | $r^2 = a^2\cos 2\theta$ |

## Parametric equations

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| Eliminate $t$ | solve for $t$ and substitute, or use $\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1$; keep restrictions |
| Segment $P \to Q$ | $x = x_1 + (x_2 - x_1)t$, $y = y_1 + (y_2 - y_1)t$, $0 \le t \le 1$ |
| Circle, center $(h, k)$, radius $r$ | $x = h + r\cos t$, $y = k + r\sin t$ (counterclockwise) |
| Ellipse | $x = h + a\cos t$, $y = k + b\sin t$ |
| Projectile | $x = (v_0\cos\theta)t$, $y = h + (v_0\sin\theta)t - \tfrac12 gt^2$ |
| Projectile, level ground | flight time $\tfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$, range $\tfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, top at $t = \tfrac{v_0\sin\theta}{g}$ |

## Complex numbers

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| Modulus | $\lvert z\rvert = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ for $z = a + bi$ |
| Trigonometric form | $z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\operatorname{cis}\theta$ |
| Product | $r_1r_2\operatorname{cis}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$ |
| Quotient | $\tfrac{r_1}{r_2}\operatorname{cis}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$ |
| De Moivre | $z^n = r^n\operatorname{cis}(n\theta)$ |
| $n$th roots | $\sqrt[n]{r}\operatorname{cis}\dfrac{\theta + 2k\pi}{n}$, $k = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1$ |

references.title: Angles and the unit circle
references.body:
## Angle measure

| Fact | Formula |
|---|---|
| Full turn | $360^\circ = 2\pi$ rad |
| Degrees to radians | multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ}$ |
| Radians to degrees | multiply by $\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ |
| One radian | $\approx 57.296^\circ$ |
| DMS | $1^\circ = 60'$, $1' = 60''$ |
| Coterminal angles | $\theta + 360^\circ k$ or $\theta + 2\pi k$ |
| Arc length | $s = r\theta$ ($\theta$ in radians) |
| Sector area | $A = \tfrac12 r^2\theta = \tfrac12 rs$ |
| Linear and angular speed | $v = r\omega$, $\omega = \theta/t$, rad/min $= 2\pi \cdot$ rpm |

## The unit circle

```plot
{"x": [-1.6, 1.6], "y": [-1.6, 1.6], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 1}], "points": [{"at": [1.0000, 0.0000]}, {"at": [0.8660, 0.5000]}, {"at": [0.7071, 0.7071]}, {"at": [0.5000, 0.8660]}, {"at": [0.0000, 1.0000]}, {"at": [-0.5000, 0.8660]}, {"at": [-0.7071, 0.7071]}, {"at": [-0.8660, 0.5000]}, {"at": [-1.0000, 0.0000]}, {"at": [-0.8660, -0.5000]}, {"at": [-0.7071, -0.7071]}, {"at": [-0.5000, -0.8660]}, {"at": [-0.0000, -1.0000]}, {"at": [0.5000, -0.8660]}, {"at": [0.7071, -0.7071]}, {"at": [0.8660, -0.5000]}], "labels": [{"at": [1.3000, -0.0300], "text": "0°"}, {"at": [1.1258, 0.6200], "text": "30°"}, {"at": [0.9192, 0.8892], "text": "45°"}, {"at": [0.6500, 1.0958], "text": "60°"}, {"at": [0.0000, 1.2700], "text": "90°"}, {"at": [-0.6500, 1.0958], "text": "120°"}, {"at": [-0.9192, 0.8892], "text": "135°"}, {"at": [-1.1258, 0.6200], "text": "150°"}, {"at": [-1.3000, -0.0300], "text": "180°"}, {"at": [-1.1258, -0.6800], "text": "210°"}, {"at": [-0.9192, -0.9492], "text": "225°"}, {"at": [-0.6500, -1.1558], "text": "240°"}, {"at": [-0.0000, -1.3300], "text": "270°"}, {"at": [0.6500, -1.1558], "text": "300°"}, {"at": [0.9192, -0.9492], "text": "315°"}, {"at": [1.1258, -0.6800], "text": "330°"}], "caption": "The unit circle: the point at angle θ is (cos θ, sin θ)"}
```
